The Second Treatise, Part I: Of Husband and Wife

Seeking Marriage

The Second Treatise, Part I: Of Husband and Wife · §§. 1–13

§. 1. Of those who may seek to be married.

Having laid down in the former treatise the foundation of all domestic duties, by expounding the words of the apostle, I now intend to set them out distinctly in order, beginning with the first and chief couple in the family, man and wife.

Here we must first speak of the persons who are to be counted true and lawful husband and wife, and then of the duties which they owe each other.

So this treatise consists of two parts.

  1. The first declares who are man and wife.
  2. The second sets out those common mutual duties which they owe one another. First, of the first.

Husband and wife are those who are rightly joined together1 by the bond of marriage,2 by which two are made “one flesh.”

To clear this point better, we will consider both the parties that may be so closely joined together, and also the manner in which they are rightly joined in so firm a unity.

About the parties we must inquire:

  1. Who may seek a mate for marriage.
  2. What kind of mate is to be taken.

1. All those who are able, without inevitable danger to their3 yokefellow, to perform the essential duties of marriage may be married.

From this proposition arise three questions to be discussed.

  1. Who are to be counted able?
  2. What danger is inevitable?
  3. Whether marriage is free for all but these?

§. 2. Of ripeness of years in those who are to be married.

1. Those are to be counted able who have4 passed the flower of their age, and are not made impotent by a defect of nature or by any other cause.

1. Ripeness of years is absolutely necessary for consummating a just and lawful marriage. Therefore, as God at first made Adam of full age, so when he sought out a wife for him, he made her of full age too: he made her a woman, not a child.5 Where the apostle advises parents to take care for the marriage of their children, he puts in this proviso: “if they are past the flower of their age.” Childhood is counted the flower of age. While the flower of the plant is sprouting, the seed is green, unfit to be sown.

Question. How long does the flower of age last?

Answer.6 The civil law, and the common law also, set down twelve years for the flower of a female’s age, and fourteen for a male’s, which is the least. For before those years they can have no need of marriage, nor are they yet well fit for marriage. So if they hold off some years longer, it will be much better for the parties themselves who marry,7 for the children whom they bring forth, for the family of which they are the head, and for the commonwealth of which they are members. Note the ages of the kings of Israel and Judah when they were first married, and we will find few of them to have been under twenty, and those few not more than one or two years under. And yet of all sorts of people the kings used to marry the soonest, so that they might have heirs early.

Objection. Solomon8 was only a child when he came to the crown, and yet9 he then had a child at least a year old.

Answer. He was said to be a child not absolutely but comparatively:10 in relation to his other brothers, who were older than he, and11 with respect to the great work he was to undertake. In the time of his reign he is said to be old,12 which could not be if he had been a child in years when he began to reign, for he reigned only forty years.

2. Objection. Ahaz was only twenty years old when he began to reign, and reigned only sixteen years, and yet when he died Hezekiah his son was twenty-five years old,13 by which reckoning Ahaz had a child when he was only eleven, or twelve years old at most.

1. Answer. Some say that this was extraordinary, and give this reason: “Ahaz, as young a father as Elizabeth was an old mother,”14 “should have hoped in Emmanuel, born of a virgin.”

2. Answer. The beginning of that reign, when Ahaz was only twenty years old, is to be referred to Jotham his father. For Ahaz was twenty years old when he (namely Jotham) began to reign, just as Jehoiachin15 was eight years old when he (namely his father Jehoiakim) began to reign: for Jehoiachin was16 eighteen when he himself began to reign.

Objection. Jotham was only17 twenty-five years old when he began to reign. How then could Ahaz his son be twenty at that time?

Answer. Jotham was twenty-five years old when his father Uzziah was struck with leprosy,18 and from that time he reigned as king, even in his father’s lifetime. But after his father was dead, the kingdom was established on him alone19 in a more solemn manner, and in this respect it is said that he then began to reign. And by then his son Ahaz was twenty years old, Jotham himself being about forty.

Contrary to this fitness of age is the practice of20 those parents, or other relatives of children, who make matches for them in their childhood, move them to consent, and so cause them to be married. Such marriages are mock marriages and mere nullities. For children cannot know what belongs to marriage, much less can they perform what is required of married persons. Their consent therefore is justly counted no consent, unless they ratify it after they come of age.

§. 3. Of impotent persons who ought not to seek after marriage.

2. Those are to be counted impotent, and in that respect unable to perform the essential duties of marriage, who (to use the Scripture phrase) “were born eunuchs from their mother’s21 womb,” or are made so by some accident: such as those who are defective or closed in their private parts, or struck with an incurable paralysis, or afflicted with frigidity, or any other such impediment.

These ought not to seek after marriage, for by those signs of impotence God shows that he calls them to live single.

Those sin against this manifestation of God’s will22 who conceal their impotence and join themselves in marriage. By this they frustrate one main end of marriage, which is the procreation of children, and do such wrong to the party whom they marry that sufficient amends can never be made.

§. 4. Of barrenness, that it does not hinder marriage.

Question. Are those who are barren to be ranked among those impotent persons?

Answer. No, there is a great difference between impotence and barrenness.

1. Impotence may be known23 and discerned by outward, perceptible signs; barrenness cannot: it is not discerned except by the lack of childbearing.

2. Impotent persons cannot render due benevolence (the marriage duty each owes the other), but those who are barren can.

3. Impotence is incurable, but barrenness is not absolutely so. Many, after they have been barren a long while, have become fruitful: and that not only by an extraordinary work of God above the course of nature (as Sarah24 and Elizabeth,25 who because of age were past the time of childbearing), but also by such a blessing as might stand with the course of nature, obtained by prayer (as Rebekah26 and Hannah),27 of which daily experience gives good evidence. For many have brought forth children after 10, 15, 20 and more years of barrenness.

On these grounds many saints who have been barren have married, and their practice in this was not disallowed, nor their marriage dissolved.28 For though the procreation of children is one end of marriage, yet it is not the only end. And the marriage bond is so inviolable that, though it is made for the sake of children, yet it must not be broken for lack of children.

§. 5. Of that inevitable danger which hinders marriage.

3. Those who are infected with such contagious diseases as spread to those who keep company with them, and infect them also, ought not to seek after marriage, for that cannot but turn to the danger of the party whom they marry. It was for the mutual good of one another29 that God ordained the law of marriage. To use it to the hurt and danger of one another is against the main end of its first institution.

The law of shutting a leper off from all society with men30 proves as much. For if lepers were not allowed to have mutual society with any man, much less were they allowed to have the society of marriage with a wife or a husband.

By contagious diseases not only will both the parties who keep company together be infected, but also their offspring. In this way their disease, which otherwise might die with themselves, is passed on to their posterity. A like restraint may be applied to such foul and loathsome diseases as make the company and society of the infected person irksome and odious to their companion.

Those sin against the end and use of marriage31 who conceal such diseases and so join themselves in marriage, to the irreparable harm of the party whom they marry.

§. 6. Of the lawfulness of marriage to all sorts of persons.

Where there is no such just impediment as has been mentioned before, it is lawful for all sorts of people, of whatever32 calling or condition, to marry. For “marriage is honorable33 in all,” or among all, namely in or among all sorts of people. That is why it is counted “a doctrine of demons” to “prohibit34 marriage.” For it is a doctrine contrary to God’s word, and a doctrine that causes much inward burning and outward pollution, and so makes their bodies, which should be temples of the Holy Spirit, sties of devils.

The disease for whose remedy marriage is sanctified is a common disease, which has infected all sorts of people. Why then should the remedy not be as common?

In this case the apostle speaks generally of all, without exception of any: “to avoid fornication, each man should have his own35 wife, and each woman her own husband.” And again: “If they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.”

Objection. “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs”36 (that is, have abstained from marriage and lived a single37 life with self-control) “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.”

Answer. That is spoken of some particular persons to whom the gift of self-control was given, not of any distinct conditions and callings, as if each and every one of this or that calling had done so, or were able to do so. That is why Christ adds this clause, “The one who can accept this should accept it,” and the apostle says to the same purpose, “each one has his own gift from God.”38

Contrary to this necessary and lawful liberty is the impure and tyrannical restraint of the Church of Rome, by which all who enter any of their holy orders are kept from marriage.

Do they not in this “test God” by placing on men’s necks “a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear”?3940 No such restraint was ever laid by God’s word on any of those holy functions which he ordained. For under the law it was lawful for high priests, ordinary priests, all sorts of Levites and extraordinary prophets to marry; and under the gospel, for41 apostles, bishops, deacons and all ministers of the word.42 Fearful have been the effects of this diabolical doctrine: fornication, adultery, incest, sodomy, bestiality, and who knows what else. Many wives have been put away from their husbands because their husbands were ministers, and many ministers put out of their calling because they had wives. Many children have by this means been born out of wedlock, and many of them cruelly murdered in their infancy.43 Six thousand heads of infants were found in the ponds of one religious house. How many more thousands have from time to time been cast into other ponds, or buried in gardens or other places, or in other ways conveyed out of sight? That doctrine must be devilish which has such devilish effects.44 Well did he wish who wished that all who cannot control themselves would take heed how they rashly profess perfection and vow virginity.

§. 7. Of the things which are absolutely necessary to make a person fit for marriage.

Those who have power to marry must be careful in choosing “a suitable helper” for themselves, for45 this was God’s care when he first instituted marriage. To make a suitable helper for marriage, some things are absolutely necessary for the very essence or being of marriage; others are necessary for the comfort and happiness of marriage.

As to the former sort, there must be chosen:

1. One of the same kind or nature. For among all the creatures that were made, “for Adam no suitable helper was found.”46 Therefore God made a woman out of his bone and flesh, of his47 own nature and kind.

Contrary to this is the detestable sin of lying with beasts, expressly forbidden by the48 law: a sin worse than beastly, for the brute beasts content themselves with their own kind. It is monstrous in its kind, and a cause of abominable monsters.49 Contrary also is that copulation which witches have with devils, than which nothing is more unnatural, nothing more monstrous and odious.

2. One of the opposite sex: the male must choose a female, the female a male. So God, having made Adam a male,50 made Eve a female, and joined them in marriage. Only a union of these different sexes is fit for the increase of mankind and the other marriage duties.

Contrary are those unnatural unions of persons of the same sex, which the apostle lists as judgments inflicted on the heathen, because “they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.”

3. One beyond those degrees of kinship by blood and by marriage which51 are forbidden by the law of God. These degrees are set out by Moses, Lev 18:6, 7, etc., and explained in a table of the degrees of kinship by blood and by marriage within which no one may marry, appointed to be hung up in every church.

Contrary is incest, a sin not only forbidden by God’s52 word, but so horrible even to the heathen that (to use the apostle’s words, 1 Cor 5:1) it is “not even named among the pagans.” That verdict is excellently confirmed by the heathen orator’s impassioned exclamation against one Sassia, who married her son-in-law, in these words: “O incredible wickedness of a woman, unheard of in any age but this! O unbridled and untamed lust! O singular boldness! Not to fear the power of God and the report of men!” etc. “Lust, shamelessness and madness overcame shame, fear and reason.”

What may we now think of the dispensations which the pope gives for incestuous marriages, allowed to great princes even by the53 Council of Trent? Does he not show himself in this to be “the man of lawlessness,” who “opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God”?

4. One who is free,54 neither married nor betrothed to another. The law of marriage shows this much in this clause: “the two will become one flesh.”55 And since56 the law inflicts the same punishment on a betrothed person who commits sexual impurity as it does on a married person, it is evident that it is unlawful to marry one betrothed to another, just as it is to marry one married to another. So binding is a betrothal contract that the law calls a betrothed maiden “a wife,” and a betrothed maiden could not be put away without a certificate of divorce.

Contrary are bigamy and polygamy, spoken of57 before. To this head may be referred marriages with those who have been betrothed to others before. These are utterly unlawful.

§. 8. Of the lawfulness of other marriages after one of the married couple is dead.

1. Question. Are those who have buried their husband or wife so free that they may marry again?

Answer. Yes, as free as those who were never married before. The law not only permits a widow to marry again,58 but if her husband died before he had any children, it commanded the nearest kinsman who was living and free to marry her, so that he might raise up offspring for his dead brother. If he refused to do so, a penalty of disgrace was inflicted on him: the rejected widow was to “remove his sandal” from his foot59 and “spit in his face” in the presence of the elders. The apostle expressly says that a woman, when her husband is dead, is free to be married (1 Cor 7:39). Yes, speaking of young widows, he says further, “I want them to marry” (1 Tim 5:14). This liberty, which the prophet of God and the apostle of Christ grant to a wife, can by no show of reason be denied to a husband. For the bond of marriage gives them a like power over each other’s body (1 Cor 7:4), and binds the one as inviolably as the other (Matt 19:6). Husbands therefore, as well as wives, have used this liberty, as Abraham did (Gen 25:1).60 The apostle who gives this liberty gives a reason for it, taken from the limit of the time in which married persons have power over one another, and that is the time of this life only: “a married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is released,” etc. On this ground all the61 reasons which warrant or move those who were never married to marry may be applied to those whose yokefellow has been taken from them by death.

2. Question. May this liberty be extended any further than to a second marriage?

Answer. We find no restraint from a third or fourth or more marriages, if by divine providence so many wives or husbands are taken away one after another while there is need for the surviving party to use the benefit of marriage. The woman of Samaria who had five husbands one after another is not blamed for having been married to so many, but for living with one (after the others were dead) who was not her husband (John 4:18). Nor did the Lord condemn the woman who was said to have had seven husbands one after another (Matt 22:25, etc.).

Contrary is the opinion of the62 Montanists and Cataphrygians, ancient heretics who counted the marriages which the survivor made after the death of a yokefellow to be adulterous. Tertullian,63 an ancient and learned church father, was so far infected with this heresy that he wrote a treatise in defense of it. It seems from their arguments that one main ground of their error was a misinterpretation of those Scriptures which forbid men to have two wives at once, and women to have two husbands at once, such as: “The two will become one flesh,” Gen 2:24; a bishop and a deacon must be “the husband of but one wife,” 1 Tim 3:2, 12; “A widow should be enrolled” who has been “the wife of one man,” 1 Tim 5:9. These are indeed express texts against such bigamists and polygamists as have been described64 before; but they make no more against second or later marriages, one mate being dead, than against first marriages. Into the roll of these heretics may be put those who deny such later marriages to any kind of ministers. So do our adversaries: they65 exclude those who have married again after one wife is dead from such functions of the inferior orders as they admit those who have married only once to. They allege many of the same Scriptures as the Montanists do (as 1 Tim 3:2, 12 and 5:9), which shows that they are infected with the same heresy, though they claim to renounce it.

§. 9. Of equality in years between husband and wife.

That the fellowship of marriage may prove a comfort, it is needful66 that there should be some equality between the parties who are married in Age, Wealth, Rank, Piety.

1. For Age: as the party who seeks a mate must be of ripe years, fit to give consent and able to perform marriage duties, so the mate who is taken must correspond somewhat67 in age: if one is young, both young; if one is of middle age, both so; if one is advanced in years, the other also. It is noted of Zechariah and Elizabeth that “they were both well along in years.” If both were old together, then both were also young together. Equality in years makes married persons more fit for the procreation of children, for a mutual performance of marriage duties to each other, and for making their company and society in every way happier.

This equality is not to be taken too strictly, as if the married couple had to be of exactly the same age, but only as some correspondence in years. There may be this even though there is a disparity68 of five or ten or somewhat more years, especially if the excess of years is on the husband’s part. For besides the fact that, in the ordinary course of nature, a man’s strength and vigor last longer than a woman’s, it is very fitting that the husband should be somewhat older than his wife, because he is a head, a governor, a protector of his wife. The Scripture notes many husbands to be older than their wives (as Abraham was ten years older than Sarah;69 and if we closely mark the circumstances of the histories of Isaac and Jacob and their wives, we will find that the husbands were older than their wives). As far as I remember, no approved example of a husband younger than his wife can be given from Scripture.

Contrary to this equality in years is the practice of many70 men and women who, being aged, to satisfy their lust or for some other ulterior motive, marry those who are only in the flower of their age. In this they often fall far short of their expectation. For those young ones, finding the company of aged folk burdensome and irksome to them, soon begin to loathe it, and so cause more grief and vexation than they ever gave comfort and contentment.

On the other side, there are others who in the prime and71 strength of their age, for wealth, honor or similar motives, marry those who with age are beginning to be decrepit and unfit to be married, hoping that they will not live long, but that with a little trouble they will gain high rank or riches, and after a while be free again. But God often repays such people in kind, by prolonging the life of those aged persons, and so making the burden much more grievous and tedious than was imagined, and by taking away those young ones sooner than they expected, so that all their hopes perish.72 The heathen observed inequality in years to be the occasion of many harms, and so prescribed rules against it.

§. 10. Of equality in wealth and rank between those who are to be married together.

2. Some equality in outward property and wealth is also fitting73 for the parties who are to be married together, so that the disparity in it (especially if it is too great) does not make the one lord it over the other more than is fitting. For if a man of great wealth is married to a poor woman, he will think to make her like his maidservant, and expect her to behave toward him in a way that does not become a yokefellow and a bedfellow, so that such a woman may rather be said to be brought into bondage than into marriage. And if a rich woman marries a poor man, she will expect to be the master and to rule him, so that the order which God has established will be utterly overturned, and the honor of marriage laid in the dust. For where there is no order, there can be no honor.

3. The same may be said of outward rank, that74 in it also there should be some equality: that princes, nobles and gentlemen marry those of their own rank, and the lower sort those of their own degree. Note what sort of wives Abraham, Isaac and Jacob married, and it will appear that they had regard to this equality. Disparity in rank, as well as in wealth, is a means to make men and women swell and lord it over others more than is fitting, yes, and to cast their former wealth and rank in each other’s teeth.

Contrary on the one side are the practices of those who aim75 to marry above their own wealth and rank, thinking to advance themselves by such marriages. This is the only thing which many seek in seeking wives and husbands, and so it often happens that they meet with the worst matches, and make their marriage a kind of bondage to them. Great portions make many women proud, fussy, lavish, idle and careless. A man would be much better off, even for the sake of his outward wealth, to marry a prudent, sober, thrifty, careful, diligent wife, though with a small portion, than such a one. A proud back, a dainty tooth and a lavish hand will soon consume a great portion; but “every wise woman builds her house,” and “a wife of noble character is her husband’s crown.” Many wives also who are married to very rich husbands are kept shorter and more pinched in their allowance than those who are married to men of lower means. It is not the means a man has, but his mind and disposition, that makes him free and generous to his wife.

Contrary are the marriages which men of great authority76 and means make with lowly women, yes, many times with their own maids, and those of the lowest rank, their kitchen maids; and those which women of noble blood and great wealth77 make with their servingmen. Do they not in this reveal much baseness of mind and violence of lust?

If it is said that such marriages are not absolutely unlawful, the rule of the civil law gives a good answer: “Always in marriages, not only what is lawful but what is honorable and fitting is to be considered.”

§. 11. Of equality in piety and religion between those who are to be married together.

4. The equality which is of greatest consequence between78 parties to be married is in piety. In this respect it is needful that, as a Christian should be married to a Christian, and one who professes79 the true faith to one who professes the same faith, so one who truly fears God should be married to one of the same mind and disposition, as is noted of Zechariah and Elizabeth:80 “Both of them were righteous in the sight of God,” etc. A worthy couple, each worthy of the other! Being both alike in such excellent qualities, they could not but reap much comfort and profit in every way from each other.

This is one of the chief points included in that proviso which the Holy Spirit gives for choosing a yokefellow, in these words: “in the Lord.”81

There is no means like this equality to increase love, preserve peace, provoke to every duty, and make them helpful to one another in all things and at all times. By it they will be made both able to do more good to one another and capable of receiving more good from one another, especially in the best things, even in those which concern their spiritual edification in this world and their eternal salvation in the world to come. For Christ is the fountain and head of all spiritual life and grace (“God was pleased to have all His fullness82 dwell in Him,” so that it is he “who fills all in all”). Now Christ imparts83 the life and grace which is in him to those who are members of his body. If then I, being a member of that mystical body, am linked by that close and inviolable bond of marriage to one of the members of that body, what great hope there is of our imparting to one another, and partaking from one another, those gifts and graces which each of us receives from Christ our head! If an unbelieving wife may be saved by a believing husband,84 and an unbelieving husband by a believing wife, much more will one believer be more and more edified by another.

Happy is that family where both its governors, husband and wife, are fellow members of Christ’s body. There the house will be made God’s church, as the house of Aquila and Priscilla was.85 God’s worship will be maintained there. Children will be trained up there in the nurture of the Lord, and servants also taught the fear of God. For those who are indeed of Christ’s kingdom will be like leaven, which86 seasons the whole lump. Take as an instance the declaration which Joshua87 makes to this purpose, and the effect which is noted of the ruler whose son Christ healed: “he and88 all his household believed.”

Here, by the way, let me exhort parents and other governors89 of children both to train up their own children in true piety and the fear of God, and also to seek such matches for them as they may have some assurance are of the same faith, and of the same mind and heart. So they will gain much happiness in marriage for their children, as Abraham did for Isaac.90

If parents ought in this respect to seek the good of their children, much more ought those who are at their own disposal, and free to marry whom they will, to have special regard to equality in piety: especially women, because they are in subjection to their husbands. Yet men ought not to be careless in this either. For wives, if the fear of God does not possess their hearts, though they are the weaker vessels, often make their husbands their plain vassals.

§. 12. Of marriages between persons of different religious professions.

Contrary are marriages with persons of different dispositions and91 different professions of religion, especially when they are made with unbelievers or idolaters.

This is one of those unequal yokes with which92 the apostle93 forbids Christians to be yoked.

Great are the dangers and harms that ordinarily follow from it. For first, “the holy seed”94 (to use the words of the Holy Spirit) is by this “mixed,” and so it comes about that “the holiness of the Lord is profaned,”95 that is, those whom God has chosen to be a holy nation and a people of his own are polluted.

Objection. “The unbelieving husband is sanctified through his believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband.”96

Answer. That is noted only as a remedy for a trouble which, once it has come about, cannot be undone. When two unbelievers are married together, and one of them is converted to the true faith while the other remains an unbeliever, then, so that the believer might enjoy the company of the97 other with some comfort, the apostle shows that for the communion of marriage the unbeliever is sanctified by the believer. But by this he gives no liberty to believers to marry unbelievers. For though God in mercy sanctifies in this way the unequal yoke which cannot be broken, yet those who, professing God’s name, knowingly take on that yoke do as much as lies in them to profane God’s holiness.

2. One who professes the true religion is in danger of apostasy by it. This reason98 the law itself presses against this point, and the Scripture gives many examples of its woeful outcome: as of Solomon,99 the wisest among men;100 of Samson, the strongest; of Jehoram,101 and others.

Objection. If I marry one of a contrary religion, I may convert a sinner from going astray and save a soul from death.

Answer. It is only a mere “may.” You have no warrant to take that risk, but are forbidden it, to avoid the contrary danger. There is great cause to fear that in an unequal yoke the worse will prevail over the better. We are by nature prone to yield to error, falsehood and every kind of evil. Truth, virtue and grace go against the current of nature. It is likely to turn out in this unequal yoke as if two oxen in one yoke should pull opposite ways against each other on the side of a hill: the ox which pulls downhill, though it is a poor, lean, weak one, will pull down the other, though that is an able, vigorous, strong one. All evil is downhill; all goodness is uphill. And because of the flesh which remains in all as long as they remain on earth, those who have some goodness in them are prone and ready to fall away, but those who are evil are very obstinate in it. Yes, evil is also of a more spreading and infecting nature. A little sour leaven will soon make a great batch of dough sour, but a great deal of sweet dough will not sweeten a little leaven. It is therefore an unwarranted pretext for anyone to marry one of a contrary religion or disposition in the hope of converting them. It is not in man’s power to convert another. It is a divine work; without God’s blessing it cannot be done. There is little ground to expect a blessing from God in a course which is directly against his own ordinance. A curse may rather be feared. And the woeful experience of all ages has shown how God has cursed such marriages.

Objection. Saint Peter102 exhorts wives so to conduct themselves that their husbands, who “do not obey the word,” may by that means “be won over without words.” And103 Saint Paul says to those who were unequally matched, “How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?” It appears therefore that an evil husband may be converted by a good wife, and an evil wife by a good husband.

Answer. These directions are given only as a remedy to redress such irreversible harms as have already happened, and not to give liberty to rush knowingly into them (as was noted before). When a misfortune has happened, necessity lies on a man, so that every means must be used to redress it. But to infer from this that a man may safely enter a course which draws him into those harms, what is that but to thrust himself into the fire, and to cast himself into temptation,104 which he is taught to pray against? Besides, the directions named above are not grounded on any express promises, but on mere suppositions.

3. Many other harms are likely to follow from this kind of unequal marriage, besides the danger of apostasy (which is nevertheless the greatest), such as:

  1. Many quarrels and contentions between man and wife.105 For how can there be mutual marriage concord between those who are of different minds?
  2. Disturbance of the family: one part siding with the man, another with the woman.
  3. Wasting of goods: the husband spending what he can on those who are of his profession of faith, and the wife what she can on those who are of hers.
  4. Hindrance of all holy duties in the house: the party who is of106 the contrary profession not enduring that there should be any.
  5. Profaneness and atheism in children. For commonly, when parents are of different religions, children are of none:107 take as an instance that cursed blasphemer whose mother was an Israelite but his father an Egyptian.

The Scripture describes such children as108 monsters and109 mongrels.

Objection. Salmon married Rahab,110 and Boaz married Ruth, both of which women were unbelievers.

Answer. They had been so, but were not so when they married them. As faith and repentance alter the disposition, so they also alter the condition of the worst that can be. Rahab’s111 faith was shown before she was married to Salmon; and Ruth112 had forsaken her country’s gods and chosen the God of Israel to be her God, and Boaz113 knew as much.

Objection. But no such thing can be said of the114 daughter of the Philistines whom Samson married.

Answer. This was an extraordinary matter, and therefore not an example for all. That he did it by an extraordinary impulse is evident from this phrase, “this was from the Lord.” That it is not an example for others is evident, because115 God’s law, the rule of example, forbids it. God moved him to it to show his own power and wisdom by it.

His power, in that he was able to work by contraries: to work enmity by friendship, utter destruction by close union. For God turned the heart of Samson, a chief man in Israel, to be drawn to and desire in marriage a daughter of the Philistines, and moved the parents of that maiden to give her to Samson in marriage: here was friendship and close union. Yet116 the history shows that by this means an occasion was given to Samson to avenge himself and the people of God on the Philistines.

His wisdom, in that he turned what had an apparent show of great evil into much good. For the fact that Samson, a Nazirite of the Lord, a chief man in Israel, should join in marriage with a daughter of idolaters, who were also spiteful enemies of the Lord’s people, had a show of evil to those who did not know the spirit of Samson or the intent of the Lord. Yet by this means God brought Samson to be a judge and deliverer of his people.

It was by such a spirit as Elijah’s, when he called for fire from heaven,117 that Samson married an idolater. If anyone shall think from this of marrying idolaters, I may say to them as Christ said to his disciples, “You+ do not know what kind of spirit you+ are of.”118 This example of Samson can be no more a warrant to others to marry idolaters than his practice of pulling down a house on his own head119 is a warrant to self-murderers. The warrant for extraordinary acts is particular, personal and belongs only to those who do them. But the warrant for acts meant as examples must be the general and known will of God in his word.

Whether this general rule may be set aside in some particular cases or not, I leave to the decision of more learned divines, and submit all to the judgment of God’s church.

§. 13. Of that mutual liking which must pass between marriageable persons before they are married.

Having shown what persons are fit to be joined in marriage, it remains to show in what manner they are to be joined.

There are in Scripture three steps or degrees commended to us, by which marriageable parties are to proceed to marriage in order.

1. A mutual liking.

2. An actual contract.

3. A public solemnizing of marriage.

I. The first liking is sometimes on the part of the parents or other relatives, and is then made known by them to the party to be married: as the family of Rebekah, liking the offer of Isaac120 which was made by Abraham’s servant, made it known to Rebekah herself. Sometimes again the first liking is on the part of the one who is to be married; and then, if that party is under the government of parents, the matter must be put to them before there is any further proceeding in it, as Samson, seeing and liking a daughter of the Philistines,121 told his father and his mother about it. Yes, even if the party is not under anyone’s government, yet it is very fitting that counsel be taken of wise and understanding friends, so that in a matter as weighty as marriage there may be the advice of more heads than one, to prevent such harms as might come about through rashness. After one party has in this way taken a liking to a fitting mate, that liking must be made known to the other party so liked, to learn whether there is a mutual affection of one toward the other. So Samson went and122 talked with the woman whom he liked to be his wife. If at first a good liking of one another is mutually and thoroughly settled in both their hearts, love is likely to continue in them forever, just as things which are well glued and set before they are shaken up and down will never come apart; but if they are joined together without glue, or shaken while the glue is wet, they cannot remain firm.

Mutual love and good liking of each other is like glue.

Let the parties to be married be well settled in this before they come to meet with trials through living together, and that love will not easily be loosened by any trials.

Contrary is the adulterous and brutish practice of those who,123 as soon as they cast their eye on anyone they like, never take advice or consult about a right and due proceeding to marriage, but at once, with all the eagerness and speed they can, like brute beasts, seek to have their desire and lust satisfied. Though, to keep themselves free from the penalty of the laws under which they live, they find means to be married, yet they show a lustful and adulterous mind. And their practice is too like the practice of the Benjamites,124 who seized wives from among the daughters of Shiloh as they were dancing, or else like the practice of the old world, which so grieved the Spirit of God125 that he regretted having made man, and so was moved to bring a flood over the whole world. Their practice was this, that “they took as wives whomever they chose”: that is, they married rashly and suddenly whomever they liked, without any consideration of their condition.

Getting Married

The Second Treatise, Part I: Of Husband and Wife · §§. 14–28

§. 14. Of a contract: what it is.

II. When both parties have shown a mutual liking126 for each other, and after mature deliberation and good advice judge each other to be a fit match, it is needful that a joint consent and absolute promise to marry one another be made before sufficient witnesses. This, rightly made, is a contract, which is the beginning of a marriage.

The right making of a firm contract consists in two things:

1. In an actual taking of each other as betrothed man and wife.

2. In a direct promise to marry each other within a fitting time. So a form of contract may be made to this effect. First the man, taking the woman by the hand, says, I, A., take you, B., to be my betrothed wife, and faithfully promise to marry you at a fit and proper time. And then the woman, in turn taking the man by the hand, says, I, B., take you, A., to be my betrothed husband, and faithfully promise to consent to be married to you at a fit and proper time. This mutual and actual taking of one another as betrothed man and wife in the present time, together with a direct promise to marry one another afterward, settles such a right and ownership of the one in the other as cannot be given away without leave from the great Judge of heaven, who by his divine ordinance has settled that right.

§. 15. Of the grounds of a contract.

Question. Is a contract absolutely necessary?

Answer. Though it has been an ancient custom, continued127 in all ages, yet I dare not pronounce it so absolutely necessary that the lack of it should nullify a marriage and make it no lawful marriage. But surely it is so fitting and needful that I would advise all Christians who desire a blessing and good success on their marriage to make a contract before they are married.

If there were no other ground for it but this, that God has sanctified it and commended it to us by his word, it would be enough to persuade those who fear God to use it.

For I ask, why does God commend anything to his church by his word, except that his church should make conscience of using it? Now that it is commended by God’s word is most evident, beyond contradiction. For I will not insist on the argument which, not without good probability, is brought for the antiquity of a contract, gathered from God’s ordering of that first ancient marriage between Adam and128 Eve. God brought Eve to Adam on the first day that they were created, to see how he would like her; and on seeing her, and on the knowledge of her that he gained at the same time by the wisdom God gave him, he then took her to himself. This taking is supposed to have been only a contract, because129 he did not know her until after his fall. If it is objected that Adam and Eve are called man130 and wife in the time of their innocence, it may be answered that those titles131 are given in Scripture to those who are only betrothed, to show the close and firm union between betrothed parties.

But not to insist on what is only probable, it is more than probable that Lot’s daughters were betrothed. For it is said that Lot132 had “sons-in-law who married” (or rather were to marry) “his daughters,” and it is also said that they “have never known a man.” It must follow, then, that they were called Lot’s sons-in-law because his daughters were betrothed to them. But most evident for this purpose is the difference which the133 law puts between a pure virgin, a betrothed virgin and a married wife. So betrothed persons are in a middle degree between single persons and married persons: they are neither wholly single nor actually married. To show that this custom of a contract before marriage continued in God’s church among the saints, it is expressly noted that Mary, the mother of the Lord134 Jesus, who lived many hundreds of years after that law, was betrothed.

§. 16. Of the reasons which show how needful a contract is.

Many good and weighty reasons may be brought to show how needful it is that a contract should go before marriage. For

1. It adds much to the honor of marriage that it should be completed and made up deliberately and with good advice, step after step, by one degree after another.

2. It puts a difference between those who intend marriage in the fear of the Lord, for such holy ends as are warranted in the word, and those who intend it only to satisfy their lust, or for other such carnal ends. For these can admit no delay, as was noted135 before. But those who use this solemn preparation of a contract before marriage show that they desire to have everything fitting for so sacred a matter duly performed; and therefore they are content to accept some delay, so that it may be the better accomplished.

3. It is a means of knitting the hearts of the two parties who are to be married more firmly and inviolably together before they come to live together. For since a contract is the beginning of a marriage, it is an evident demonstration of God’s counsel concerning the betrothed parties, that God has prepared them for each other to be man and wife. So after the contract is made, they may pray for each other absolutely and without condition, that God would bless them to one another, to live together in comfort and happiness. Before a contract is made, they can pray for one another only on a supposition (if God has appointed them to be man and wife). For it often happens that after many great hopes and likelihoods of going forward with this or that match, it is broken off completely by some occasion or other. But a lawful contract ties so firm a knot that it cannot be broken, so that a man who is betrothed to a woman may conclude that she will be his wife, and a woman may conclude the same of a man. Considering this will further move them to observe more closely what good qualities, or what other things that may make them more lovely to one another, are in each other.

4. It is a means to make them prepare themselves beforehand to perform such marriage duties as God’s word requires of man and wife. For a contract gives them assurance of marriage if they live to see it. So they cannot help knowing that it is high time for them to think how they are to conduct themselves when they come to live in a house together, and also to consider what crosses ordinarily accompany the married state, so that they may be prepared beforehand wisely to pass through them or patiently to bear them.

5. It may be a means of revealing many hidden and secret hindrances which otherwise would never come to light. For many friends, fearing that revealing some evils which are kept secret should make a breach between themselves and their friends, will not make them known until they see some urgent necessity moving them to do so. Though the evil is such that, if it were known, it would hinder the marriage, yet until they see some sure evidence that the couple will indeed be married (if no just objection is raised), they will hope that some other occasion may arise to hinder the marriage, and for that reason they conceal their objection. But because a contract is the beginning of marriage, once they have notice of it they will not hold back from disclosing what they know. It is for this end that the contract is openly published in the church three separate times, so that if anyone knows any just cause why such betrothed persons may not lawfully proceed to marriage, they may make it known. It is a commendable custom, and a great pity that it is so much neglected as it is.

6. It may prevent many plots and schemes of enticing or stealing away young women and widows. For it often happens that when parents or other relatives have provided a good match for their daughter, or for someone else under their government, and everything has been well settled on all sides, the wedding day appointed, and all things fitted and prepared for solemnizing the wedding, some who want to forestall that marriage get the bride away by secret and cunning devices a few days before, if not on the very morning of the intended wedding day, and marry her at once to another man. What makes men so bold is that they know that a clandestine marriage, once completed, will stand firm in law. But a legal contract prevents such injuries, because it makes such a furtive marriage utterly void. No one, therefore, who knows that a contract has been lawfully made beforehand will be so bold, or rather so mad, as to attempt to frustrate a marriage in any such way.

7. It is a means to stir up the parties who are to be married to provide beforehand, more carefully and diligently, all things fitting for their living together and for the good ordering of their household, so that they are not left looking for necessities when they ought to be using them. For being betrothed, they know that it cannot be long before they must come to live together.

§. 17. Of abusing, or neglecting a contract.

There are two extremes contrary to the doctrine of a contract set out above: one of attributing too much to it, the other of detracting too much from it. Many make it a marriage in itself, and so have a greater solemnity at their contract than136 at their marriage. Yes, many take the liberty after a contract to know their spouse as if they were married: an unwarranted and unchaste practice. Lot’s daughters were137 betrothed to husbands, and yet it is said that they “have never known a man.” The law calls her who is betrothed “a virgin,”138 to show that she ought to keep herself a virgin until the marriage is completed. Therefore Mary is described this way: “a virgin pledged in marriage.”139 But it is the common course of most people to make light of this warranted and honorable way of proceeding to marriage by a contract. There are few, compared with the multitudes who are married, who make any conscience of it. They think it needless and utterly neglect it. No wonder they meet with many injuries and troubles, when the means of preventing them are not used. Let such people duly weigh the reasons given in the previous section.

§. 18. Of the length of time between the contract and marriage.

Question. What length of time must pass between the making of a contract and the completing of the marriage?

Answer. This must be left to the wise consideration of the betrothed parties and of their friends, for the same time cannot be precisely prescribed for all. Occasions may arise either for hastening or for putting off the marriage. Only the extremes on both sides must be avoided. The marriage ought neither to be solemnized too suddenly after the contract (then the ends and reasons of a contract, mentioned before, are made void), nor yet to be put off too long (then Satan may take occasion to tempt them through their lack of self-control). The commendable custom of our church and other churches shows that at least three weeks must pass between contract and marriage. For the contract is140 to be published three times, and that only once a week, before the wedding is celebrated. And we read that the virgin Mary was betrothed for at least three months before Joseph took her as his wife. For when the angel first came to her she was141 betrothed; after that she went to her relative Elizabeth, with whom she stayed three months; and then, when she had returned home, Joseph was warned by an angel to take her as his wife.142 I do not note this as a rule for everyone to follow precisely. For the virgin Mary had a just occasion to stay three months with her aged relative Elizabeth, and so others may have occasions to put off their marriages. This may be lawful, provided the marriage is not put off too long, and that there is a mutual and joint consent of both parties. For after the contract is made, neither the man nor the woman has power over their own body.

Contrary to this is the unwarranted course which many take, to143 be betrothed and pledged to a wife, and then to travel overseas, or to any other place, and be absent from their spouse a year, or two, or three, or perhaps more years. If a man was not allowed to go to war, nor to be charged with any business that would draw him away from his wife, in the first year of his marriage, much less may he absent himself for any long time after he is betrothed but not married. This may be a means of turning the heart of his spouse away from him forever.

§. 19. Of a religious consecrating of marriage.

III. The last degree in completing a marriage is its open and public solemnization, which consists in a religious consecration and a civil celebration of it.

A religious consecration of marriage is performed by the blessing of a public minister of the word, openly before the church, in the daytime. This has been the practice of Christians from of old, and it is still continued among us. Though we have neither an express precept nor a particular pattern in God’s word for this manner of solemnizing a marriage (for no particular form of it is set down in the Scripture), yet since it agrees with the general rules of Scripture, we ought in conscience to subject ourselves to it.

The general rules are these: “Everything must be done decently144 and in order”; the churches of God have such a custom; “Submit145 yourselves+ for the Lord’s sake to every human ordinance,”146 and the like. But the manner of consecrating marriage described above is very decent and in good order, a commendable custom of the churches, and an ordinance of the rulers under whom we live. Therefore it is warranted, and to be observed. Nor is this order, custom and ordinance appointed without just and weighty reasons. For

1. Marriage is a kind of public action: its good or bad ordering tends greatly to the good or harm of family, church and commonwealth. For by marriage families are set up, and church and commonwealth are increased and continued.

2. “Marriage is honorable.”147148 It is the most sacred and inviolable bond that knits any two persons together.

3. Marriage is149 God’s covenant, in which he himself has a main and principal hand. For God is the chief agent in joining man and woman in marriage.

On these grounds it has been thought very fitting that marriage should be solemnized in the daytime (as a work of light that need not be done covertly and secretly), and in a public place, where anyone who wishes may have free access, either to object to it and hinder it (if there is just cause) or to be a witness of it and add his blessing to it. And among public places the church is thought the fittest, because it is the house of prayer, where persons and actions are most solemnly blessed. And of all persons a public minister is thought the most fitting to celebrate marriage and to join150 the parties to be married together, because he stands in God’s place, and in and by his ministry God joins them together and blesses them. So after the minister has rightly joined man and wife together in marriage, it may well be said, “What God has joined together, let man not separate.” The form of consecrating marriage which is prescribed in our liturgy, or Book of Common Prayer, sets down so distinctly, clearly and fully whatever is to be observed and done by the parties to be married, their parents or other guardians, and the minister who joins them together, that I can add nothing to it. There the grounds, ends and uses of marriage are declared. There open proclamation is made whether anyone can object to the intended marriage. There each party is solemnly charged, if either of them knows any impediment why they may not lawfully be married, to disclose it. There also each party is openly asked whether they will freely and willingly take one another as man and wife. There the duties of married persons are declared, and they are each asked whether they will subject themselves to them or not. When all this has been openly professed, the parent, or someone in his place, is called forward to give the bride to the bridegroom. Then, when the two of them have actually taken each other as man and wife, and testified to it by express words and by mutual pledges, the minister joins them together in God’s name, pronounces them to be lawful husband and wife, and by prayer asks God’s blessing on the action and on their persons. In this way the marriage is consecrated, and the two of them are made one flesh, that is, lawfully joined together by the inviolable bond of marriage.

§. 20. Of clandestine marriages.

Contrary to this are clandestine marriages, such as are made in private houses or other secret places, or in churches without a sufficient number of witnesses, or in the nighttime, or without a lawful minister of the word, and the like. As such seeking of secrecy takes much away from the honor and dignity of marriage, so it implies some evil clinging to it: for “everyone151 who does evil hates the light.” There is little hope that such marriages should have any good success. For where such means as are sanctified for obtaining a blessing on marriage are neglected, what blessing can be expected from it?

§. 21. Of a civil celebrating of marriage.

Though by the consecrating of marriage named above it is fully complete in its substance, yet for the greater solemnity of so honorable a thing it is very fitting that a civil celebration of it should be added as well, under152 which I include all the lawful customs that are used to set forth its outward solemnity, such as the meeting of friends, accompanying the bridegroom and bride both to and from the church, putting on one’s best clothing, feasting, and other tokens of rejoicing. For these we have express warrant from God’s word.

As to the general point, that the time of marriage is a time of rejoicing, some gather it from the derivation of the word, as if it were called marriage from merry age. But to let that pass, the Scripture is accustomed to set forth a time of rejoicing by the joy of the bridegroom, “as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride,”153 and it speaks of “the sounds of joy and gladness, the voices of the bride and bridegroom.”154 And on the other hand it counts it a judgment when155 joy is taken away from the bridegroom and the bride.

As for the meeting of friends at the time of marriage, it is noted that “Laban invited all the men of that place”156 when his daughter was married. And when Samson was married, “they selected thirty men to accompany him.”157 And when a friend of the virgin Mary was married,158 Jesus and his disciples, besides many others, were invited to it. And in the parable of the wedding of the king’s son, it is noted that many guests were invited to the wedding.159 In all these histories it is further noted that feasts were made at the solemnizing of those marriages. And the words the prophet uses, “as a bridegroom adorns himself with ornaments, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels,”160 give warrant for putting on the best clothing at that time.

Here, by the way, let good heed be taken that the things which may lawfully be used are not unlawfully abused, as marriage festivities commonly are, and especially in feasting.

§. 22. Of ill or well ordering marriage feasts.

Marriage feasts are abused,161

1. When they are held at an unseasonable time:162 such as on the Lord’s day, or in a time of mourning.

2. When they exceed the means of him who makes the163 feasts.

3. When the abundance prepared is taken immoderately,164 even to gluttony and drunkenness. The wicked practice of drinking toasts to the bridegroom and bride often causes much excess in drunkenness.

4. When too much time is spent on them.165

5. When God is completely forgotten in them, and the company is poisoned166 with corrupt talk, unchaste songs and the like.

6. When the needy and distressed are not remembered167 at them.

To prevent these abuses, a seasonable time for celebrating168 marriage must be chosen, and moderation used both by him who makes the feast and also by those who share in it: moderation, I say, in the measure of eating and drinking, and in the time spent on it. That time must be sanctified with such talk as is “helpful for building up” and “bringing grace to those who listen.” And for more cheerfulness in it, clever questions and puzzling riddles may be posed (as Samson did)169 to exercise the understanding and judgment of the guests. There may also be the singing of “psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs,” the guests making music in their hearts to the Lord. Yes, further, so that the marriage meeting, mirth and feasting may be the better sanctified, a good choice is to be made of the guests who are invited to it. Of this we have a worthy pattern in those who were married in Cana of Galilee,170 and invited Jesus, his mother and his disciples to their feast. Guests such as Jesus will give occasion for wholesome and sanctified talk, by which all the guests may be much edified. Such as the virgin Mary will be a good example of modesty, sobriety and other such Christian graces. Such as the disciples will be far from scorning and mocking sound and good instruction, but will rather give all diligent heed to it, and lay it up in their hearts.

Above all, so that the mirth and joy of marriage is not dampened as Belshazzar’s was,171 let those who are married, and all who come to rejoice with them, make sure that they have true assurance of their spiritual marriage with Christ, and of a good right in him to the created things which they use. Otherwise their sins will be like that handwriting which appeared to Belshazzar on the wall.

Finally, because of the liberty which God gives, with plenty and abundance, to eat what is rich and drink what is172 sweet, let the poor who scarcely have enough be remembered.

So by a right celebrating of marriage it is much honored, and man and wife are brought together with much honor.

§. 23. Of the honor of marriage with respect to its first institution.

There is great reason why marriage should be solemnized with such honor. For it is a most honorable thing: honorable in its institution, ends, privileges and mystery. No ordinance was more honorable in its first institution, as is evident from its Author, the place where it was instituted, the time when it was instituted, the persons who were first married, and the manner of joining them together.

1. The Author and first founder of marriage was the Lord173 God. Could there have been a greater, or in any way a more excellent, Author?

2. The place was Paradise, the most fair, glorious, pleasant, honorable, well-provided and in every way most excellent place that ever was in this world. Place, though it is only a circumstance, adds much to the honor of a thing. Solemn ordinances are made in honorable places. So with us marriages are solemnized in churches, not in private houses.

3. The time was the most pure and perfect time that ever was in the world, when no sin or pollution of man had stained it: the time of man’s innocence. Purity adds much to the honor of a thing.

4. The persons were the most honorable that ever were: the first father and mother of all mankind, those who had absolute power and dominion over all creatures, and to whom all were subject. No one but they ever had a true monarchy over the whole world.

5. The manner was with as great deliberation as was ever used in instituting any ordinance. For first, the three glorious174 persons in the Trinity meet to consult about it. For “the Lord God also said,” and to whom should he speak? Not to any created power, but to him who was begotten of himself, the “Wonderful Counselor,” etc. In this consultation this ordinance is found to be very needful (“It is not good for the man to be alone”), and so a decision is set down, to make “a suitable helper” for man. To carry this out the better, the Lord proceeds to it very deliberately, by various steps and degrees.

  1. All the creatures that lived on the earth or breathed in the air are brought before man, to see if a suitable helper for him might be found among them.
  2. Each of them being thoroughly viewed and found unfit, another creature is made, and that out of man’s substance and side, and after his image.
  3. This excellent creature, so made, is presented to man by its maker, to see how he would like it.
  4. Man showing a good liking for her, she is given to him to be his wife.
  5. The inviolable law of the close and firm union of man and wife together is enacted.

Let all the branches named above concerning the first institution of marriage, expressly recorded by the Holy Spirit, be well weighed, and we will easily see that there is no ordinance now in force among the sons of men so honorable in its institution as this.

§. 24. Of the Ends of Marriage.

2. The ends for which marriage was ordained add much to its honor. They are chiefly three.175

1. That the world might be increased, and not merely increased, but with legitimate offspring and distinct families, which are the seedbeds of cities and commonwealths. Yes, and also that the church in the world might be preserved and propagated by a holy seed, Mal 2:15.

2. That men might avoid fornication (1 Cor 7:2) and control their own bodies in holiness and honor. Because of that176 proneness to lust which is in man’s corrupt nature, this end adds much to the honor of marriage. It shows that marriage is like a haven for those whose salvation is in jeopardy through the gusts of temptation to lust. No sin is more hereditary; there is none in which more children of Adam share than this. Well might Christ say (Matt 19:11), “Not everyone can accept this word.”

Of all the children of Adam that ever were, not one in a million of those who have come to ripeness of years has been a true eunuch all his lifetime. Against this hereditary disease no remedy is so sovereign as this. Yes, for those who do not have the gift of self-control, this is the only warranted and sanctified remedy.

3. That man and wife might be a mutual help to one177 another (Gen 2:18): a help both in bringing forth and in bringing up children, and both in setting up and in well governing their family. A help also in well ordering prosperity and in well bearing adversity. A help in health and sickness.178 A help while both live together, and when one is taken from the other by death. In this respect it is said (Prov 18:22), “He who finds a wife finds a good thing,” which by the rule of relation is also true of a husband.179

Man can have no such help from any other creature as from a wife, nor a woman as from a husband.

§. 25. Of the Privileges of marriage.

III. If180 it is asked (as it once was of circumcision) what is the privilege, advantage and profit of marriage, I answer, “Much in every way.”

1. By it men and women are made husbands and wives.

2. It is the only lawful means to make them fathers and mothers.

3. It is the ordinary means to make them masters and mistresses. All these are great dignities, in which the image and glory of God consists.

4. It is the most effectual means of continuing a man’s181 name and memory in this world that there can be. Children are living monuments and vivid representations of their parents.

5. In ancient times many privileges were granted to those who were married.182 In pleading cases or giving sentence they had the first place, and in the choice of men for offices they were preferred.183 In assemblies they had the place of honor.184 And if they had many children they were exempt from night watches and other such burdensome duties. Among us, if the younger sister is married before the elder, pre-eminence and precedence are given to the younger.

The privileges and honors which are given to married persons were, without question, the ground of the custom of his country which Laban mentions:185 that the younger was not to be married before the elder.

§. 26. Of the mystery of Marriage.

IIII. Great is the mystery which is set forth by marriage: namely, the sacred, spiritual, real and inviolable union between Christ and his church. It is excellently portrayed in Solomon’s Song and in Psalm 45, and expressly noted in Eph 5:32.

By this, man and wife who love one another wholeheartedly, as they ought, have an evident demonstration of Christ’s love to them. For as parents, by the affection which they bear their children, may better discern the mind and intent of God toward them than those who never had a child, so married persons may better know the disposition of Jesus Christ, who is the spouse of every faithful soul, than single persons.

§. 27. Of Marriage and single life compared together.

Let the admirers and praisers of the single state now bring out all their reasons and put them in the other scale against marriage. If these two are duly balanced and rightly weighed, we will find single life too light to be compared with honorable marriage. All that can be said for the single state is grounded on incidental circumstances. Saint Paul, who of all the writers of holy Scripture has spoken most for it, brings all his commendations under the head of expediency, and limits them all to the186 “present necessity.”

Objection. He uses these words187 (good and better).188

Answer. Those words relate not to virtue but to expediency. Nor are they spoken in opposition to vice and sin, for then it would follow that to marry (which is God’s ordinance, and honorable in all) is evil and sinful. That is to revive189 that ancient heresy that “marriage is of the devil.”190 Of old, those who called lawful marriage a defilement have been said to have the apostate dragon dwelling in them. But the apostle calls that good which is advantageous, and that better which is more expedient; and yet not absolutely more expedient, but to some persons at some times. For if any do not have the gift of self-control, it is not only advantageous or more expedient that they marry, but also absolutely necessary. They are commanded to do so (1 Cor 7:9). Yet on the other side, if any have the gift of self-control, they are not absolutely barred from marriage; there are other occasions, besides avoiding fornication, to move them to marry. It is therefore truly said that “virginity is not commanded, but advised.”191 “We have no precept for it, but leave it to the power of those who have that power.” So far as men and women see just occasion for abstaining from marriage (being at least able to do so), they are persuaded by the apostle to use their liberty and keep themselves free. But all the occasions which192 move them to remain single arise from the weakness and wickedness of men: the wickedness of those who stir up troubles against others, and the weakness of those who allow themselves to be disquieted and too much distracted with the affairs of the family, care for wife, children and the like.193 Were it not for the wickedness of some and the weakness of others, to please a husband or a wife would be no hindrance to pleasing the Lord. If, therefore, man had stood in his whole and innocent state, no such wickedness or weakness would have seized on him, and then the single state could in no respect have been preferred194 before the married. But since the fall, virginity (where it is given) may be of good use; and therefore the church gives due honor both to virginity and to marriage.

§. 28. Of celebrating marriage with sorrow.

Contrary to the joyful celebrating of marriage described above are all those crooked courses which bring much grief, trouble and vexation to it: such as forced, stolen, unequal or in any other way unlawful marriages; marriages without the consent of parents or other governors and friends; or marriages rushed through to avoid the danger of the law for impurity committed before, and the like. Many, by their disorderly and improper performing of so weighty a matter, not only cause great trouble and disquiet on the wedding day, but also much sorrow all the days of their life. If such people find no joy, comfort or help in marriage, but rather the contrary, let them not blame God’s ordinance, but their own folly and perverseness.
