The Second Treatise, Part II: Of Their Common Duties

Marital Unity and Sexual Faithfulness

The Second Treatise, Part II: Of Their Common Duties · §§. 1–9

§. 1. Of the heads of those common-mutual duties.

In the first part of this treatise concerning man and wife, it has been declared who are to be counted as such. In this second part their common-mutual duties are to be set out. These are either absolutely necessary195 for the being and abiding of marriage, or196 needful and requisite for its well-being and well-abiding, that is, for the good condition of marriage, and for a commendable and comforting life together.

There are two kinds of the former:

  1. Marital unity.
  2. Marital chastity.

The latter may also be brought under two heads: for they are either such as the married couple are to perform mutually, each to the other, or such as both of them are to perform jointly to others.

Those mutual duties are:

  1. A loving affection for one another.
  2. A provident care for one another.

Under that provident care I include both the means by which it may be better carried out (which is cohabitation) and the matter in which it consists:

And this concerns the soul, the body, the good name, and the property of each other.

The joint duties which are to be performed to others concern those who are in the house and those who are outside the house.

Those who are in the house are:

  1. Members of the family.
  2. Guests who come to the family.

Many more particulars are included under these general heads, which I intend to deliver one by one as I come to them, each in its own proper place.

§. 2. Of marital unity.

The first, highest, chief and most absolutely necessary common-mutual duty between man and wife is marital unity, by which husband and wife count one another to be one flesh, and accordingly preserve the inviolable union by which they are knit together. This is the duty which the apostle commands husbands and wives in these words: “A wife197 must not separate from her husband,” and, “A husband must not divorce his wife.” He speaks there of renouncing each other, and of making the marriage bond void and of no effect. He would have that bond kept firm and inviolable, and would have the two who are made one by it constantly remain one, and not make themselves two again. This marital unity is so necessary that it must not be broken up or dissolved, even though one is a Christian and the other a pagan. “If a brother198 has an unbelieving wife,” says the apostle, “he must not divorce her. And if a woman has an unbelieving husband, she must not divorce him.”

There are two chief reasons for this inviolable union: one taken from the author of marriage, the other from its nature.

1. The author of marriage is God.199 It is his ordinance, and it is he who by his ordinance has made two into one flesh. Now note the consequence which Christ draws from this, as a settled case and an undeniable principle: “What God has joined together,200 let no man separate.” If no man, then neither wife nor husband himself.

2. Such is the nature of the marriage bond that it makes two into one, and201 binds those two together more firmly than any other bond can bind any other two together. How then should they be two again?

§. 3. Of desertion.

The vice contrary to marital unity is desertion. It is when one of the married couple, out of indignation against the true religion and utter detestation of it, or some other such cause, openly renounces all marital unity, withdraws himself or herself from all society with the other, and lives among infidels, idolaters, heretics or other such persecutors, among whom a faithful Christian cannot live with safety of life or a good conscience. And though every good means that can be thought of is used to win back the party who has departed, nothing will prevail, but that party obstinately persists in renouncing all marital fellowship.

This desertion is so grave in the case of marriage that it202 frees the innocent party from any further seeking after the other. In this respect the apostle says, “If the unbeliever leaves, let him go. A brother or sister is not under bondage in such cases,” 1 Cor 7:15. By bondage he means the subjection of marriage (because of which neither of the married persons has power over his own body, but each over the other’s). Now those who are not under this bondage are not bound to seek after it. Therefore that desertion on the offender’s203 part is such a dissolution of marriage as frees the innocent party from its bondage. In many reformed churches overseas desertion is held to dissolve the very bond of marriage so far that liberty is given to the forsaken party to marry another. And it is also applied to other cases than the one mentioned above: as when an204 infidel, idolater or heretic departs from one of the true religion for other causes than hatred of religion; or when both man and wife have lived as idolaters among idolaters,205 and one of them, being converted to the true faith, leaves his home among idolaters and goes to those who profess the true faith, but can by no means get the other party to move; or when one of the true religion departs from another of the same profession of faith, and will by no means be brought to live with the party left behind, but openly shows a stubborn obstinacy. In such cases, the matter being heard and judged by the magistrate, the marriage bond may be broken, and liberty given to the forsaken party to marry another. But because our church has no such custom, and our law has not settled such cases, I leave them to the custom of other churches.

§. 4. Of marital chastity.

The second necessary common-mutual marriage duty is marital chastity. Chastity in a broad sense is taken for every kind of purity in soul or body: in this sense the apostle calls the church of God “a chaste virgin.”206 But in the sense in which we use it here, it belongs especially to the body. It is that virtue by which “we possess our vessels”207 (to use the apostle’s phrase) “in holiness and honor”; or, more plainly to our purpose, by which we keep our bodies undefiled.

Chastity thus restricted to the body is that of

  • Single life.
  • Wedlock.

That of single life is opposed to fornication. It is either the chastity of those who were never married: such a one was Saint Paul, and in this respect he wishes that all were as he was, 1 Cor 7:7. Or it is the chastity of those who are lawfully freed from the bond of marriage: such a one the apostle calls208 “a true widow.” The chastity of wedlock is that virtue by which married parties, observing the lawful and honorable use of marriage, keep their bodies from being defiled with another’s flesh. So the apostle commands wives to be “chaste,” Titus 2:5. So209 those who keep the laws of wedlock are as chaste as those who abstain altogether.

Here, by the way, note the folly of our adversaries, who think there is no chastity except that of single persons. So in their speeches and writings210 they set chastity and marriage against one another as two contraries.

Some of their holy fathers and popes, and those not the least learned nor of the worst repute among them, have inferred in their arguments against priests’ marriage that marriage is a living in the flesh, a sowing to the flesh, a pollution of the flesh.211 To that purpose they urge Saint Paul’s advice to man and wife to abstain so that they may give themselves to fasting and prayer: but this is directly contrary to the apostle’s intent. For,

1. He speaks there of extraordinary humbling. 2. He adds this limitation, “for a time.” 3. He does not say simply, “that you+ may pray,” but “so you+ may devote yourselves+” (or have212 leisure) “to prayer”: as if it only hindered prayer, but did not pollute it.

But how can the spots and blots on marriage named above agree with the beauty and glory with which the apostle sets it out in these words, “marriage is honorable in all,” Heb 13:4? If marriage were what the papists make it out to be, the marriage bed would be very unfittingly called “undefiled.”

See how contrary the spirits of Saint Paul and of their popes were! Far more contrary, I know well, than chastity and marriage are.

But to return to our matter: it is clear that married persons may be chaste, and accordingly they ought to be chaste. To this end the apostle, counseling men and women to have wives and husbands in order to avoid fornication, inserts this word OWN (“each man should have his OWN wife,213 and each woman her OWN husband”), by which he implies that they should have relations with no one else. What214 Solomon says of a husband must, by the rule of relation, be applied to a wife. As the man must be satisfied at all times with his wife, and even enraptured with her love, so the woman must be satisfied at all times with her husband, and even enraptured with his love. By the same rule husbands must take the command given to wives, “to be chaste,”215 as directed to themselves also, and be chaste. Isaac and Rebekah faithfully and mutually performed this duty to each other.

1. It was one main end for which marriage was ordained (especially since the216 fall of man): to live chastely. The apostle implies this where he says, “to avoid fornication,” let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband.217 And again, “If they cannot control themselves, let them marry.”

2. By chastity a godly seed is preserved on earth. With this reason the prophet Malachi urges this duty. For after he had said that the Lord “made them one,” meaning that he made two into one flesh218 by marriage, he draws this exhortation from it: “So guard yourselves+ in your+ spirit, and let no one break faith with the wife of his youth.”

3. A special part of the honor of marriage consists in219 chastity. So the apostle, having given marriage this high commendation, that it is “honorable in all,” adds this clause (“and the bed undefiled”) to show the reason for that honor. It is as if he had said, Because the marriage bed is in itself a bed undefiled, marriage is therefore in itself honorable, and it remains honorable just so far as the bed remains undefiled.

§. 5. Of adultery.

The vice contrary to marital chastity is adultery, one of the most grievous vices in that state: a vice by which the way is opened to divorce. This is clear and evident from the ruling of Christ himself on that point, first220 set out in his Sermon on the Mount, and again221 repeated in his conference with the Pharisees, where, condemning unjust divorces, he makes an exception of divorce for adultery.

And there is great reason for it. For222 the adulterer makes himself one flesh with his harlot. Why then should he remain one flesh with his wife? “The two,” says the law, “will be one flesh”: not three. The same may be said of a wife who commits adultery.

§. 6. Of pardoning adultery on repentance.

Question. Since adultery gives just cause for divorce, may this fault, on the repentance of the guilty person, be so forgiven that the innocent person seeks no divorce, but both continue to live together in wedlock as before?

Answer. Though it is not fitting in this case to impose it on the innocent party as an inviolable law to keep the guilty party because of repentance (for we have no direct and strict warrant for it), yet I do not doubt that they may do so if they will; and, where there is no just objection to the contrary, they ought to do so. For the law of divorce did not require anyone to sue for the bill of divorce, but only gave them liberty to use that punishment if they saw cause. I do not doubt that, as warrant for this liberty, we may take God’s pattern in keeping churches and people after they have committed spiritual adultery, and Christ’s forgiving the woman who had committed adultery. For “since Christ said to an adulteress, ‘Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more,’ who cannot see that a husband ought to forgive what he sees the Lord of both husband and wife has forgiven, and that he ought not to call her an adulteress whose fault he believes has been blotted out by the mercy of God on her repentance?”223

§. 7. Of the difference between adultery in a man and in a wife.

Question. Is the bond of marriage violated as much on the224 man’s part when he commits adultery as on the woman’s when she does?

Answer. Though the ancient Romans and the canonists have made the woman’s fault in this kind far heavier than the man’s, and given the man more privileges than the woman, yet I do not see how that difference in the sin can stand with the tenor of God’s word. I do not deny that more troubles may follow from the woman’s fault than from the man’s: such as greater disgrace before men, worse disturbance225 of the family, more mistaking of legitimate and illegitimate children, and the like. The man cannot know which are his own children as well as the woman can. He may take illegitimate children to be his own, and so settle the inheritance on them; and he may suspect his own to be illegitimate, and so deprive them of their patrimony. But the woman is free from all such mistakes. Yet with respect to the breaking of wedlock and the transgression against God, the sin of either party is the same. God’s word makes no difference between them. At the beginning God said of them both, “the two will be one flesh”:226 not only is the woman made one flesh with the man, but the man also with the woman.227 Their power over one another in this respect is also the same. If on just occasion they abstain,228 it must be by mutual consent. If the husband leaves his wife,229 she is as free as he would be if she left him. Accordingly the punishment230 which by God’s law was to be inflicted on adulterers is the same, whether the man or the woman is the offender (Deut 22:22). If any difference is made, it is fitting that adulterous husbands be punished all the more severely, since it belongs to them all the more to excel in virtue and to govern their wives by example.

§. 8. Of the heinousness of adultery.

But to return to showing how heinous adultery is: I find no sin in the whole of Scripture set out so conspicuously in all its separate colors as this one. For besides being231 forbidden by name in the Ten Commandments, it is further expressly branded as committed:

1. Against each person of the holy Trinity: the Father (whose232 covenant is broken), the Son (whose233 members are made the members of a harlot), and the Holy Spirit (whose234 temple is polluted).

2. Against one’s neighbor: the235 party with whom the sin is committed (for this sin cannot be committed by one person alone); the husband and wife of each party236 (who cannot rest content with any satisfaction); the children237 born in adultery (whom the adulterers brand with an indelible mark of disgrace, and deprive of many privileges they might otherwise enjoy); the relatives by marriage238 and friends of each party (to whom the grief and disgrace of this foul sin reaches); the whole family belonging to either of them (for239 this is like a fire in a house); the town, city and nation where such unclean birds roost (for240 all of them lie open to the vengeance of God for this sin); and the very church of God (whose241 holy seed is hindered by this sin).

3. Against the parties themselves who commit this sin, and that against their242 souls,243 bodies,244 name,245 property, and all that belongs to them.

As this sin is in itself a sinful sin, so by the bitter and246 cursed fruits that come from it, it is made sinful beyond measure. For

1. By it the affection of husbands and wives (which of all others ought to be the most inviolable) is so alienated that it is seldom reconciled again.

2. By it the property of the family is much wasted: the adulterous husband spends on his harlot what he should provide for his family with, and the adulterous wife steals what she can from her husband.

3. By it husbands and wives are stirred up to wish for, and long for, one another’s death: and not only to wish it inwardly in their hearts, but also to carry it out outwardly in deed.

4. If a galling and terrifying conscience does not arise from this sin (as it often does), then something worse does: a seared conscience, a hard heart, a reprobate mind, and a shameless face.

So God deals with such sinners accordingly. In247 his soul248 he hates them. By his word he has denounced many fearful judgments against them, both in249 this world and in250 the world to come (against no sin more). This sin is reckoned one of the chief causes of the greatest judgments ever inflicted in the world: of the251 universal flood; of the252 fire and brimstone which destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah; of253 Canaan’s spewing out its inhabitants; of the254 plague which destroyed 24,000 in one day; and of the255 Israelites’ captivity, and the like. By all these we see that fearful sentence proved true: “God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.”256 Now consider this:257 “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”

§. 9. Of remedies against adultery, and in particular of due benevolence, and of defect or excess in it.

For preventing this heinous sin, God’s word has prescribed many other remedies, which I pass over: such as258 a diligent keeping of the heart (so that lustful thoughts do not come from it); of the eyes259 (so that they do not wander to the beauty or handsomeness of anyone’s person, or to lascivious pictures, or any other such allurements); of the ears260 (so that they do not listen to any enticements of others); of the tongue261 (so that it utters no unchaste and corrupt talk); of the lips262 (so that they take no delight in wanton kisses); of the hands263 (so that they use no wanton caresses); of the feet264 (so that they do not carry you too near the place where adultery may be committed); of your company265 (so that you are not defiled with others’ wantonness and impurity); of your diet266 (so that it is not immoderate); of your clothing267 (so that it is not gaudy and lascivious); of your time268 (so that it is not spent in vanity and idleness). These and other such remedies, I say, I pass over. One of the best remedies that can be prescribed to married persons (next to a269 reverent fear of God, and a continual setting of him before them wherever they are) is that husband and wife delight in each other mutually, and maintain a pure and fervent love between themselves, yielding to one another that due benevolence270 (the marriage duty each owes the other) which is warranted and sanctified by God’s word, and ordained by God for this particular end. This due benevolence (as the apostle calls it) is one of the most distinctive and essential acts of marriage, and necessary for its main and principal ends: for the preservation of chastity in those who do not have the gift of self-control, for increasing the world with legitimate offspring, and for linking the affections of the married couple more firmly together. These ends of marriage, at least the first two, are made void unless this duty is performed.

As it is called271 benevolence because it must be performed with good will and delight, willingly, readily and cheerfully, so it is said to be272 due because it is a debt which the wife owes to her husband, and he to her. “The wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife.”273

I have my warrant from the apostle to prescribe this duty as a remedy against adultery. For “to avoid fornication,”274 he advises man and wife to “render due benevolence” to one another. If, then, this question is raised (How will marriage keep men and women from adultery?), this answer may be given from the apostle’s words: (by rendering due benevolence). He presses this home further by declaring the injury that may follow from neglecting this duty, namely their casting themselves into the snares of Satan.275 Well might he press this duty for that end, because no other means has the same force: not fasting, not keeping vigil, not hard lodging, not long travel, not much labor, not cold, not solitude, nor anything else.276 Some who have labored hard by these means to beat down their bodies and subdue lust (but neglected the remedy named above) have nevertheless felt lust boiling in them.

There are two extremes contrary to this duty: one in the defect, the other in the excess.

Defect in it is when, in case of need, it is not asked for; or, being asked for by the one, it is not yielded by the other. Some make modesty their pretext for not asking for it. But in a duty so warrantable and needful, a pretense of modesty is (to say the least) a sign of great weakness, and a cause of much iniquity. To deny this duty when it is rightly asked for is to deny a due debt, and to give Satan great advantage. The punishment inflicted on Onan (Gen 38:9, 10) shows how great a wrong this is. From that punishment277 the Hebrews gather that this sin is a kind of murder. It is all the more heinous when hatred, stubbornness, squeamishness, fear of having too many children, or any other such motive is the cause of it.

Excess is either in the measure or in the time. In the measure, when husband or wife is insatiable, provoking lust rather than assuaging it, and weakening their natural vigor rather than suppressing their unnatural appetite. Many husbands and wives are much oppressed by their bedfellows’ insatiable demands in this matter.

In the time, when it is against piety, mercy or modesty.

1. Against piety, when no day or duty of religion, not even extraordinary days and duties of humbling, will make them forbear.278 The prophet’s bidding the bridegroom and bride come out of their chamber on the day of a fast, and279 the apostle’s making an exception for prayer and fasting where he commands this duty of due benevolence, show that in the time of a fast it must be forborne.

2. Against mercy, when one of the married couple is weak through sickness, pain, toil, travel, or any other such cause, and through that weakness is not well able to perform his duty, and yet the other will have it performed all the same. “I desire mercy, not sacrifice,” says the Lord. Shall God’s sacrifice give way to mercy, and shall not man’s or woman’s lust? For so I may well call this unseasonable desire.

Question. What if a husband or wife remains sick, or otherwise weak, for so long that the other cannot exercise self-control?

Answer. In such cases of necessity the body must be beaten down, and earnest prayer made for the gift of self-control. For assuredly the Lord who has brought you to that necessity will give you sufficient grace.

3. Against modesty,280 when husbands require this duty at the time which under the law was called the time of a wife’s separation for her sickness (Lev 15:19, etc.). For what can be expected from such polluted intercourse but a leprous and loathsome offspring? This kind of intemperance is expressly forbidden (Lev 18:19), and a capital punishment was inflicted on those who offended in it (Lev 20:18). Abstinence at this time is set in the list of those marks which show a man to be righteous (Ezek 18:6), and the contrary intemperance is put in the roll of the abominations which provoked God to spew out the Canaanites (Lev 18:28) and to forsake his own inheritance (Ezek 22:10).

To this kind of intemperance281 some refer a man’s knowing his wife after she has conceived. But I find no such thing condemned in God’s word, and I dare not make that a sin which is not condemned there.282 Certain sects among the Jews are branded for this error.

1. Objection. No other animal will do so, so it may seem to be against nature.

Answer. 1. I deny the argument: though some forbear, not all do.

2. I deny the consequence: for other animals are not bound one male to one female as a husband is to his own wife.283 Besides, what beasts are bound to by nature must be left to man’s discretion.

2. Objection. Once a woman has conceived, no more conceptions can be expected until she is delivered.

Answer. Conception is not the only end of this duty: for it is to be rendered to those who are barren.

Question. What if the wife is nursing her child? Ought not her husband then to forbear?

Answer. Because nursing is a mother’s duty, a man ought to do what he can to restrain himself.

Living Together in Love

The Second Treatise, Part II: Of Their Common Duties · §§. 10–17

§. 10. Of mutual love between man and wife.

So much for those common-mutual duties which tend to preserve the very being of marriage, and are in that respect absolutely necessary. The other common-mutual duties (though they are not of such absolute necessity as the former) are in their kind necessary for the good condition of marriage, and for better preserving that knot. If they are not performed, the end and right use of marriage will be perverted, and that state made comfortless and very burdensome. The first of these is love. A loving mutual affection must pass between husband and wife, or else no duty will be well performed: this is the ground of all the rest. In some respects love belongs properly and distinctively to a husband, as284 I intend to show when I come to speak of a husband’s particular duties. But love is also required of wives, and they are commanded “to love their husbands,” just as husbands are commanded “to love their wives.”285 So it is a common-mutual duty belonging to husband and wife alike: and that is true wedlock, when man and wife are linked together by the bond of love. Under love all other duties286 are included, for without it no duty can be well performed. “Love is the fulfillment of the law,”287 that is, the very life of all the duties which the law requires. It is “the bond of perfect unity,”288 which binds together all the duties that pass between one party and the other. Where love abounds, all duties will be performed readily and cheerfully. Where love is lacking, every duty will either be wholly neglected, or performed so carelessly that it might as well not be performed at all. For this reason the apostle commands, “Do everything289 in love.” As love provokes the party in whom it rules to do all the good it can, so it stirs up the party loved to repay good for good. It is like fire, which is not only hot in itself, but also conveys heat into what is near it: and from this arises a reflection of heat from one to the other. Note how wonderfully this is set out between Christ and his spouse in the Song of Solomon; and it is further shown in the examples of all the good husbands and wives noted in Scripture: they bore a very loving affection for one another.

Though love is a general duty which everyone owes to another,290 even to his enemy, yet the more closely God has linked any together, the more they are bound to this duty, and the more they must abound in it. But of all others291 man and wife are most closely and firmly linked together. Of all others, therefore, they are most bound to it, and that in the highest degree possible, even like Jonathan’s love, who loved David292 “as himself.” Solomon says, “He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the Lord.” By the rule of relation this is also true of a husband: “She who finds a husband finds a good thing and obtains favor from the Lord.” Man and wife, therefore, are to each other a special pledge of God’s favor, and in this respect are to be loved above all others under God. If this is the ground (as it ought to be) of their mutual293 love, their love will be fervent and constant. Neither the lack nor the withering of any outward attractions, such as beauty, figure, family, friends, riches, honors or the like, will withhold or withdraw, extinguish or diminish their love. Nor will any excellencies of nature or grace in other husbands and wives draw their hearts from their own to those others. Nor again will the love of a former yokefellow, dead and gone, lessen in the least the love of the living mate.

I have mentioned this instance all the more because in many294 who are far from setting their affection on another’s flesh, the love of a former husband or wife who has died is so firmly fixed in their heart that they can never again love any other so entirely. Those who are so minded are not fit to be joined to another yokefellow after they are released from one. If they marry again and show such a mind, they plainly show that they regard this or that person more than God’s ordinance. By God’s ordinance man and wife are bound to one another no longer than they live together. Death is an absolute severing, and makes an utter dissolution of the marriage bond. “If her husband295 dies, she is released from the law of marriage,” so that she may take another man. The same liberty is also given to the man. Being now free, if they marry another (that other being now a true husband or wife), their love must be as entire toward that other as it was toward the former; indeed, more entire, if there was any defect in the former. For as children married out of their parents’ house must not keep such a love for their parents as swallows up their love for the party to whom they are married, but must, according to the law, leave father and mother and hold fast to their yokefellow, so neither must the love of a former husband or wife prevail when they are married to another. This other must be held fast as closely as if they had never been joined to a former one. The living husband or wife is the present pledge of God’s favor. He is now your own husband, and she is now your own wife, and not the party who is dead. I do not deny that the memory of a virtuous husband or wife ought to be precious to the surviving party, for “the memory of the righteous is a blessing.”296 But as the virtue of a deceased person must not be buried with the dead body, so neither must the person be kept above ground with the memory of his or her virtue. This is done in a sense when love of the deceased party either takes away or lessens the love of the living. This is to give the dead dominion over the living, which is more than the law commands.

§. 11. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual hatred, contrary to love.

There is a generation of so sour and crooked a disposition297 that they cannot love, but rather hate one another, because they are man and wife. For many husbands who have wives, and wives who have husbands, worthy in every way to be loved, will nevertheless say, to the astonishment of their hearers, “I have indeed a good husband, but I cannot love him,” or “I have a good wife, but I cannot love her.” And when they are asked for a reason, they do not hesitate to reply openly and shamelessly, “I think I could love him if he were not my husband,” or “I think I could love her if she were not my wife.” O more than monstrous impudence! Is not this directly to oppose God’s ordinance, and the order which he has set between man and woman? Is it not to trample God’s favor underfoot? Even if there were nothing else to move love but this, that such a one is your husband, or such a one is your wife, yet this should be motive enough. And shall this be the ground of your hatred? Assuredly such a spirit is a plainly diabolical spirit, contrary to the spirit which is from above; and if it is not cast out, it will cast those whom it possesses into the fire of hell.

§. 12. Of mutual peace between man and wife.

Among other means of maintaining an inward loving affection between man and wife, outward mutual peace, concord and agreement is one of the chief. So the apostle exhorts us “to keep the unity of the spirit through the bond298 of peace”: for peace is a bond that ties one to another, and makes them as one, even one in spirit; just as, on the other side, outward discord divides men’s spirits. We are commanded to “pursue peace with everyone”:299 how much more, of all persons, ought husbands to have peace with their wives, and wives with their husbands! They are nearer than brothers and sisters. See then how good and pleasant a thing it is for them to dwell together in unity.300 Dwell together they must: but without peace there is no dwelling together. “Better to dwell on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife.” Persons at variance would be far better out of sight and apart than present together. Man and wife must not be out of sight and apart; at peace, therefore,301 they must be. Mutual peace between them is a great refreshment to their minds when they have been battered by the discords of others. It is said that a wife is in this respect like a haven to a man (and how much more a man to his wife!). If the haven is calm, and free from storms and tempests, what a refreshment it will be to the sailor who has been tossed on the sea by winds and waves!

For maintaining peace:

1. All offenses must be avoided as far as possible.302 The husband must watch over himself so that he gives no offense to his wife, and so must the wife on her side. Offenses cause contentions.

2. When an offense is given by one party, it must303 not be taken by the other, but rather passed over; and then peace will not be broken. The second blow makes304 the fray.305

3. If both are angered together, the fire is likely to be the greater; so they must both labor all the faster to put it out. Wrath must not lie in bed306 with two such bedfellows; nor must they part beds for wrath’s sake. So that this fire may be quenched the sooner, they must both strive to be the first to offer reconciliation. The glory belongs to those who begin first, for they are most properly the blessed peacemakers.307 Not to accept peace when it is offered is worse than heathenish; but when wrath is kindled, to seek reconciliation is the duty of a Christian, and a grace that comes from above.

4. Neither children, nor servants, nor anyone else in the family must be308 backed by the one against the other. The husband’s siding with anyone in the house against his wife, or the wife’s against her husband, is a common cause of contention between man and wife.

5. They must refrain from taunting one another309 with the husbands or wives of other persons, or with their own former husbands or wives (if they have had any before). Comparisons of this kind are very odious. They stir up much anger and cause great contentions.

6. Above all they must beware of rash and unjust jealousy,310 which is the bane of marriage, and the greatest cause of discontent that can arise between man and wife. Jealous persons are ready to pick quarrels and to look for occasions of discord: they will take every word, look, action and gesture in the worst sense, and so take offense where none is given. Once jealousy is kindled, it is like a flaming fire that can hardly be put out.311 It makes the party whom it possesses implacable.

7. In all things that are consistent with a good conscience they must endeavor to please one another, and each312 of them must allow their own will to be crossed rather than cause discontent to the other. Saint Paul notes this as a common313 mutual duty belonging to them both, and expresses their care for it by a word that signifies more than ordinary314 care, and implies a dividing of the mind into various thoughts, casting this way and that way and every way how best to please the other.

§. 13. Of contentions between man and wife.

Contrary to mutual peace are contentions between man and wife. They are all too frequent in most families, and by them315 the common good is much hindered. Discord between man and wife in a house is like contention between the master and the pilot in a ship: is not great danger and much injury justly to be feared from it? We heard before that a man is like a haven to his wife, and she to him. Now we find by experience that if the haven is stormy, it is much more troublesome and dangerous to the sailor than the wide sea. Therefore let man and wife be of the same mind toward one another as Abraham was toward Lot, and when occasions of discord arise, say, “Let there be no strife between you and me, for we are man and wife: no longer two, but one flesh.”

§. 14. Of husbands and wives dwelling together.

From a mutual affection of love comes a mutual provident care in husband and wife for one another. In handling it we will first note the means by which their mutual provident care may be better carried out and shown, and then the matter with which it must be concerned. The means, in one word, is cohabitation. For it is a duty that man and wife dwell together. The phrase used in setting out the woman’s creation (he built a woman, which hints at the setting up of316 a family) implies as much. So does the law of marriage, by which a man is commanded to “leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife,” that is, to go out of his father’s house and dwell with his wife. And so does this phrase (“forget317 your father’s house”), taken from the duty of a wife and applied mystically to the church. Saint Peter expressly charges husbands318 to “dwell with their wives,” and Saint Paul lays it as319 a charge on both husbands and wives not to leave one another, but to dwell together, even though one of them is an unbeliever. Surely it was conscience of this duty that made the320 Levite go after his wife, who had gone away from him, to bring her home again; and that made Jacob’s321 wives leave their father’s house and go with their husband.322 The word in which Saint Peter sums up this duty is a title reserved for a husband, and a corresponding title is reserved for a wife: and the derivation of our two usual English words (husband, housewife) is not much different.

The power which each has over the other’s body, and323 the advantage which they give to Satan by living apart (both of which are expressly noted, 1 Cor 7:4, 5), show the necessity of this duty; and the many benefits that come from it further urge its rightness. By husbands’ and324 wives’ dwelling together all marriage duties are better performed; mutual love is better bred, preserved and increased; the good gifts of each are better observed by the other; better help and relief are given by each to the other; and in short they are made more able to do good to one another, and to receive good from one another. Why then should they have any mind to live apart, unless they are forced by extraordinary occasions, such as captivity, close imprisonment, contagious sickness and the like? These are no faults of theirs, but crosses to be borne with grief; and earnest prayer, together with all other good means, is to be used to bring them together again. Indeed, if the imprisonment, banishment or other such absence325 is such that one may come to the other if they will, the party who is free ought to go to the other, at least if that other asks for it.

§. 15. Of the reasons for which man and wife may live apart for a time.

Question. May there be any just causes for man and wife willingly to live apart?

Answer. There neither can nor ought to be any cause for utterly forsaking one another, which is a kind of326 desertion. But there may be just causes for living apart for a time, such as:

1. Weighty and urgent affairs which concern the good of the church or commonwealth: as when a man is sent out to war, or on an embassy (in which case, though he may take his wife with him, he is not necessarily bound to, especially if the place he is sent to is far off, the journey there difficult and dangerous, and his stay there not long). When Reuben, Gad,327 and half the tribe of Manasseh crossed over the Jordan to help their brethren in their battles against the Canaanites, they left their wives behind them in their families.328 When Uriah went to war, he left his wife at home. And329 when Moses was to bring Israel out of Egypt, his wife stayed at her father’s house.

2. The main duties of their particular calling: as of sailors, who must often be at sea; merchants who trade in other countries; lawyers who attend the public courts of justice; courtiers, who in their months or quarters attend on their prince; attendants of women recovering from childbirth and of sick persons; and other nurses.

Provided always that in these and other such cases there is330 a joint and mutual consent of both parties. For if man and wife must not deprive one another for a time to give themselves to fasting and prayer “except by mutual consent,” much less may they live apart for any time, for lighter reasons, without331 consent. Provided also that they take no delight in living apart, but are rather grieved that they are forced to do so; and that, as evidence of this, they take every occasion they can to show their longing for one another by letters, messages, tokens and other such kindnesses, and return with all the speed they can. No distance or absence ought to lessen their mutual love in the least.

§. 16. Of the error of papists about a man and wife’s separation.332

Contrary to the duty of cohabitation is the doctrine of the papists, in which they teach that

Separation may be made between man and wife for many causes, from bed or cohabitation, for a certain or uncertain time. The Council of Trent boldly pronounces anathema on those who say the church errs in this. If the many causes which they allege besides adultery are well weighed, we shall find them wholly without warrant from God’s word.333 They bring them under two heads: 1. Mutual consent. 2. Demerit.

By consent (they say) of both married parties, in order to attain a greater and more perfect state, a consummated marriage may be loosed from bed and cohabitation.

Answer. 1. In marriage there is a covenant of God (Prov 2:17) as well as of the two parties: the consent of the parties, therefore, is not sufficient to break it.

2. No state in this world can be greater or more perfect than is fitting for married persons. Adam and Eve in their best state were married; and now “marriage is honorable in all.”334

3. The states which they count more perfect are either such as are not in man’s power (as perpetual self-control), or such as may be carried out as well by married persons as by single persons (as ecclesiastical offices), at least if they are such as are warranted by God’s word. High priests and other priests, all sorts of Levites, extraordinary prophets and apostles were married. What offices are greater than these?

The causes which, they say, make a separation for demerit are: 1. Adultery. 2. Departing from the Catholic faith. 3. Soliciting or driving to sin.

Concerning335 adultery, we do not deny that it gives just cause for divorce; but we also say (as336 we have good warrant from Christ’s words) that it is the only cause of just divorce. For to make a separation for departing from the Catholic faith337 is directly contrary to the doctrine of Saint Paul and Saint Peter, 1 Cor 7:12, 13, 14. 1 Pet 3:1.

As for soliciting and driving to sin, though it may be a cause to move a husband or a wife to walk more warily and338 wisely, and in extremity to avoid each other’s company for a time, or to complain to the magistrate for relief (who may see fit to put the offending person in prison, or else keep them apart in some other way until the offender is reclaimed and brought to a better mind), yet it is no sufficient cause to dissolve marriage finally with respect to bed and cohabitation.

They urge that if the right eye causes one to stumble, it must be plucked out.

Answer. 1. That is only a metaphor, and may be applied in various other ways.

2. The words are to be taken not absolutely but by way of comparison: rather pluck it out than be made to stumble by it.

3. Plucking out, applied to the point in hand, may be done in many other ways than by dissolving marriage.

4. That general prohibition (“anyone who divorces his wife339 … brings adultery upon her”), limited only by the exception of fornication, admits neither this nor any other such cause for dissolving marriage.

§. 17. Of husbands’ and wives’ unlawfully absenting themselves from one another.

Contrary also to the duty of cohabitation named above is the practice of many men who, living themselves in one place (say, at London), send their wives off to some country house, and there even cage them up like hawks, never caring to come to them; and they are merriest when their wives are farthest off. If their wives live at home, they will be away, taking their meals and their lodging where their wives cannot know. Their own house is like a prison to them: they are not well except when they are out of it. Of the same wicked notion and practice are many wives who, for no other reason than sheer looseness, eager in pursuing their pleasures and satisfying their lusts, gad out of their own houses by day, lie out of them by night, and stay in other company days and nights together; or at least are glad when their husbands have occasion to be away from home: not unlike the loose woman whom Solomon describes, Prov 7:10, etc. I speak of matters too famous, or rather infamous. I wish there were no just cause to rebuke this looseness. But let those who desire to approve themselves to God or man beware of these heinous and worse than heathenish vices. “Though you prostitute yourself, O Israel, may Judah340 avoid such guilt!”

Those come too near to the unlawful separation named above341 who, though they both live in one house, yet make that house like two houses by estranging themselves from one another: the man staying in one end of it, his wife in another. So they have separate rooms, separate tables, separate servants, everything separate. Or if the smallness of their house will not allow them to divide the other rooms like this, they will still have separate bedrooms, or at least separate beds: so that whoever calls them bedfellows only gives them a false name. In this way they rob each other of that due benevolence, the marriage duty which they owe one another; they expose themselves to the devil’s snares; they estrange their hearts more and more from one another; and they deprive themselves of the mutual comforts and helps which they might give to and receive from one another through the fellowship of marriage.

Caring for Each Other’s Souls

The Second Treatise, Part II: Of Their Common Duties · §§. 18–28

§. 18. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual prayers.

The matter with which the mutual provident care of husbands and wives ought to be concerned is, in general, the good of one another: that each of them should do for the other what Solomon applies in particular to a wife, namely, “good and not harm all342 the days of” their life. Now the good of man extends to his soul, body, good name, and goods.

A general duty tending to the good of all these is prayer.343 Peter requires such conduct of man and wife toward one another that their prayers may “not be hindered.” By this he takes it for granted that prayer is a mutual duty which one owes to the other; and Isaac performed this duty for his wife.344 In this, man and wife may be helpful to each other in all things needful to either of them: for it is the means which God in wisdom345 has sanctified for obtaining every needful blessing for ourselves or others. Many count it only a slight duty and of little use; but the truth is that to perform it rightly, in truth and faith, is both difficult in the doing and powerful in the effect. It is the best duty that one can perform for another, and the one that should least be neglected. We heard before that Isaac prayed for his wife; and to show the good he did her by it, it is noted that “the Lord heard his prayer,” so that she, being346 “barren” before, by that means “conceived.” All the medicine in the world could not have done her so much good.347 “At all times,” therefore,348 “without ceasing,” this duty is to be performed. Whenever man and wife make any prayer, they must be mindful of one another in it. Yes, and they must often purposely take occasion to make prayers specially for one another, and that both when apart and also in each other’s presence.

This latter especially concerns the husband, who is like a priest to his wife, and ought to be her mouth to God when the two of them are together. Yet I do not doubt that the wife may pray in her husband’s presence when the two of them are alone, either for trial (so that he may know her ability and gift in that kind) or for help (if the wife is much better able to perform that duty than the man is, as many wives are). Not without cause, therefore, have I counted this among the common mutual duties.

§. 19. Of the things for which husbands and wives are to pray alone.

There are various needful blessings which husbands and wives are to pray for that belong only to themselves, and are most fitting to be mentioned in private prayer between themselves, such as

1. That as the two of them are one flesh, so they may also be one spirit: that their hearts may be as one, knit together by a true, spiritual, marital love; always delighting in one another, ever helpful to one another, and ready with all willingness and cheerfulness to perform all those duties which they owe to one another.

2. That their marriage bed may be sanctified; and that, as it is by God’s ordinance, so it may remain to them, through their right use of it, a bed “undefiled.” There is nothing else for which mutual prayer in private between man and wife is more needful; and all the more because of the natural heat of lust which is in most people. If this is not assuaged by prayer (the best means for that purpose), it may prove a defilement349 of the undefiled bed, and man and wife may become adulterers to one another. As other things, so this also is “sanctified by the word … and prayer.” The word gives a warrant and direction for its use; prayer both seasons it and obtains a blessing on it.

3. That they may have children, and such as may be heirs of salvation and live in this world to their own and others’ good: that they may be comely and well-proportioned children, not idiots in understanding, nor monsters in bodily shape, nor yet wicked and infamous in their lives. That could not but be a grief to their parents, and might also open the mouths of the wicked against them.

4. That God would give them a sufficiency of this world’s goods, and other good means to nourish, nurture and settle their children well; and enough for the support of their family, and of the condition in which God sets them.

5. That such needful gifts and graces as are lacking in either of them may be worked in them, and such vices and infirmities as they are subject to may be corrected.

These and many other such things give man and wife occasion in a special way to pray for one another, and with one another.

§. 20. Of husbands’ and wives’ hateful curses and wishes against one another.

Contrary to that holy and heavenly duty of prayer are those dreadful and hellish imprecations and curses which commonly pass out of the mouths of many husbands and wives against one another (and that many times on very slight occasions), cursing the day that they ever knew one another, and wishing that one of them had been under the ground before they came together. These and similar curses are most hateful in any man’s mouth, but more than most hateful in the mouths of man and wife against one another.

Many who for outward shame refrain from belching out such rotten, stinking speech make little conscience of wishing the same in their hearts. If a husband is at all harsh, and a wife shrewish; or if through sickness or some other such occasion they seem burdensome to each other; or if some dislike of the one arises in the heart of the other; or if their hearts are set on others; or if the survivor is to carry away the goods and lands, their hearts will be filled with a thousand wishes for one another’s death. Yes, many times those who have very good husbands or wives, without any show of reason (only through an inward corruption of their heart and the malicious prompting of Satan, not recognizing their own good), are ready to wish they were in heaven. By this they make a pretense of the eternal bliss of the one for whom they wish it, whereas in truth their only desire is to be loosed and freed from them. God often deals with such wicked wishers (and so shows how hateful such wishes are to him). For sometimes, according to their wish, he takes away good husbands and wives from those who are evil; and when they are gone he makes their loss so keenly felt that those ungodly wishers repent of their rash wishes (as we say) in every vein of their heart. Yes, to make their misery all the greater, he gives them such sour and perverse husbands and wives in the place of those good ones (for a better seldom comes) that they are forced with many deep sighs and groans to wish (but all in vain) their former wives and husbands350 alive again, and so to prove the proverb true, A good thing is not so well recognized by enjoying it as by lacking it. Sometimes again God in anger crosses their wishes, and first takes away those who wished the death of others; or else he prolongs the life of both, to351 their greater vexation.

§. 21. Of husbands’ and wives’ neglect of mutual prayer.

The very neglect of mutual prayer by husbands and wives for each other is also a sin contrary to the duty of prayer named above. If all who are guilty of it were as well known to man as to God, how many more unkind husbands and wives, careless of one another’s good, would be noted than are now! Rare are those husbands and wives who have their set times to pray alone together, if they ever pray for one another at all. Though in outward courtesies they may seem very kind, and in the outward things of this world very provident, yet if they do not pray for one another, they are neither kind nor provident. Hearty, fervent, frequent prayer is the greatest token of kindness, and the best part of provident care, that there can be.

§. 22. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual care for one another’s salvation.

From the general duty of prayer, which is profitable for all things, I come to the particular branches of a man and wife’s352 mutual provident care. And I will begin first with what is to be sought first, the good of one another’s soul. The apostle suggests that this is a thing to be sought after where he says, “How do you know, wife, whether you will353 SAVE your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will SAVE your wife?” Peter354 charges wives to do their best to “win” their husbands; and Paul355 sets before husbands the pattern of Christ’s love, which had special regard356 to the soul and its salvation. So this is a mutual duty belonging to them both, which Peter further implies where he calls them “fellow heirs of the grace of life.”

It is the greatest good that one can possibly do for another, to be a means of furthering his salvation. And there is357 nothing that can more soundly and firmly knit the heart of one to another than to be a means of it.

§. 23. Of husbands’ and wives’ care to win one another, when one of them is not called.

So that the salvation of the soul may be better brought about, regard must be had to the present and particular condition of husband or wife. If one is a believer and the other is not, the believer must use every means possible to draw the other to believe also. If both are believers, their mutual care must be to edify one another in their most holy faith.

For the first, it is the main aim of Peter’s exhortation to358 believing wives about their conduct, to draw their unbelieving husbands to the true faith. His phrase (“they359 may be won,” or gained), as it refers in general to the salvation of their souls, so in particular it refers to their first conversion. Now if this duty belongs to a wife, much more does it belong to a husband, who is appointed a head to his wife, and a savior. To this end Paul advises believing husbands and wives who360 are married to unbelievers to live with them.

For what a woeful thing it is that two who in this world361 are so closely linked together as to make one flesh should in the world to come be as far separated from one another as heaven is from hell! This indeed will happen to many: for Christ has expressly foretold that of “two” who were “in one bed” together (and who are more fitly described by this phrase than man and wife, who are most usually called bedfellows?) “one will be taken” (to mercy and glory), “and the other left” (forsaken, left to endless and unrelieved torture and torment). But though it is foretold that it will turn out this way with many a couple, yet our care must be, and that with our utmost power,362 to prevent it, both in ourselves and in our bedfellow.

If it pleases the Lord to give such a blessing to the endeavor of a husband or wife as to make it a means of the conversion of their bedfellow, then the party converted will both love the other wholeheartedly and also heartily bless God (as there is just cause) that they were ever so closely linked together.

This duty of winning one another is to be applied to those who are married not only to outright infidels, but also to papists or other such idolaters, to atheists or any other profane persons, to heretics, separatists, schismatics, or any who do not believe rightly.

§. 24. Of husbands’ and wives’ edifying one another.

The second duty tending to the soul’s salvation is that two believers, being married together, endeavor mutually to build one another up more and more.363 One Christian owes this duty to another: much more do man and wife. “See to it,”364 says the apostle, “that no one falls away from the grace of God.” If no one, then neither wife nor husband.

A spiritual edifying of one another is the best use which365 we can make (and ought to make) of those “joints”366 and “bonds” by which we are knit to one another. By virtue of them “the body”367 (namely the mystical body of Christ) “grows and builds itself up,” and “grows as God causes it to grow.”368 Now since the bond of marriage is the firmest of all, and the one by which we are most closely knit together, by virtue of what bond should we edify one another, if not by virtue of the marriage bond?

§. 25. Of husbands’ and wives’ hindering sin in one another.

Two things are required for spiritual edification.

One concerns the hindrances to growth in grace.

The other its helps.

The hindrances to grace are all kinds of sins. Sin is to grace as water is to fire: it slakes its heat, and if it is poured on without stint, it will put it out entirely. Because of this there ought to be a mutual care in husbands and wives both to prevent sin before it is committed, and also to make what redress they can after it is committed.

That it is a mutual duty for husbands and wives, as far369 as they can, to prevent sin in one another is evident from the reason which the apostle uses to keep them from depriving one another, in these words, “so that Satan will not tempt you+.”370 For out of the aim and matter of those words this general doctrine may be gathered: husbands and wives ought to take care to keep one another from the temptations of Satan, that is, from sin, to which all his temptations tend. Rebekah371 performed the duty of a good wife in keeping Isaac from blessing Esau; if he had done it, he would have sinned against372 God’s express word. Though she failed in the manner of doing it, yet her end was good.

As the love they owe to one another, so the care which they373 ought to have for themselves requires as much. For sin provokes God’s wrath, his wrath sends down vengeance, and the vengeance which falls on the husband can hardly miss the wife, nor that which falls on the wife miss the husband; and that because of their close union. Though it does not fall on both their heads, yet it cannot but greatly affect, and even afflict, the party who escapes. The wives of those rebels who were374 swallowed up alive in the wilderness perished in the same way as their husbands. For those who are as close as husbands and wives, and do not do what they can to prevent one another’s sins, make themselves accessories to them.

For the better carrying out of this duty, husbands and wives375 must be watchful over one another, and observe what sins either of them is given to, or what occasions are offered to draw either of them into sin. If either of them is hot-tempered or prone to sudden anger, the other must endeavor to take away all occasions of offense. And if both should be touchy and quick to wrath, when the one sees the other moved first, the party whose anger is not yet stirred ought all the more to be settled and composed to all meekness and patience, so that the whole household is not set on fire by both being provoked together. If either of them is given to drunkenness, covetousness or any other sin, the other ought by wise and gentle persuasion to keep them (as much as they can) from those sins. Yes, they may also get others who are discreet and able to dissuade them, or use whatever other good means they can for that purpose.

§. 26. Of husbands’ and wives’ redressing sin in one another.

When either husband or wife has fallen into any sin, it is a mutual duty for the other to use whatever remedy there may be for that sin: as if one of them were wounded, the other must take care to heal that wound. Abigail376 performed her duty in this kind when, after she had heard what churlish treatment her husband gave to David’s servants, she hurried to carry plenty of provisions to David, and humbled herself before him, and so moved David to assuage his wrath. Yes, she also took a fitting time to tell her husband his fault, and the danger into which he brought himself by it.

More directly, and with better success, Jacob redressed the superstition, or rather idolatry, of his wife Rachel, as may be gathered by comparing Gen 31:19, 34 with Genesis 35:2, 4.

A brother in general must not allow sin to lie on his brother;377 much less may husband or wife allow it to lie on the other.

“You must not harbor hatred against your brother” (says the law) “and allow378 sin to lie on him.” To do this, then, is a token and fruit of hatred. If a husband should see his wife, or a wife her husband, lying in the fire or the water, ready to be burned or drowned, and not give their best help to pull them out, might they not justly be thought to hate them? But sin is like fire and water, which will burn and drown men in perdition.

This duty may be performed by meek instructions, pithy persuasions, gentle reproofs; yes, and by the help of some379 good minister, or other discreet and faithful friend.

§. 27. Of husbands’ and wives’ furthering the growth of grace in each other.

So much for preventing and redressing the hindrances of grace. To this must be added a furthering of its growth, which man and wife must mutually endeavor to bring about in one another. The care which Elkanah had to take his380 wives with him to the tabernacle of the Lord year by year shows that his desire was to uphold them in the fear of God. Yes, the gifts and portions which he used to give them at that time imply the care he had to encourage them to keep on serving the Lord. It was without question the main end at which the Shunammite aimed in381 providing lodging for the prophet, that both she and her husband might be built up in grace.

This duty may be better carried out by the following means.382

1. By taking notice of the beginning and the least measure of grace, and approving of it.

2. By frequent conversation about the things that concern it: mutually putting questions to one another about them, and answering them.

3. By their mutual practice and example: making themselves a pattern of piety to each other.

4. By performing exercises of religion together, such as praying, singing psalms, reading the word, and the like.

5. By maintaining holy and religious exercises in the family.383 Though this duty belongs especially to the husband, yet the wife must remind her husband of it if he forgets it, and stir him up if he is reluctant. So did the good Shunammite, 2 Kgs 4:9, 10. No man’s persuasion in this kind can prevail so much with a man as his wife’s.

6. By stirring up one another to go to the house of God,384 to hear the word, partake of the sacrament, and conscientiously perform all the parts of God’s public worship.

There is great need that husbands and wives should endeavor to further the growth of grace in each other, because we are all so prone to fall away and grow cold, just as385 water does if the fire goes out and more fuel is not put under it.386 And of all others, husbands and wives may be most helpful in this, because they can soonest spot the beginning of decline through their close and continual familiarity together.

§. 28. Of the sins of husbands and wives contrary to a mutual care for one another’s salvation.

The vices contrary to that general mutual duty of husbands and wives in furthering the salvation of one another, and to the particular branches included under it, are many, such as

1. A careless neglect of it: when husbands and wives387 so mind earthly things that they think it enough if they are provident for one another in the things of this life. Most who live on this earth are guilty of this, and among others, even many of those who have the name of very good and kind husbands and wives. But whatever the opinion of others about them may be, the truth is that if they fail in this point, they go no further than the very heathen have done, and their kindness may be like the ape’s kindness, which causes death.

2. The unworthy walk and unchristian conduct of a believer388 who is married to one who does not believe: by this the unbeliever is kept from embracing the gospel, and made to dislike and detest it all the more. If a popish or profane husband is married to a wife who professes the truth of the gospel, and she is stubborn, proud, wanton, waspish, wasteful, or given to any other such vices, will he not be ready on that account to rail against the religion she professes, and utterly protest against it? So also a popish or profane wife, if she is married to such a husband.

3. Negligence in observing one another’s disposition or conduct:389 by which it comes about that they do not hold back or restrain one another from running into any sin, but show themselves such husbands and wives to one another as Eli showed himself a father to his sons. From this it came about that God’s severe vengeance fell on the neck of both the one and the other. Pilate’s wife, though a heathen woman, will rise up in judgment against many such wives, for she did what she could to keep390 her husband from shedding innocent blood.

4. A flattering indulgence of one another’s whims, and seeking391 mutually to please one another in all things, without regard to good or evil. Scripture calls such people392 men-pleasers. So it comes about that husbands and wives are so far from drawing one another away from sin that the better rather yields to the worse, and both run into393 evil: as Adam was persuaded by his wife to transgress against God’s express charge, and wise Solomon was drawn by his wives into idolatry, 1 Kgs 11:4, and Sapphira consented to the sacrilege of Ananias her husband, Acts 5:2.

5. An undue fear of offending one another by Christian instruction,394 admonition, reproof and the like. Many who are often moved in conscience to make known to their husbands and wives the sins in which they live, and the danger in which they lie because of them, nevertheless refrain and hold back from doing so through careless and causeless fear.

6. An impious and envious disposition, by which many husbands395 and wives are moved to mock and scoff at the holy zeal and eagerness which they observe in their bedfellows: as Michal, who likened David to a fool, or396 a vulgar fellow, because he showed his zeal by dancing before the ark. In this way many nip the work of the Spirit in the very bud, and cause grace soon to wither. But cursed be that husband or wife who thus perverts the main end of their close union.
