Guarding Each Other’s Health, Reputation, and Property

The Second Treatise, Part II: Of Their Common Duties · §§. 29–39

§. 29. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual care over one another’s body.

After the good of the soul follows the good of the body, in which husband and wife must show their provident care for each other, and do what lies in them to further the welfare of one another’s person, and to nourish and cherish one another’s body. The apostle lays down this duty under the comparison of a body, which he calls flesh, saying, “No man ever yet hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it.”397 Now man and wife are “one flesh.”398 The apostle applies this duty in particular to husbands. At the first institution of marriage it was applied in particular to the wife, whom God made to be “a helper suitable for” man.399 So it is a mutual duty belonging to both. It seems that Rebekah400 was so attentive to Isaac in this respect that she could readily make “tasty food” for him, such as he loved.

This duty extends to every condition, both of prosperity and adversity, of health and sickness. For they mutually covenant and promise as much when they are first joined together in marriage: “I take you,” each says to the other, “for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish.” Therefore they ought mutually both to rejoice in one another’s welfare, and also in all distress to help and comfort each other, putting their shoulders under one another’s burden, and helping to ease one another as much as they can. What Solomon said of a friend and a brother may fitly be applied in this case to husband and wife: “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.”401 That is, a trusty and faithful friend is constant in his goodwill, and ready to perform all duties of kindness at any time, whether in prosperity or adversity. The change of outward condition makes no alteration in his loving affection and friendly conduct. Yes, he seems to be as it were born and brought forth for the time of trouble and affliction, because then his provident care and tender affection are most clearly shown. Of all friends, none ought to be more caring, none more faithful to one another, than man and wife. How much, then, ought they to love at all times, and, if any trial comes to either of them, the other to conduct himself so that it may truly be said they were joined together for adversity!

In this way they will confirm the truth of that which moved God to create mankind male and female, namely that “it is not good for the man to be alone,”402 but that it was rather good, that is, needful, profitable and strengthening, for man and woman to be together. In this respect the wise man says, “He who finds a wife finds a good thing”;403 and by the rule of relation we may infer, she who finds a husband finds a good thing.

§. 30. Of husbands’ and wives’ reluctance to help one another in time of need.

Contrary to this duty is a certain lack of natural affection in various husbands and wives, who greatly begrudge providing the things that are needful for one another. The man commonly thinks the cost too great, the woman thinks the pains too much. They are disposed toward one another as if they were mere strangers; indeed, many strangers will be more ready to perform, and more cheerful in performing, needful duties (as occasion is offered) than such heartless husbands and wives. If a little sickness or some other such trial falls on one of them, the other thinks, “No one ever had such a burden,” and by their discontent they make the burden much heavier than it would otherwise be: just as when two oxen are in one yoke and one holds back, the pulling is made much harder for the other. In this way they pervert one of the principal ends of marriage, which is to be a continual comfort and404 help to each other, and to ease the burdens of one another; in which respect they are made yokefellows. Job’s wife405 by her heartless conduct toward him in his affliction greatly added to his misery. When he stood most in need of her help, she gave him the least. It appears from Job’s complaint of her, in these words, “My breath is alien to406 my wife,” that she altogether neglected him in his misery. The common saying of many, after a husband or wife who has long lain sick has died, betrays their lack of natural affection. Their saying is this: “If my husband” (or wife) “had died so much sooner, I would have saved so much money.” What does this suggest but that they would have been content for their husband (or wife) to die sooner, so that they might have saved the more?

§. 31. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual regard for one another’s good name.

The provident care of husbands and wives ought further to extend to the reputation and good name of one another. The good name of the wife ought to be as dear to the husband, and that of the husband to the wife, as their own.407 The great regard that Joseph had for the reputation of Mary, his betrothed wife, made him think of putting her away secretly when he observed her to be with child and did not know by whom: for he was unwilling “to make her a public example.”408 The same regard moved Bathsheba409 to send secretly to David and tell him that she was with child. The commendation which the good husband410 (noted by Solomon) gives of his wife, being approved by the Holy Spirit, shows how man and wife ought in that respect to honor each other; and that on good grounds. For

1. A good name is a most precious thing: “better than fine perfume,”411 which gives a sweet scent, and412 “more desirable than great riches.”413

2. So closely are husbands and wives joined together that the good name of the one cannot but tend to the honor and reputation of the other; so in this they seek their own honor also.

§. 32. Of husbands’ and wives’ preventing each other’s discredit.

For direction in this, let us consider how this duty may be414 performed, and how it may be shown.

For the better performing of it, care must be taken both to prevent and redress a bad name, and also to gain and preserve a good name.

To prevent a bad name, regard must be had to these three things following:415

  1. What one says of the other, and how.
  2. What hearing they give to things reported by others.
  3. What judgment they pass on one another.

For the first, husbands and wives must in no case delight to416 reveal to others, and spread abroad, the infirmities and imperfections of one another, or anything that may tend to the discredit of either of them; but rather cover and conceal them as much as they can with a good conscience. It is expressly said that Joseph, “being a just man,”417 labored to conceal the blemish which he imagined to be in his wife; so this may stand with justice. Yes, it is also a part of love, for “love covers over a multitude of sins.”418

For the second, husbands and wives must not have their419 ears wide open to hear every tale and report that is brought to one against the other, but rather show themselves displeased and offended with those who are ready to relate things of evil report. If a husband or wife shows a willingness to listen for tales and reports about one another, the devil will stir up instruments enough to fill their heads with tales, and those for the most part both frivolous and forged. Not only strangers, but children, servants, and those who are of the same household will always be telling some tale or other, to curry favor, as we say. But an utter dislike of such flattering talebearers will take away their occasion for telling untrue or trivial reports.

For the third, the judgment and verdict which husbands420 and wives give of one another must be either very charitable or very sparing. If one hears some notorious crime of the other reported, they must not be overhasty or quick to judge and condemn, not even though they think they see some evidence of it, but rather suspend their judgment. This seems to have been the mind of Joseph: though he observed Mary to be with421 child, yet he would not at once judge her to be a notorious adulteress, or condemn her as a hypocrite, unworthy to live, and therefore he would not make her a public example.

In brief, so that husbands and wives may be more sparing in judging one another, they must not rashly believe any evil report of one another, but rather suppress all slight suspicions as much as they can.

So that the judgment which they give of one another may be charitable, in judging they must carefully observe the properties of love, which are: 1. To interpret doubtful things in the better sense. 2. To mitigate, as far as truth and justice will allow, the faults which are evident. Michal422 offended against the first in a high degree, and was cursed. Abigail423 observed the latter, and was blessed.

§. 33. Of the wisdom of husbands and wives in redressing one another’s bad name.

To redress a bad name, husbands and wives must first give one another notice of the report that goes about concerning them, and endeavor424 to work in them both a sight and also a sense of those evils which are in the mouths of others. After notice is given, they must labor to bring them to repentance for the sins for which they are badly spoken of, and to a showing of repentance by doing things fitting for repentance: that is, by a zealous and conscientious practice of such virtues as are directly contrary to the vices for which they were spoken evil of. It may with good probability be gathered from the history of the Levite,425 whose wife played the whore, that he dealt with her in this way. And in this way Abigail endeavored to deal with her husband.426

§. 34. Of husbands’ and wives’ care in gaining one another’s good name.

To gain a good report, husbands and wives must427 First, take notice of the good qualities which are in one another, and, as one has occasion to speak of the other, make those good qualities the subject of their speech: as we428 heard it commended before in the husband of that wife whom Solomon describes.

Secondly, they must lend a willing and joyful ear to those who (so far as they can tell) truly and sincerely, without flattery or hypocrisy, speak anything in commendation of the one or the other: not thinking themselves dispraised (which is the notion of many) when their bedfellow is praised, but rather having their hearts all the more enlarged to praise God for bestowing on them such an excellent token and pledge of his favor.

Thirdly, they must imitate those good things which they see, or hear to be, in one another, and imitate them in such a way that those who knew both husband and wife beforehand may say, “She learned this from him,” or, “He learned this from her.”

§. 35. Of husbands’ and wives’ wisdom in preserving each other’s good name.

To preserve a good name, it will be fitting for a husband or429 wife wisely and at the right time to give one another notice of the good report that is raised of them, in order to provoke them both to give glory to God for it430 (as the apostle thanks God for the report which was spread abroad of the faith and love of the Colossians), and also to walk worthy of that good report (as the apostle, who had given great testimony of the generosity of the Corinthians, earnestly urges them to complete their generous gift: “Otherwise,” he says, “we … would be ashamed431 of this confident boasting”). For if those of whom a good report has once been raised decline, grow cold, fall back, or fall into notorious and scandalous sins, they will utterly extinguish and put out their good name among men, and turn it into an evil report, according to what Solomon says, “As dead flies bring a432 stench to the perfumer’s oil, so does a little folly to him who is esteemed for wisdom and honor.”433

§. 36. Of husbands’ and wives’ fellow feeling for one another’s reputation.

In the last place, to show a mutual provident care for one another’s good name, husbands and wives must be so moved by the report that goes about of either of them as if the report were of themselves. If the report is good, they must be glad of it and rejoice at it; if it is evil, they must be grieved, and troubled at it in a holy manner. In this way they will show a true sympathy and fellow feeling for one another’s reputation, according to that general rule of the apostle, “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.”434

§. 37. Of the vices contrary to that mutual care which man and wife should have for one another’s reputation.

The vices contrary to these duties concerning the good name of435 a husband and wife are, in general, two.

One is a readiness to disgrace and discredit one another,436 like Michal the wife of David,437 of whom we heard before. This is a hateful and detestable vice, which cannot stand with true marital love, but rather shows an utter dislike and a plain hatred of one another.

Husbands and wives discredit one another either by bringing on a bad name or by hindering a good name.

A bad name is brought on by the following means.

1. By spreading abroad one another’s infirmities: as when438 tattling gossips meet, their usual chatter is about their husbands, complaining of some vice or other in them. “My husband,” says one, “is covetous: I can hardly get anything from him: he makes me go dressed as nobody else does.” “And my husband,” replies another, “is so furious that no one knows how to speak to him.” So one after another goes on in this track, some revealing infirmities which should be concealed, others (which is worse) plainly slandering their husbands. In the same way husbands, when they meet with their boon companions, make their wives the common subject of all their talk, one accusing his wife of one vice, another his of another. There are two reasons why this vice (most detestable in itself) is made more hateful in a husband or a wife. 1. Because they know more of one another’s infirmities than anyone else does, so that if they are so evilly minded, they may discredit one another much more than anyone else can. 2. Because by their close union they are most bound to conceal and cover each other’s imperfections. Ham439 was cursed for revealing his father’s nakedness. But husbands and wives who do this deserve a more horrible curse.

2. By opening their ears to, and giving credence to, every slight440 report that anyone raises. More secret resentment of one against the other, and more open quarrels and contentions between them, commonly arise from this than from anything else.

3. By twisting and misinterpreting one another’s actions,441 words, yes, and thoughts also: taking everything in the worst sense.

4. By concealing from one another the common evil rumors442 which are raised about them, and are in every man’s mouth. Of all others, bedfellows are most fit to disclose such things to one another, and most bound to do it: most fit, because of their mutual familiarity; most bound, because of their close union.

Many husbands and wives hinder one another’s good443 name by envying the good report that is made of the other, and contradicting it, as if the credit of the one must necessarily turn to the discredit of the other. Thus, as water quenches hot iron, so this envious disposition is a means to extinguish the heat of fame, and to put out the glorious light of a good name. And as by this they impair the reputation and honor of one another, so they monstrously discredit and dishonor themselves.

The other general vice of this kind is a careless disregard,444 or plain neglect, of one another’s reputation: when the husband is in no way moved by any report that goes about of his wife, nor the wife by any of the husband, but, as if they were mere strangers to one another, they pass by all reports made of one another. What mutual love can there be in such people? However their hands have been joined together, surely their hearts were never united; so that it would have been better if they had never known one another, unless the Lord afterwards knits their hearts and unites their affections more closely and firmly together.

§. 38. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual provident care of the goods of the family.

There remains yet one thing more about which husbands445 and wives ought to show a mutual provident care for each other, and that is the goods of this world. Although the husband, while he lives with his wife, has the truest ownership of them and the greatest title to them, yet I refer this to those mutual duties which man and wife owe to each other, in three respects.

First, because in conscience they belong to the wife’s use as well as to the husband’s.

Secondly, because the wife is appointed by God’s providence a joint governor of the family with the husband, and in that respect ought to be a help in providing such a sufficiency of the goods of this world as is needful for the condition in which God has set them, and for the charge which God has committed to them.

Thirdly, because the wife, if she outlives the husband, ought to have such a portion of those goods as is fitting for her place and charge.

In these respects we see that it is needful, indeed a binding duty, that husband and wife, even in mutual regard for one another, be as provident as they can be with a good conscience in getting, keeping and disposing of sufficient goods and riches for one another’s mutual good. Concerning the husband’s duty in this respect, no question is raised. The practice of all good husbands mentioned in Scripture, the care of providing for their own446 enjoined on them, their place and office as their wives’ head, with many other such arguments (of which we will speak more distinctly when we come to set out the particular duties of husbands), prove as much. The greatest question concerns the wife, whether she is bound to take any care about the goods. But if the Scripture is thoroughly searched, we will find proof enough to show that she too is bound to it. For, first, the general end at which God aimed in making the woman (namely, to be “a helper”447 to man) implies as much: for in this she may be a very great help, as we will soon see in various particulars. 2. That general property attributed to a wife, to be “a good thing,”448 confirms as much: for what is profitable is called good; and it is one respect in which a wife is called a good thing, that by her provident care and diligence she may bring much profit to her husband. Therefore in this respect, among others, the good wife whom Solomon describes is said449 to bring her husband “good” all the days of her life: for by her industry and provident care she so preserved and increased his goods that “the heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value.”450 If the particular actions by which that good wife is described are well noted, we may easily observe that she was a special help to her husband, even in his outward condition. From all this we may infer these two points. First, that this provident care about outward, temporal goods is lawful, not unbecoming a Christian man or woman. Secondly, that it is a mutual duty belonging to both husband and wife.

For the first: how needful the goods of this world are for the preservation of life and health, the standing of the family, the good of church and commonwealth, the relief of the poor, and similar uses, no man can be ignorant. God has given them as blessings to his children, and that often in great abundance; and his children have accordingly been thankful for them. So a provident care about them is not unlawful, but very advisable and needful.

For the second: if there were not a joint care in this, the care and pains of the one might be altogether in vain. For suppose a husband is industrious, as Jacob451 was, and gets much abroad: if the wife, either by her lack of thrift, idleness, negligence or similar vices, allows what is brought home to be embezzled and wasted, or by her prodigality, love of finery or love of vain company consumes it herself, where will the profit of the husband’s pains be? Or on the other side, if a wife should be as hardworking and prosperous in getting as452 the good housewife mentioned before was, and the husband should waste it all away by card-playing, dicing, drinking, reveling or other such means, what fruit would remain of the wife’s provident care? In this mutual provident care of husband and wife, each of them must keep an eye on their own place. Affairs abroad belong most to the man, and are especially453 to be ordered by him; what the wife is especially to care for is the business of the house. For the apostle lays it down as a rule for wives (as we will declare more particularly hereafter) that they be “keepers at home”454 and “govern their households.”455 By this means they may be very profitable to each other.

§. 39. Of the vices contrary to the good provident care of husband and wife for the goods of the family.

Contrary to that duty are the following vices.

1. Covetousness, and excessive care for themselves: as456 when a husband so rakes and scrapes and hoards up for himself that he neither gives his wife as much as is457 fitting for her place while he lives with her, nor thinks of providing sufficient support for her if she outlives him, but rather thinks how to cheat her of what the law settles on her. Or when a wife secretly hoards up whatever she can get, either by her own industry or else by stealing from her husband: sometimes selling grain, wares, household goods or other such commodities so secretly that the husband will never know it; sometimes taking money out of his till, box, bag, chest or the like, so that either it will not be missed, or, if it is, it will not be known who had it. There are many who, distrusting their husbands’ provident care, or disliking them, or for some other ulterior motives, commit whatever they can get to the trust and keeping of others. By this it often comes about that they themselves, meeting with deceitful friends, are utterly cheated, simply because they dare not make their own fraud known. As covetousness is a hateful sin in itself, so it is made much more heinous by defrauding husband or wife, who ought to be as dear to each other as themselves.

2. Prodigality, and too lavish spending on themselves,458 and on the things most agreeable to their own corrupt appetite: as when husbands, without any moderation or measure, spend their goods abroad in hunting, hawking, card-playing, dicing, eating, drinking or the like, and allow their wives to go in need at home; and yet they took wives whom they undertook to support, and for that reason received their portion. Or when wives bring their husbands into debt, and weaken, if not utterly overthrow, their estate by gorgeously decking and adorning their houses, by fine and costly clothing, by dainty fare, by gadding about to gossip, and the like. Many wives are so violent in this that if their desire and whim are not satisfied, their husbands will have no rest (of course they brought a portion, and maintained they must and will be; it does not matter whether their husbands’ estate can bear it or not), so much so that many are forced knowingly, for the sake of peace, to let their estate sink. O foolish and wretched wives! How little they consider that they were married to do their husbands good, and not harm, all the days of their life! Is this to be a help to man? Or rather, is it not utterly to thwart God’s counsel and pervert his purpose? Can we think that God will hold back, and not be avenged on them? Yet God will be avenged much more on the husbands named above, because of that image of himself which he has placed in them, and because of the place and authority in which he has set them. The apostle expressly says of them that each “is worse than an unbeliever”;459 and since that is so, they must look for the greater judgment.

3. Idleness, and a careless neglect of their estate. Many460 men spend day after day like a bird that flies up and down, as it happens, from tree to tree, from twig to twig. They go from place to place, but do not know for what end. As they meet with any company, so they stay as long as the company stays, and then look for other company, and are ready to go with anyone to the alehouse, tavern, playhouse, bowling alley or other such places. Many women also spend the whole morning lying in bed and dressing themselves, and the afternoon, as occasion offers, sitting idly at home or walking out to little purpose, only to wear away the time, paying little regard to their husbands’ estate, whether it increases or diminishes. Thus by the idleness and carelessness of husband and wife fair estates many times come to ruin, and both of them are brought to poverty and beggary.

Serving Together in Family Ministry

The Second Treatise, Part II: Of Their Common Duties · §§. 40–45

§. 40. Of husbands’ and wives’ joint care in governing the family.

So far I have set out such common duties as concern the husband and wife mutually, and are to be performed by each to the other. There are other common duties which they are both jointly bound to perform to other persons: either to members of the family, or to strangers coming to the family.

Concerning the members of the family: though there are some distinctive duties belonging to the master and some to the mistress, some to the father and some to the mother, of which we will speak in their due place, yet in general the government of the family and of its separate members belongs to both husband and wife (if, at least, they have a family). And it is a joint, common duty of theirs to be helpful to one another in it.

Objection. Since it is not necessarily required that a husband and wife should have a family to govern, for two may be married and have neither children nor servants (as many are) and yet be true husband and wife, why is this care of a family ranked among the duties of husband and wife?

Answer. 1. Because ordinarily, when two are married, they gather a family and are its governors. So though it fails in some particular cases, yet for the most part it holds.

2. Because the joint government of which I speak in this place is by virtue of the marriage bond. For if a man and a woman should live together in a house and, by mutual consent, have a joint authority and government, this would be very offensive to all who should know of it or hear of it. Nor would they be bound by any ordinance of God to be as helpful to one another as husband and wife, nor would the members of a family be so bound to subject themselves to both.

3. The duty of which I speak, though it is about the government of a family, yet concerns a husband as he is a husband, and a wife as she is a wife: namely, that by virtue of their marriage bond and close union they should be helpful to one another in well ordering the things of the family.

Whether the man ought to see to the good government of his house is a question beyond all question. He is the highest in the family; he has authority over all, and the charge of all is committed to him. He is like a king in his own house: as a king is to see that the land where he is king is well governed, so is he who is the chief ruler in a house. The duty which the apostle applies in particular to bishops and deacons belongs in general to all husbands:461 that each “must manage his own household well”; and again,462 that each be “a good manager of his children and of his own household.” The care of many husbands in this respect is commended in Scripture: that of Abram,463 of Jacob,464 of Joshua,465 of David,466 of the467 ruler at Galilee, and of many others. That the wife also ought to be a help to him in this is very evident. For the apostle expressly lays it to the charge of wives468 that they “govern their households.” Would the wise man have so highly commended a wife469 for governing her husband’s house well if it had not belonged to her? It is very likely that wise Abigail had a great hand in governing Nabal’s house: because the servants complained to her of Nabal’s churlishness; because she had the servants at her command, ready to do what she wanted of them; and also because she could so readily prepare such a store of provisions for David and his men as she did. That is why the wife is called mistress of the house,470 just as the husband is called master of the house.471

Objection. A woman is not to teach or to usurp authority over a man.472

Answer. 1. That branch about teaching refers to public assemblies and churches, in which she must not teach, but not to private families, in which she may and ought to teach. For Bathsheba473 taught Solomon. When Apollos474 was brought to the house of Aquila, Priscilla, the wife of Aquila, helped to explain to Apollos the way of God more accurately.

2. The other branch, concerning authority, does not refer to the inferior members of the family, over whom the wife of a household governor has authority, but only to the husband: if she takes any authority over him, she usurps it. Therefore neither this place of Scripture nor any other excludes the wife, considered jointly with the husband, from ruling and governing those in the family who are under them both.

2. Objection. This joint government of the wife greatly impairs the dignity and authority of the husband.

Answer. Not at all. For she is subordinate to her husband, and must rule others in such a way that she is subject to her husband, and does not command anything against his command (provided that his command is not against the Lord and his word). We see that in every state the king or highest governor has other magistrates under him, who have command over the subjects; and yet the king’s supreme authority is not in the least impaired by this, but rather is the better established, and he is the more honored. So it is in a family.475

Therefore let husbands and wives assist one another in this, for so they may be very helpful to one another and, by their mutual help in governing, bring much good to the family. The husband, aiding his wife by his help, adds much authority to her, and so ensures that she is not despised or lightly regarded. The wife by her help causes many things to be noticed, and so set right, which otherwise might never have been found out. For two eyes see more than one, especially when one of them is closer at hand and present, as the476 wife is in the house.

Besides, there are many things in governing a family well which are more fit for one to deal with than for the other. It is more fit for the husband to deal with the great and weighty affairs of the family (such as performing God’s worship, appointing and settling good orders, providing fitting house room and other necessities for the family, keeping children in awe when they grow477 older or become stubborn, ruling menservants, and the like). And it is more fit for the wife to deal with some lesser but very needful matters, such as nourishing and instructing children when they are young, adorning the house, ordering the provisions brought into the house, ruling maidservants, and the like. Yes, further, as the man especially is to perform the very acts of prayer, reading the word, catechizing and other such duties in the family, so the wife may be a great help: by putting her husband in mind both of the duty itself and of the time for performing it, and encouraging him to do it; by gathering the family together and exhorting them to be eager; by making herself an example to the rest through her diligent and reverent attention; by often urging and pressing on her children and servants such points of instruction as her husband has taught; yes, by praying, reading, teaching and performing such exercises herself, as far as she is able, when her husband is absent, or negligent and careless and will not do them himself, or perhaps is not able to do them; or, if she does not perform them herself, by getting someone else to perform them.

§. 41. Of the vices contrary to a joint care of governing the family.

The mind and practice of many, both husbands and wives,478 is contrary to this duty.

Many a husband, because the wife’s office is especially to479 stay at home, will hand over all government to the wife. He leaves it to her not only to order the things in the house, but also to bring in all needful things, to order and govern the children both young and old, yes, even to provide for them too, and to take in, put out and use all sorts of servants as she pleases. Yes, if servants are stubborn and defiant toward her, he will take no notice of it, nor bear to be told of it, much less give her his assistance, but lets her be disgraced and despised. As for religious duties, he will have nothing at all to do with them. Oh base-minded men, unworthy to be husbands and heads of wives! Shall your+ wives, who were made to be a help to you+, have no help from you+, no, not in those things which especially belong to your+ charge? Shall the weaker vessels bear all the burden? Certainly, as the man carries away the greatest reputation and honor when a family is well governed (though it is by the joint care and wisdom of his wife), so he lies most open to the judgment of God if its government is neglected, and through that neglect children and servants grow ungodly. Take as an instance Eli480 and David.481 For as in a commonwealth the greatest honor of good government, victorious battles, happy peace and prosperity, and the greatest dishonor and damage of the contrary, fall to the king, so it is with the man who is chief governor in a family. For it is presumed that all who do any good are instruments of the highest governor, and that if any evil or injury happens, it is through his negligence.

On the other side, because the husband is the chief,482 many wives think that the government of the family does not belong to them at all. So they are careless of its good, and will not stir their least finger to set anything in order; but if anything is amiss, they lay all the blame on their husbands. Do not such wives pervert the main end for which God made them, which is to be a help? Do they not behave most unworthily of the place in which God has set them, namely to be joint governors with their husbands and partakers of their dignities? As by their negligence they make themselves accessories to all the evil that happens in the family, so they will surely have their part in those judgments which are executed on its head.

Most contrary to the duty named above is the practice of483 those who are hindrances to one another in governing the family. So it is when wives are not only negligent themselves in coming to religious exercises, but keep back children and servants too, and so are a great grief to their devout husbands; or when they use any of the children or servants as instruments of iniquity; or when they are themselves unquiet and troublesome in the house, like her of whom Solomon speaks in this proverb: “Better to live on a corner of the484 roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife.”

Husbands also are often a hindrance to the good government which their wives would help to further, when they scoff and scorn at the good counsel their wives give them for that purpose, or when they will not allow their wives to deal with anything at all, nor bear that they should find any fault, much less undertake to set right anything that is amiss. These and similar perverse dispositions are found in husbands and wives, and through them it comes about that those who were joined together to be a mutual help to each other prove heavy, yes, intolerable burdens.

§. 42. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual help in hospitality.

The next common duty of husband and wife concerns those who come to their house but are not particular members of it, whether they are kindred, relatives by marriage, acquaintances or strangers, especially if they are saints, to whom hospitality,485 that is, a kind and courteous welcome, is due. In this, therefore, husbands and wives must be helpful to one another. For as it is required of486 husbands, so also of487 wives, to be “hospitable”: namely, while they are married, together with their husbands, and when they are widows, by themselves. Abraham488 and Sarah were a help to one another in this when the three angels came to their house in the shape of men; so were489 the Shunammite woman and her husband when Elisha the prophet came to their house.

As for hospitality, that it is a commendable duty belonging490 to those who are householders and able to entertain guests is evident from the precepts and examples specified above, and also from the blessing which God has brought on this account to the houses of those who were given to it. The apostle hints at this in these words: “by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it.”491 Now therefore, since husbands and wives are (as we have heard) joint governors, as in other things so in this they ought to lend a helping hand to each other, and that for these reasons.

1. Because in entertaining guests there are various492 things to be done, some of which belong to the husband’s place and some to the wife’s. To see to the provision of things outside the house is more fit for the husband: Abraham493 did it. To order the smaller things inside the house is more fit for the wife: that was left to Sarah.494

2. Because it is fitting that guests should know they are welcome495 to both the husband and the wife, so that they may be all the more cheerful.

3. Because mutual consent and cheerful help in this will496 be a special means both to show their mutual affection and to hold the hearts of man and wife firm and close together, and to make them like and love each other the better. This is especially so if the husband shows himself as ready and willing to entertain his wife’s friends and kindred as his own, and the wife likewise her husband’s (as they ought). For as they themselves are made one flesh, so each of them ought to regard the other’s friends as their own.

4. Because in this way they show a mutual desire to bring497 God’s blessing on each other and on their whole family.

§. 43. Of vices contrary to mutual help in hospitality.

Contrary to this duty, for the most part, is covetousness in the husband and laziness in the wife. The man, because the charge of the family lies on him, distrustfully fears that he will not have enough for his own.

I do not deny that a provident care for our own, and especially for those of our family, is needful and commendable: he who does not provide for them “is worse than an unbeliever.”498 So a man may be too lavish in entertaining guests, if he goes beyond his means, impoverishes his estate and disables himself from providing for his own, as many do. Yet when a man has enough, yes, and abundance, and there is no just cause but only an undue fear, then to pinch too fretfully and distrustfully, and to begrudge entertaining anyone, is unbecoming in a Christian; yes, it is even to be worse than an unbeliever, not worthy to have a house or anything fit for entertaining guests, no, nor worthy of common society.

The woman, on the other side, resents the pains she must take and the trouble she must undergo in entertaining guests, and so is unwilling that anyone should ever come to their house.

Concerning a wife, I do not deny that a husband may be too burdensome to her in this way, by being too jovial, as they say, and bringing guests into the house too often, especially if they are guests of no good name, and by that means make her even weary of her life. But for a wife to refuse all pains of that kind, and to be discontented when her husband invites any friends, or when any come (as the three angels came to Abraham) unexpectedly, does not show that there is a loving affection in her, or a wifely subjection to her husband.

These faults are all the greater when the husband or wife is free and eager in entertaining their own kindred and friends, but reluctant and grudging about entertaining each other’s friends and kindred. From this commonly arises much resentment of one against the other, yes, much discord and contention between them; and from disliking one another’s practice in this, there often follows a dislike of one another’s person. So, as the fault is bad in itself, it proves to be much worse in the injuries that follow from it.

§. 44. Of husbands’ and wives’ mutual help in relieving the poor.

The last common and joint duty in which husband and wife ought to be helpful to each other concerns those who are outside the house, namely the poor, and such as stand in need of their help, who are to be relieved and supported. Because man and wife usually eat their meals together, and are joint partakers of the good things God has created, they must put one another in mind of that precept of charity which was given to the Jews when they were at their meals: “send out portions to those who have nothing prepared.”499 The good wife, who is set forth by the Holy Spirit as a pattern and example for others to follow, and her husband are noted as being helpful to one another in this duty. For it is said of her that she stretches out her hand to the poor and to the needy;500 and it is said of him that he “praises her,”501 by this encouraging her to keep on doing the good things she did. What liberty the wife has, or how far she may be restrained if her husband utterly refuses to give consent, we will set out502 later in the particular duties of wives. The point noted here is this: that the husband himself must be bountiful to the poor according to his ability, and allow his wife, yes, urge her, to be so too, and also give her the means to be bountiful; and that the wife also must stir up her husband to generosity in this respect, and herself open her hand to the poor in the things which she may lawfully give.

There is nothing by which a man or wife can bring more profit to the house than by giving to the poor. What is given to the poor is “a loan to the Lord,” and he will repay it with great increase.503 It is like seed,504 which, being liberally sown, will bring forth a plentiful harvest. Yes, it is a means to make us friends,505 who will speak a good word for us at the bar of Christ’s judgment seat. And it brings not only the blessing of men,506 but that of God507 also, even the greatest blessing of all, the508 blessing of eternal life. For it is a sacrifice with which “God is pleased.”509 The apostle notes this as one of Christ’s own sayings, which he left to his disciples by word of mouth: “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”510

Besides, husbands and wives, in distributing alms, may receive511 good direction from one another: the husband by telling the wife who are fit to be relieved (for husbands commonly know better those who are outside the family), the wife by telling the husband what things are best to give away. For wives commonly know which things there is the greatest store of, and what can best be spared in the house.

§. 45. Of husbands’ and wives’ unmercifulness to the poor.

Contrary to this is the unmercifulness of many husbands, who512 are not only hard-hearted themselves (never giving anything unless they are forced by the law of the land, and then they part513 with what is given so grudgingly that it is not at all acceptable to God, for “God loves a cheerful giver”)514 but also tie their wives’ hands and allow them to give nothing. In this515 they bring on their own necks both the cry of the poor and the groans and grief of a merciful wife who is restrained like this, and aggravate their sin to a high degree.

On the other side, the unmercifulness of many wives is also contrary to the duty named above. For there are many who, though they have liberty to give from the common goods, and also an allowance of their own from which they may give, yet covetously hoard up all they can get and do not give a penny’s worth. They would rather let food and other things perish in the house, and throw them away when they have gone bad, than let anything be given out of the house while it is good. Shall not the created things that are spoiled in a house, and the poor who have gone without, raise a loud cry in the ears516 of the Lord against them? Yes, further, many wives are grieved at their husbands’ generosity, and are always urging them to shut their hands and give no more. Are they not plain devils in this, opposing what is good?
