The Third Treatise: Of Wives

A Wife’s Respect for Her Husband

The Third Treatise: Of Wives · §§. 1–16

§. 1. Of the general heads of this treatise.

Eph 5:22.

Wives, submit yourselves+ to your+ own husbands as to the Lord. v. 23. For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the church; and He is the Savior of the body. v. 24. Therefore, as the church is subject to Christ, so let wives be subject to their husbands in everything.

In the particular declaration of wives’ duties, the apostle notes two points:

  1. The duty required.
  2. The reason to enforce it.

In setting out the duty, he declares

  1. The matter in which it consists.
  2. The manner in which it is to be performed.

In the matter we may note:

  1. The thing required,517 subjection.
  2. The persons it concerns, their518 own husbands.

The manner concerns the quality and the extent of that subjection.

To declare the quality of wives’ subjection to their husbands, two rules are set down.

1. That it is to be such a subjection as519 should be performed to Christ.

2. That it is to be such a subjection as the520 church performs to Christ.

The extent of wives’ subjection stretches very far, even to all things.521

The reason to enforce all these points is taken from that place of eminence and authority in which the husband is set above his wife. This reason is

1. Set forth under the metaphor of a head (“for the husband is the head of the wife”).

2. Amplified by the resemblance he has in this to Christ.

In this resemblance two points are noted.

1. That the husband, by virtue of his place, carries the very image of Christ (“as Christ is the head of the church”).

2. That the husband, by virtue of his office, is a protector of his wife (“and He is the Savior of the body”).

§. 2. Of a wife’s subjection in general.522

The first point to be handled in the treatise of wives’ particular duties is the general matter of them all (subjection), under which all the other particulars are included. For it has as large523 an extent as that honor which is required in the fifth commandment, when it is applied to wives. When the Lord first declared her duty to the woman, he set it down in this phrase: “Your desire will be subject to your husband” (Gen 3:16).

Objection. Was that not a punishment inflicted on her for her transgression?

Answer. It was a law too, for the testing of her obedience; and if it is not kept, her nature will be more depraved and her fault more increased. Besides, we cannot help thinking that the woman was made before the fall so that the man might rule over her. On this ground the prophets and apostles have often urged the same. Sarah is commended for this, that she was subject to her husband (1 Pet 3:6). By this the Holy Spirit would teach wives that subjection ought to be like salt, to season every duty which they perform to their husbands. Their very opinion, feeling, speech, action, and all that concerns the husband, must taste of subjection. Contrary to this is the disposition of many wives, whom ambition has tainted and corrupted within and without. They cannot bear to hear of subjection: they imagine that it makes them slaves. But I hope that partly by what has been delivered before about those common duties which man and wife mutually owe each other, and partly by the particulars which are included under this general, but most of all524 by the duties which the husband in particular owes his wife, it will plainly appear that this subjection is no servitude. But even if it were more than it is, seeing God requires subjection of a wife to her husband, the wife is bound to yield it. And it is good reason that she who first drew man into sin should now be subject to him, so that she does not fall again through the like womanish weakness.

§. 3. Of a husband’s superiority over a wife, to be acknowledged by a wife.525

The subjection which is required of a wife to her husband implies two things.

  1. That she acknowledges her husband to be her superior.
  2. That she respects him as her superior.

That acknowledgment of the husband’s superiority is twofold:

  1. General, of any husband.
  2. Particular, of her own husband.

The general is the ground of the particular. For until a wife is taught that a husband, by virtue of his place, is his wife’s superior, she will not be persuaded that her own husband is above her, or has any authority over her.

First, therefore, concerning the general, I will lay down526 some clear and undeniable proofs to show that a husband is his wife’s superior and has authority over her. The proofs are these.

1. God, by whom “the authorities that exist have been appointed,”527 has power to place his image in whom he will; and whatever superiority and authority God gives to anyone ought to be acknowledged as their due. But God said of the man to the woman, “he will rule over you” (Gen 3:16).

2. Nature has placed an eminence in the male over the528 female, so that where they are linked together in one yoke, it is given by nature that he should govern and she obey. The heathen observed this by the light of nature.

3. The titles and names by which a husband is set forth imply a superiority and authority in him, such as “lord”529 (1 Pet 3:6),530 “master” (Esth 1:17),531 “guide” (Prov 2:17),532 “head” (1 Cor 11:3),533 “the image and glory of God” (1 Cor 11:7).

4. The persons whom the husband by virtue of his place, and the wife by virtue of hers, represent prove as much most clearly. For a husband represents Christ, and a wife the church (Eph 5:23).

5. The circumstances the Holy Spirit notes at the woman’s creation imply no less: that she was created after man, for man’s good, and out of man’s side (Gen 2:18, etc.).

6. The very534 attire which nature and the custom of all times and places have taught women to put on confirms the same: long hair, veils, and other coverings over the head. The apostle himself uses this argument and the one before it for this very purpose, 1 Cor 11:7, etc.

The point, then, being so clear, wives ought in conscience to acknowledge as much: namely, that a husband has superiority535 and authority over a wife. The acknowledgment of this is a main and principal duty, and a ground of all other duties. Until a wife is fully instructed in it and truly persuaded of it, no duty can be performed by her as it ought to be. For subjection has relation to superiority and authority; the very derivation of the word implies as much. How then can subjection be yielded if husbands are not acknowledged as superiors? It may be forced, as one king conquered in battle by another may be compelled to pay homage to the conqueror. But because he still thinks to himself that he is in no way inferior, he will hardly be brought to yield a subject’s duty to him willingly, but will rather wait for a time when he may free himself and take revenge on the conqueror.

§. 4. Of a foolish notion that husband and wife are equal.

Contrary to the subjection named above is the opinion of many wives, who think themselves in every way as good as their husbands, and in no way inferior to them.

The reason for this seems to be that small inequality536 which there is between the husband and the wife. For of all the degrees in which there is any difference between person and person, there is the least disparity between man and wife. Though the man is like the head, yet the woman is like the heart, which is the most excellent part of the body next to the head, far more excellent than any other member under the head, almost equal to the head in many respects, and as necessary as the head. As evidence that a wife is to man as the heart to the head, she was at her537 first creation taken out of the side of man, where his heart lies. And though the woman at first “came from man,”538 created out of his side, yet “man is born of woman.” Ever since the first creation man has been born and brought forth out of the woman’s womb, so that “man is not independent of woman, nor is woman independent of man.” Yes, “the wife does not have power over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have power over his own body, but the wife.”539 They are also540 “fellow heirs of the grace of life.” Besides, wives are mothers of the same children of whom their husbands are fathers (for God said to both, “Be fruitful and multiply”),541 and mistresses of the same servants of whom their husbands are masters (for Sarah is called “mistress”).542 And in many other respects there is a common equity between husbands and wives. From this many wives gather that in all things there ought to be a mutual equality.

But to infer a general rule from some particulars is a very weak argument.

1. Does it follow that because in many things there is a common equity between judges of assize, justices of the peace and town constables, there is therefore an equality between them in all things?

2. In many things there is not a common equity: for the husband may command his wife, but she is not to command him.

3. Even in those things in which there is a common equity, there is not an equality. For the husband always has a superiority, even in all things: if there is any difference even in the instances named above, the husband must have the final say. So in giving the name of Rachel’s youngest child, when the wife wanted one name and the husband another, the name which the husband gave stood (Gen 35:18).

However little disparity there may seem to be, yet since God has so expressly appointed subjection, it ought to be acknowledged. And543 though husband and wife may serve one another mutually through love, yet the apostle does not allow a woman to rule over the man.

§. 5. Of a wife’s acknowledgment of her own husband’s superiority.544

The truth and life of that general acknowledgment of husbands’ honor consists in its particular application to their very own husbands.

The next duty, therefore, is that wives acknowledge their545 own husbands, those to whom they are joined in marriage by God’s providence, to be worthy of a husband’s honor and to be their superiors. This is what the apostle intends by that word of restriction546 (own), which he uses very often. So does Saint Peter,547 exhorting wives to be in subjection548 to their own husbands, and restricting to this the commendation of the good wives of old, that they were in subjection to their own husbands.

Objection. What if a man of lowly place is married to a woman of eminent place, or a servant is married to his mistress, or an aged woman to a youth? Must such a wife acknowledge such a husband as her superior?

Answer. Yes, truly. For in giving herself to be his wife, and549 taking him to be her husband, she raises him above herself and subjects herself to him. It makes no difference what either of them was before marriage. By virtue of the marriage bond the husband is made the head of his wife, though before marriage the husband was a very beggar, of lowly parentage, and the wife very wealthy and of a noble stock; or though he was her apprentice or her slave. This also holds in the case of an aged woman and a youth: for the Scripture has made no exception in any of these cases.

2. Objection. But what if a man of wicked and beastly character, such as a drunkard, a glutton, a profane swaggerer, an impious swearer and blasphemer, is married to a wife who is a sober, religious matron? Must she account him her superior, and worthy of a husband’s honor?

Answer. Surely she must. For the evil quality and disposition550 of his heart and life does not deprive a man of that social honor which God has given him. Though because of his evil qualities a husband may carry the image of the devil, yet with respect to his place and office he bears the image of God. So do magistrates in the commonwealth, ministers in the church, and parents and masters in the family. Note for our present purpose the exhortation of Saint Peter to Christian wives who had unbelieving husbands: “Be subject to them; let your+ conduct be coupled with fear.”551 If unbelievers do not carry the devil’s image, and are not vassals of Satan as long as they are unbelievers, who are? Yet wives must be subject to them, and fear them.

§. 6. Of wives denying honor to their own husbands.

Contrary to this is a very perverse disposition in some552 wives, who think they could subject themselves to any husband better than to their own. Though in general they acknowledge that a husband is his wife’s superior, yet when it comes to applying it to themselves they fail, and cannot be brought to grant that they are their husbands’ inferiors. This is a vice worse than the former. For to acknowledge no husband as superior over his wife, but to think man and wife equal in all things, may proceed from ignorance of mind and error of judgment. But for a wife who knows and acknowledges the general rule, that a husband is above his wife, to imagine that she herself is not inferior to her husband arises from monstrous conceit and intolerable arrogance, as if she herself were above her own sex, and more than a woman.

Contrary also is the practice of such553 women as purposely marry men of far lower rank than themselves, for this very end, that they may rule over their own husbands; and of others who, being554 aged, marry youths, if not mere boys, for the same end. It is a mind and practice very unseemly, and flatly thwarting God’s ordinance. But let them think of ruling555 as they please; the truth is that they make themselves subjects by both God’s law and man’s, and such wives often feel the heaviest burden of this subjection. Solomon notes this as one of the things under which the earth trembles: “a556 servant who becomes king.” Now when can a servant domineer more than when he has married his mistress? As for aged women who are married to youths, I may say (as was said in another case), “woe to you, O wife, whose husband is a child.”557 It is unfitting for an aged man to be married to a young maid, but much more unfitting for an aged woman to be married to a youth.

§. 7. Of a wife’s inward fear of her husband.558

So much for a wife’s acknowledgment of her husband’s superiority. Next we are to speak of the corresponding respect which she ought to bear toward him.

A wifely respect for her husband consists in two points:

  1. Reverence.
  2. Obedience.

The reverence which she owes him is559

  1. Inward.
  2. Outward.

Inward reverence is a respect full of awe which a wife has in her heart for her husband, esteeming him worthy of all honor for the sake of his place and office, because he is her husband. Doubtless Sarah had in her heart a reverent regard and honorable esteem for her husband when,560 being alone and thinking of him in her very thought, she gave him this title, “lord.” This inward reverence the Scripture includes under this word fear, as where our apostle says,561 “let the wife see that she fears her husband,” and where562 Saint Peter exhorts wives to have their conduct “coupled with fear.” It is no slavish fear of her husband which ought to possess the heart of a wife, dreading blows, frowns, spiteful words or the like; but such a respect full of awe for him as makes her (to use the apostle’s word) “care … how she can please her husband.”563 This wifely fear shows itself in two effects. One is joy, when she gives her husband contentment and sees that he is pleased with what she does. The other is grief, when he is justly offended and grieved, especially with anything that she herself has done.

Unless this inward reverence and due respect for a husband564 is first placed in the heart of a wife, either no outward reverence and obedience will be performed at all, or, if it is performed, it will be very unsound, only for show, hypocritical and deceitful; so that it is as good not to do it at all as to be never the better for it. For the outward action and conduct will be shaped according to one’s inward feeling and disposition. Michal565 first despised David “in her heart,” and from this it followed that she566 uttered most irreverent and vile speeches about him, even to his face. Therefore, after the judgment of a wife is rightly informed of a husband’s superiority, and her will persuaded to account her own husband her head and guide, it is very needful that her heart and feelings be seasoned accordingly with the salt of good respect and high esteem, which breeds fear. And so that her heart may be seasoned in this way, she ought often and seriously to meditate on his place and office, and on that honor which the Lord by virtue of it has planted in him. And if he has gifts worthy of his place, such as knowledge, wisdom, piety, temperance, love and the like, she ought to take notice of them, and to think him worthy of double honor.

§. 8. Of a wife’s low esteem of her husband.

Contrary to this inward reverence of the heart is a low and vile esteem which many have of their husbands, thinking no better of them than of other men, no, worse than of others, and despising their husbands in their heart, like Michal, of whom we heard before. As this is in itself a vile vice, so it is also a cause of many other vices, such as presumption, rebellion,567 yes, and many times of adultery itself; and it is also a main hindrance to all duty.

It commonly arises either from conceit (by which wives think too highly of their own gifts, thinking them so excellent568 that they need no guide or head, but are rather fit to guide and rule both their husband and the whole household. Of this proud and presumptuous spirit Jezebel seems to have been, who with a bold and shameless face said to Ahab her husband, “Do you not reign over Israel? Get up … I will get you the vineyard of Naboth.”569 So also were all those wives who are noted for drawing their husbands’ hearts away from the Lord, such as the wives of Solomon,570 Jehoram571 and others, who learned it from their great-grandmother Eve572); or else from some infirmities of mind or body, or of life, which they see in their573 husbands (which is how it comes about that many husbands who are highly honored and greatly esteemed by others are much despised by their wives, because their wives, always living with them, are privy to such infirmities as are hidden from others); or, worst of all, from unjust surmises574 and suspicions, suspecting their husbands of many evil things of which they are in no way guilty, and misinterpreting and perverting things well done, as Michal575 perverted David’s holy zeal.

To remedy this monstrous vice, wives ought first, with respect576 to themselves, to purge pride and conceit out of their hearts, thinking humbly and lowly of themselves, even because of their sex and its weakness. And if the Lord has endowed them with any gift above the ordinary sort of women, they ought to note well their own infirmities and set them beside their eminent gifts: so, by looking at their black feet, their proud peacock feathers may be brought down. Yes, also, when they see any infirmities in their husbands, they ought to turn their eyes back on their own infirmities, which perhaps are just as many and as grievous, if not more in number and more heinous in their nature and kind. At least let them consider that they are subject to the same, if God leaves them to the sway of their own corruption.

Secondly, wives ought, with respect to their husbands, to suspect no evil of which they have no sure proof and evidence, but rather take everything in the better sense, and follow the rule of love, which “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.”577 If they note any defects of nature and deformity of body, or any gross and notorious vices in their husband, then they ought to turn their eyes and thoughts from his person to his place, and from his vicious qualities to his honorable office (which is to be a husband). This will lessen that vile esteem which might otherwise be occasioned by the means named above.

§. 9. Of wifely sobriety.578

A wife’s outward reverence toward her husband is a showing of her inward due respect for him. Now, seeing579 the intent of the heart and the inward disposition cannot be discerned by man in themselves, so that the husband may know his wife’s good feeling toward him, it is needful that she show it by her outward reverence.

A wife’s outward reverence consists in her reverent

  • Bearing.
  • Speech.

As for the first, that a reverent bearing and conduct of herself toward580 her husband, and in her husband’s presence, becomes a wife was implied of old by the veil which the woman used to put on when she was brought to her husband, as is noted in the581 example of Rebekah. The apostle alludes to this in these words: “a woman ought to have a sign of authority on her head.”582 As that covering on the woman’s head implied subjection in general, so in particular it implied this kind of subjection, namely a reverent conduct and bearing. But this duty is set down most expressly by583 Saint Peter, who exhorts wives to order their conduct before their husbands so that it is pure, with reverence.

This reverent conduct consists in a wifely sobriety, mildness, courtesy, and modesty.

By sobriety I mean such a seemly, serious and gracious bearing as gives evidence to the husband that his wife respects his place and the authority which God has given him. Sobriety in general is required of all women because of their sex, and surely it well becomes them all; but it becomes wives much more, and most of all in their husband’s presence.584 The apostle requires it in particular of deacons’ wives, yet not as belonging only to them, but as belonging to them in a further respect, not only as wives, but as the wives of deacons.

Contrary to this sobriety are flightiness and wantonness. These vices in a wife, especially before her husband, show little respect for him, if not a plain contempt of him.

Objection. In this way all delightful familiarity between husband and wife will be taken away.

Answer. Though the sobriety named above is opposed to flightiness585 and wantonness, yet it is not opposed to marital familiarity. This is permitted to man and wife so far that if any other man and woman behaved toward each other as a husband and wife lawfully may, it might justly be counted flightiness and sin. Take the example of Isaac and Rebekah,586 who so caressed each other that Abimelech, knowing them to be people who feared God, gathered from that caressing that they were man and wife: for he thought that otherwise they would not have been so familiar together.

This587 familiarity proves both liking and love, and shows that the man and wife delight in one another’s person. But the flightiness here condemned in a wife is not so much a mutual familiarity with her husband, with his good liking, as a wanton dallying with others, to his grief and disgrace.

§. 10. Of wifely mildness.588

Mildness in a wife also has to do with the ordering of her expression, bearing and whole conduct before her husband, by which she shows a pleasingness toward him, and a contentment and willingness to be under him and ruled by him. This is excellently set forth in the spouse of Christ, whose eyes are said to be “like doves,” her lips to “drip sweetness like the honeycomb,” and589 she herself every way “pleasant.” From this it is noted that she appeared to her husband “like the dawn,” and that his heart was wounded by her. Surely the clear sky is not more pleasant in time of harvest than a mild and amiable expression and conduct of a wife in her husband’s presence.590 And though her husband should be of a harsh and cruel disposition, yet by this means he might be made meek and gentle. For the keepers of lions are said to bring them to some tameness by handling them gently and speaking to them kindly.

Contrary to this mildness are a frowning brow, a scowling eye, a sullen look, a pouting lip, a puffed-up face, a mocking mouth, a scornful toss of the arms and hands, a disdainful turning of the body this way and that, and a fretful flinging out of her husband’s presence. All these and other like contemptuous gestures are like thick clouds spreading over the sky on a summer’s day, which make it very cheerless. They often stir up much anger in the man, and bring much harm on the wife herself.

§. 11. Of wifely courtesy and gestures of respect.591

Courtesy is that virtue by which a wife takes occasion to testify her acknowledgment of her husband’s superiority by some outward gesture of respect toward him. Rebekah, as soon as she saw Isaac, whom she had taken for her husband, got down from her camel and came to him on foot, which was a kind of gesture of respect. This is not to be taken as if no difference were to be made between the bearing of a servant or child and that of a wife, or as if a wife should bow at every word that she speaks to her husband. Though in the kind and extent of many duties the same things are required of wives as of children and servants, because God has made them all inferiors and demanded subjection of all, yet in the manner and measure of many duties there is a great difference. So it is in this one: the gestures of respect of children and servants ought to be more submissive and more frequent. Yet because God has placed authority in the husband over his wife, she is in every way to testify her reverent respect for her husband. Therefore at some times and on some occasions (as when he is going away from her on a journey for a time, or when he returns home again, or when she has a solemn and great request to make to him, or when he offers her an especial and extraordinary favor, or (as I have observed in such wives as know what becomes their place, and are not ashamed to show as much) when she sits592 down at table or rises from it) she is to declare her reverence by some gesture of respect. This cannot but work much on the heart of a good and kind husband, and make him respect his wife all the more when he sees this evidence of her respect for him. Yes, it cannot but be a good pattern to children593 and servants, and a motive to stir them up to show every submissive gesture of respect both to her husband and to herself. For it may make them reason with themselves like this: “Shall594 we scorn or begrudge giving our father or master what our mother or mistress does not begrudge giving her husband? Shall she bow to him, and shall we not much more bow to her?” In this way a wife’s honoring of her husband by showing him gestures of respect makes both him and herself more honored by others.

Of a contrary mind are those who not only omit595 this duty altogether, but also jeer and scoff at the very mention of it, saying, “So wives will be made no better than children or servants.” But though scornful dames deride these outward evidences of their subjection, yet wives who fear the Lord ought not to be hindered by this from doing their duty: for by such evil examples they might be discouraged from every good duty. It is enough that such holy women as trusted in God behaved themselves so. But as for this particular, we know that equals do not scorn, when occasion offers, to perform this kind of courtesy in making gestures of respect to one another: how much less should wives, who are their husbands’ inferiors!

§. 12. Of wifely modesty in clothing.596

The modesty that belongs to a wife is shown much in her clothing. Saint Paul requires this modesty of all sorts of women in general, but Saint Peter presses it in particular on wives. For as it well becomes all women, so it becomes wives in a distinctive way: namely, in dressing themselves, to have regard to their husband’s place and condition rather than to their own birth and parentage, and much rather than to their own mind and fancy. A wife’s modesty therefore requires that her clothing be neither above her husband’s means in costliness, nor unbecoming his calling in its elaborateness. As a poor man’s wife must not seek costly clothing, so neither must the wives of ministers, grave counselors, wise magistrates, no, nor of conscientious professing Christians, hunt after new fashions, or dress themselves in frivolous and garish clothing. It is a token of great reverence in a wife toward her husband to have an eye to his place and condition in her clothing.

On the contrary, such proud dames as must have their own way in their attire, and think it is no business597 of their husbands to order them in it, and do not care what their husband’s means or his place and calling are, show little respect and reverence to their husbands. Such are those who are not at all moved by their husband’s example: though the man’s clothing is plain and grave, yet the wife’s must be costly and garish. Yes, there are many who stand somewhat more in awe of their husband’s sight, but show him little more respect. They have their silk gowns, beaver hats and other such attire not suited to their place and condition lying in the country, if they are of the city, or in the city, if they are of the country, in a friend’s house where their husbands will598 not know of it; and when their husbands are not with them, they wear them, paint their faces, do up their hair, and follow the fashion in everything. What can those who see this think, but that such a wife’s care is more to please other flighty, vain people than her grave, discreet husband, or that her husband can have no influence at all with her? As this stains her own good name, so it leaves a blot of dishonor even on him. If a wife’s care were to give evidence of the reverence which she bears her husband, his desire and example would in this matter prevail more with her than the fancies of her own heart.

§. 13. Of a wife’s reverent speech to her husband.599

As by bearing, so also by speech must a wife’s reverence be shown: this must correspond to that. For the feeling of the heart is shown by words as well as by deeds: “out of the overflow of the heart, the mouth speaks.”600 A wife’s reverence is shown by her speech both in her husband’s presence and in his absence. To this end, in his presence her words must be few, reverent and meek. First, few: for the601 apostle requires silence602 of wives in their husbands’ presence, and enforces that duty with a strong reason in these words: “I do not permit a woman to usurp authority over a man, but to be in silence.” The way the latter clause is drawn from the former shows that he speaks not only of a woman’s silence in the church, but also of a wife’s silence before her husband. This is further cleared by another like place, where the same apostle commands wives to learn from their husbands at home.603 The reason mentioned before for silence implies on the one side a reverent subjection, as on the other side too much speech implies a usurping of authority.

Objection. Then it seems a wife must always be mute before her husband.

Answer. Not at all. For silence in that place is not opposed to speech, as if she should not speak at all, but to loquacity, to talkativeness, to too much chattering. Her husband’s presence must somewhat restrain her tongue, and so her very silence will testify a reverent respect. Otherwise silence, as it is opposed to speech, would imply haughtiness of spirit and stubbornness of heart, which is an extreme contrary to loquacity. But the middle way between both is for a wife to be sparing in speech, to wait for a fit time and just occasion to speak, and to be willing to listen to the word of knowledge coming out of her husband’s mouth. This shows reverence. Elihu604 showed the reverent respect which, as a younger man, he bore toward his elders by holding back from speaking while they had anything to say. How much more ought wives to do so, because both of their sex and of their place?

Contrary is the practice of those who must and will do all the605 talking. If their husbands have begun to speak, their slippery tongues cannot wait and hold back until he has finished. If (as they are very hasty and eager to speak) they do not speak before their husbands, they will surely take the words out of his mouth before he has finished. So they disgrace themselves and dishonor their husbands.

§. 14. Of the titles which wives give their husbands.606

As their words must be few, so those few words must be reverent and meek. Both are also implied under the word named above,607 silence, which in the original also means608 quietness.

Reverence has to do with the titles by which a wife names her husband; meekness with the manner of framing her speech to him.609

As for the titles which a wife gives her husband in speaking to him or naming him, they must be such as signify superiority, and so savor of reverence. Such are the titles by which husbands are named in the Scripture;610 they are titles of honor. Such also are the titles which the church (whom our apostle makes a pattern for wives in all subjection) gives to her spouse Christ Jesus, as may be gathered from the Song of Songs. It is likely that Sarah usually gave this title “lord” to her husband. For when she had occasion to think of him, this title “lord”611 was at once in her heart; and it would not have risen up so readily if she had not ordinarily used it. When we have occasion to think of anyone, we name them in our hearts according to the usual titles we give them. Among all the other titles, the name “husband,” as it is the most usual, so it is the fittest and most suitable title. It suggests reverence, and does not smack of fussiness and oddity, as these titles do: “Head,” “Guide,” “master,” “man” and the like. Though these are lawful titles, because the Scripture gives them to husbands and they signify superiority, yet because they are unusual and smack of oddity, they are not so fitting. Common use and practice have made it more fitting to add the husband’s surname to this title “master.”

Saint612 Peter proves by this argument that Sarah obeyed Abraham: because she called him “lord.”

Contrary to these are those forms of address which suggest equality or inferiority rather than superiority, such as “brother,” “Cousin,” “Friend,” “man,” etc. If a stranger is present, how can he tell by this form of address that the one you are speaking to is your husband? If he notices any marital familiarity between you and your husband, what else can he judge it to be but flightiness and wantonness? Remember the fearful outcome that nearly followed from such forms of address given by Sarah613 and Rebekah614 to their husbands. Not unlike these are such as “Sweet,” “Sweeting,” “Heart,” “Sweet-heart,” “love,” “Joy,” “Dear,” etc.; and such as “Duck,” “Chick,” “Pigsny,” etc.; and husbands’ Christian names, such as “John,” “Thomas,” “William,” “Henry,” etc. If these are shortened (as many shorten them, like this: “Jack,” “Tom,” “Will,” “Hall”), they are much more unseemly: servants are usually called so.

But what may we say of those titles given to a husband by his wife, not only often in anger but usually in ordinary speech, which are not fit to be given to the basest men there are, such as “Grub,” “Rogue” and the like, which I am even ashamed to name, except that the sins of women are to be cast like dirt in their faces, so that they may be the more ashamed?

Objection. Many of the titles named above are titles of friendship and familiarity.

Answer. Subjection is the mark which wives are directed to aim at in their thoughts, words, deeds and whole conduct toward their husbands. Such tokens of familiarity as are not also tokens of subjection and reverence are unbecoming in a wife, because they swerve from that mark.

§. 15. Of wives’ meekness in their speech.615

Meekness in a wife’s manner of framing her speech to her husband also commends her reverent respect for him. This is a special effect of that meek and quiet spirit which Saint Peter requires of wives, a duty he strongly enforces by this weighty argument: “which is precious in God’s sight.”616 Is a wife’s meekness precious in God’s sight, and shall wives not hold it both a binding duty and a becoming ornament and grace to them? As the form of words which a wife uses in asking or answering questions, or in any other kind of conversation which she holds with her husband, so her moderation in persisting, arguing and pressing matters, yes, and the mild composure of her expression in speaking, declare her meekness. If she wants to obtain anything from him, she must ask for it kindly, as the Shunammite did.617 If she would move him to perform a binding duty, she must persuade him mildly. If she would restrain him and keep him from doing what is evil, even that she must do with some meekness, as Pilate’s618 wife did. If she has occasion to tell him of a fault, she ought in this to show humility and reverence by observing a fit season and doing it in a gentle manner, as Abigail did.619 As she behaved wisely in this respect with her husband, in observing a fit season, so she did also with David, by hinting at his fault rather than plainly reproving him, when she said, “my lord will have no remorse or guilt of conscience over needless bloodshed.” This meekness also requires silence and patience, even when she is reproved.

Contrary is the waspish and shrewish disposition of many620 wives toward their husbands, who do not care how hastily and rashly they speak to them, like Rachel;621 nor how angrily and scoldingly, like Jezebel;622 nor how disdainfully and spitefully, like Zipporah;623 nor how scoffingly and jeeringly, like Michal;624 nor how reproachfully and disgracefully, like Job’s625 wife. If they are reproved by their husbands, their husbands will be reproached by them, and they are ready to answer back, not only word for word, but ten for one. Many wives by their shrewish speech show no more respect to their husbands than to their servants, if as much. The least occasion moves them not only to be inwardly angry and fret against them, but also to show it outwardly by scolding and brawling. The very target on which many wives usually spit out their venomous words is their husband: when they are full of resentment, they must vent it on their husbands, and in this their fault is doubled.

Let wives therefore learn, first, to moderate their anger, and then to keep in their tongues with bit and bridle, but most of all to take heed that their husbands do not taste its bitterness, no, not even if they should be provoked by some oversight of their husbands. It is to be noted how Solomon calls the quarrels which are between man and wife “the contentions of a wife,”626 by which he suggests that she is commonly the cause of them, either by provoking her husband or by not bearing with him.

§. 16. Of a wife’s speech about her husband in his absence.627

The reverence which a wife bears toward her husband must further be shown by her speech about him in his absence. So Sarah showed her reverence,628 and so must all who desire to be counted the daughters of Sarah. The church, speaking of her spouse,629 does so with as great reverence as if she had spoken to him. It was for honor and reverence’s sake that the Virgin Mary called Joseph the father of Jesus630 when she spoke of him.

This shows that a wife’s reverent speech in her husband’s presence and to his face is not flattery, to please him and fawn on him, but sincerity, to please God and perform her duty.

Those therefore act contrary to their duty who in their husbands’ presence631 can offer the fairest and meekest speech that may be to their husbands’ faces, but632 behind their backs speak most reproachfully of them.

A Wife’s Not Going Against Her Husband’s Will (I)

The Third Treatise: Of Wives · §§. 17–32

§. 17. Of a wife’s obedience in general.

Thus far we have spoken of a wife’s reverence; next we must speak of her obedience. The first law that was ever given to woman since her fall laid this duty of obedience to her husband on her, in these words: “Your desire will be to your husband, and he will rule over you.”633 How can a husband rule over a wife if she does not obey him? The principal part of that submission which is required of a wife in this634 text, and in many other places, consists in obedience. And therefore it is expressly commended to wives in the example of Sarah, who635 “obeyed Abraham.” In the same way, it is by obedience that the church shows her subjection to Christ.

The place in which God has set a husband, namely, to be a head;636 the authority which he has given him, to be a lord637 and master;638 the duty which he requires of him,639 to rule: all these require obedience of a wife. Is not obedience to be yielded to a head, lord and master? You+ take away all authority from a husband if you+ exempt a wife from obedience.

Contrary to this is the stubbornness of such wives as must have their640 own will and do as they please, or else there will be no quiet in the house. Their will must be done; they must rule and overrule everything; they must command not only children and servants, but husbands also, if the husband at least wants to have peace. Look into families, observe the state and condition of many of them, and then tell me if these things are not so. If a husband is a man of courage, and seeks to stand on his right and maintain his authority by requiring obedience of his wife, it is strange to see what a hurly-burly she will make in the house. But if he is a milksop, and weakly gives in to his wife and allows her to rule, then perhaps there will be some outward quiet. The ground of this is an ambitious and proud disposition in women, who insist on ruling, or else they think themselves slaves. But let them think what they like: in this they certainly thwart God’s ordinance, pervert the order of nature, deface the image of Christ, overthrow the ground of all duty, hinder the good of the family, become a bad pattern to children and servants, lay themselves open to Satan, and incur many other harms which cannot but follow from violating this main duty of obedience. If this is not performed, how can other duties be expected?

§. 18. Of the cases in which a wife has power to order things of the house without her husband’s consent.

A wife’s obedience requires

  • Submission.
  • Contentment.

Submission in yielding to her husband’s mind and will.

Contentment641 in resting satisfied and content with his condition and means.

That submission consists in two things.

First, in abstaining from doing things against her husband’s mind.

Secondly, in doing what her husband requires. The first of these requires that a wife have her husband’s consent for the things which she does. To make this clearer, we must consider:

1. What kind of husbands they must be whose consent is required.

2. In how many ways his consent may be given.

3. What the things are about which his consent is to be looked for.

As for the first: on the one side it often happens that a wise,642 provident and religious man is married to a foolish woman, an utter idiot who has no understanding, and of her there can be no question that such a wife is to do nothing by herself and on her own initiative, but is to be wholly ordered by her husband. So on the other side it often happens that a wise, virtuous and gracious woman is married to a husband destitute643 of understanding: to a born fool (as we say), or a madman, or to one made very dull and stupid, unfit to manage his affairs, through some disorder, wound or sickness. In such a case the whole government lies on the wife, so that her husband’s consent is not to be waited for.

Question. What if the husband is a wicked and profane man, and so blinded and stupefied in his soul? Does not this spiritual blindness and dullness give a religious wife as much liberty as natural stupidity does?

Answer. Truly, no. For Peter exhorts believing wives644 who were married to unbelieving husbands “to be subject” to them, and that “in fear.”

The reason is clear. For spiritual blindness does not disqualify a man from civil government. Indeed, nothing that such a man does is acceptable to God, or of any avail to his own salvation; but yet it may be profitable to man. A wicked man may be provident enough for wife, children and the whole family in outward, temporal things.

Again, it often happens that a husband is645 far away from the house for a long time: sometimes because of his calling, as an ambassador, soldier or sailor; sometimes also carelessly or willfully neglecting house, goods, wife, children and all. And in his absence he has left no instructions for ordering things at home. In this case also there is no question that the wife has power to manage matters without her husband’s consent, provided that she observes those rules of God’s word concerning justice, equity, truth and mercy which a husband ought to observe in managing them.

The first of these cases shows an incapacity in the husband; the other an impossibility for him to order matters. Therefore, since the wife is next to the husband, the power of ordering things passes to her: she is not bound to have his consent.

§. 19. Of various kinds of consent.

II. A consent may be general or particular. A general646 consent is given when, without specific reference to this or that particular thing, liberty is granted to a wife by her husband to do all things as seems good in her own eyes.647 That excellent good wife and notable good housewife who is set forth by the wise man had such a consent. For first it is said, “The heart of her husband trusts in her”;648 and then it is concluded that she orders all the things of the house, many particulars of which are specified there. From this I gather that her husband, seeing her to be a godly, wise, faithful and industrious woman, gave her power and liberty to do what she thought good in the household affairs (he being a public magistrate, for “he is known at the city gate, where he sits among the elders of the land”),649 and that she used her liberty accordingly.

A particular consent is one which is given to one or more particular650 things, such as the consent651 which Abraham gave to Sarah about Hagar, and652 the one which Elkanah gave to Hannah about staying at home till her child was weaned.

This particular consent may be expressed or implied. An expressed consent is when the husband makes known his approval by word, writing, message or sign, and that whether his consent is asked (as was noted in the example of Elkanah) or freely offered.

An implicit consent is when it may be gathered by any likely inference that the husband’s will is not against such a thing,653 though he has not made known his mind about that very particular. This implicit consent may be gathered either from his silence when he is present to see a thing done, or otherwise knows of it; or else, when he is absent, from his past conduct or disposition in other similar cases. The Scripture counts a husband’s silence to be a consent when he knows of a thing and could forbid it, but does not: as654 in the case of a wife’s vow. For all we read to the contrary,655 the Shunammite had no other consent to prepare a room for the prophet, and to go to him, than her husband’s silence, and his not forbidding it when he knew of it.

As for the other kind of implicit consent, it may be set out in the following instance. Suppose a good wife has a husband whom she knows, from his past conduct and disposition, to be a compassionate and charitable man, who takes every occasion to show mercy; and in his absence a fit and needful occasion of showing mercy arises. If she takes that occasion to show mercy, she has an implicit consent, for she may well think that if her husband knew of it he would approve of what she does. We may suppose that Hannah656 vowed her child to God on some such ground. For it is not likely that she who would not stay at home to wean her child without her husband’s consent would vow him to the Lord (which was a far greater matter) without some persuasion that her husband approved of it. Now, so that a wife may show that she deals uprightly in this case, from a true persuasion of her heart about her husband’s mind, she ought (when she reasonably can) to make known to her husband what she has done: as Hannah without any question did. And this much may be gathered from the words which Elkanah spoke to Hannah: “May the Lord confirm His word.”657

§. 20. Of the things about which a wife must have her husband’s consent.

The things about which a husband’s consent is to be looked for are such as he has power to order by virtue of his place and authority: for example, ordering and disposing of the goods, livestock, servants and children of the family, and receiving strangers; yes, even ordering his wife’s going out of the house, and her making of vows, and the like. Now then, to set out distinctly a wife’s duty in this first branch of obedience, it is this:

A wife must do nothing which belongs to her husband’s authority wholly without, or directly against, his consent. Do not these words of that old law (“Your desire will be to your husband”)658 imply as much? I do not deny that there may be various things that belong to a wife as her own, in which I will not restrain her liberty; and therefore I use this phrase, (which belongs to her husband’s authority.) And I grant that the general and implicit consent named above is a true consent, so that there is no need of an express, particular consent for everything; and therefore I have added these clauses, (wholly without, or directly against consent.)

That is done wholly without consent which is done without any warrant from the husband, and so secretly that she is afraid it should come to his notice, imagining that he would by no means like it: as Rachel’s taking her father’s idols659 without any consent of Jacob.

That is done directly against consent which is expressly forbidden and disallowed by the husband.

But to come down to the particulars mentioned before. First, concerning the goods of the family: it is a disputed question whether the wife has power to dispose of them without or against the husband’s consent.

Before I settle the question, I think it needful to declare 1. what goods, and 2. what occasion of giving, the question is about.

§. 21. Of the things which a wife may dispose of without her husband’s consent.

1. As for the goods, some belong to the wife as her own;660 others are common. Goods that are the wife’s own are those which, before marriage, she herself or her family reserve from the husband for her sole and personal use and disposal, and to which he also agrees; or those which, after marriage, he gives her to dispose of as she pleases: say some rent, annuity, fees, gratuities, or the like.

These kinds of goods are excluded from the question661 at hand: the wife has liberty to dispose of them as she pleases without any further consent than she had by virtue of her husband’s former grant.

To these I may add other goods, but of another nature: namely, such as someone close to her, say her father, mother, brother or anyone else, seeing her husband to be a very hard man, who does not allow enough for herself, much less to give to charitable uses, gives her to dispose of as she pleases, charging her not to let her husband know of it. Now because it is in the power of a free donor to order his gift as he pleases, and because he orders this gift in such a way that he will not have her husband know of it, I do not doubt that she may dispose of such goods by herself, according to the donor’s mind, without her husband’s consent. In this she is only like a trustee.

Again, of the common goods, some are set aside by the husband to be spent on the family; others he reserves as a stock, or to lay out as he himself sees occasion.

Concerning those which are set aside to be spent, I do not doubt that the wife has power to dispose of them; nor is she bound to ask any further consent of her husband. For it is the place and duty of wives to guide, or “govern their households,”662 and by virtue of this a wife, providing sufficiently for the family, may give from such goods as are set apart to be spent to the poor, or otherwise, as she sees good occasion.

I have noted this for those tender consciences who think they cannot give a bit of bread or a scrap of food to a poor person, or make a dish of broth or a hot drink for a sick person, unless they first ask their husband’s consent.

This is provided that, if her husband expressly forbids this liberty, she does not take it unless necessity requires it.

But our question concerns such goods as the husband has not set apart, but has reserved to his own disposal.

§. 22. Of a wife’s liberty in extraordinary matters.

II. As for the occasion of disposing of goods, it may be ordinary or extraordinary. Extraordinary, for the good of the husband himself and others in the family, or of those who are outside the family. If an extraordinary occasion arises in which the wife, by disposing of the goods without or against her husband’s consent, may bring a great good to the family, or prevent and keep a great injury from it, she is not to wait for his consent: take as an instance the example of Abigail.663 So a faithful, provident wife who sees her husband given to wild living, spending all he can get on cards, dice and drink, may without his consent lay up what goods she can for her husband’s, her own, her children’s and the whole household’s good. This is no part of disobedience, but a point in which she may show herself a very good help to her husband:664 the end for which a wife was first made.

Concerning those who are outside the family: if they are in great need and require immediate relief, then, though the wife knows her husband to be so hard-hearted that he will not allow her to relieve such a person, yet she may relieve him without his consent. The ground of this and other such cases is the rule laid down by the prophets and by Christ himself, namely, “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”665 If God waives a duty owed to himself in a case of mercy, will he not much more waive a duty owed to a husband?

§. 23. Of a wife’s restraint in disposing of goods without her husband’s consent, and of the ground of that restraint.666

From all these things set down beforehand, I gather the true state667 of the question in dispute, concerning the power of wives in disposing of the goods of the family, to be this:

Whether a wife may, secretly and wholly without, or openly and directly against, her husband’s consent, give away such common goods of the family as her husband reserves to his own disposal, when there is no extraordinary necessity?

The most ancient and common answer to this question has been negative, namely, that a wife does not have power to do so; and for my part I subscribe to it.

The ground of this answer is taken from that primary law of the wife’s subjection: “Your desire will be to your husband.”668 How is her desire subject to her husband if, in the case put forward, she does not wait on his consent? It is further confirmed both by the669 proofs named above and by all the other proofs that might be produced out of the Scripture concerning the subjection of wives to their husbands. If she does not yield subjection in ordering the goods of the family, in what will she yield it?

Against this foundation some object that670 the same law of subjection is laid on a younger brother in the very same words, and yet a younger brother was not bound by it671 to have his elder brother’s consent in disposing of his goods.

Answer. The law of the royal right (if I may so speak) and preeminence of the first-born was ordained under those words; and therefore a younger brother was made a subject to his elder while he remained in the family, as a son to the father. The elder brother was like a lord over his other brothers. That is why, when Isaac conferred the right of the first-born on Jacob (thinking he was his eldest son Esau), he used these words: “Be lord over your brothers, and may the672 sons of your mother bow down to you.” This being so, without question the younger brother could not dispose of the goods of the family wholly without or directly against the elder brother’s consent. So this objection establishes the argument named above all the more strongly.

Again, it is objected that that old law is to be understood of weighty matters.

Answer. The apostle,673 who was guided by the spirit of the lawgiver, extends that law to everything. But is not this matter of disposing of goods a weighty matter? The consequences which I will shortly note as following from it will show it to be a matter of importance.

§. 24. Of the example of the Shunammite in asking her husband’s consent.674

As another reason, the Shunammite’s pattern may be cited: she asked her husband’s consent before she prepared the things that were thought fitting for receiving the prophet, and before she used the things that were fitting for her journey.

Objection. It is indeed commendable for wives to seek their husbands’ consent as she did; but where such consent cannot be had, it is not necessary.

Answer. Since this example is grounded on a law (as we showed675 before), it declares not only what may be done, but also what ought to be done. And if a wife is bound to have her husband’s consent for doing a thing, it follows by consequence that she is barred from doing it without her husband’s consent.

2. Answer. Those who object to this reason taken from example use the same kind of reason themselves on other points, such as the examples of Abigail, Joanna and Susanna for the contrary.

2. Objection. In the Shunammite’s example there was more than a merciful relief of the prophet, namely, bringing him into the house to eat and to lodge, in which the husband must have the chief say.

Answer. The word of God makes no such difference between relieving and receiving: it extends a wife’s subjection to everything. Therefore the husband has the chief say in the one as well as in the other.

§. 25. Of the law of a wife’s vow.

A third reason is taken from the law of a wife’s vow,676 by which it is implied in general that a wife could not make a vow without her husband’s consent. From this it follows, as an argument from the greater to the less, that she must not dispose of the goods without his consent. Yes,677 the law further says expressly that, though she has vowed, yet her husband has power to annul her vow. Note here how the Lord will rather give up his own right (if I may so speak) than have the order which he has appointed between man and woman broken. The Lord’s right was to have what was vowed to him performed; the order which he appointed was to have the wife subject to her husband. Rather than have the wife do what the husband would not have done, the Lord released a wife from her vow in case her husband would not consent to have it performed. Now then I ask: is the disposing of goods a greater matter than the performing of a vow? Or does a wife have more liberty in these days than in former days? If she does, by what law? Was there ever, under the law, a stricter charge laid on wives than this: “Let wives be subject to their husbands in everything”?

Objection. That point of a woman’s subjection in performing her vow is a particular case expressly ruled, but this of disposing of goods is not.

Answer. By particular laws and examples the Scripture gives directions for other cases like them; and arguments drawn by just and necessary consequence are counted as sound as express testimonies. As for the claim that this particular in question is not expressly decided, I take the reason for it to be this: in former times they marked the extent of the general law of a wife’s subjection so well that it never came into question with them to do this or other such things without their husbands’ consent. Good wives did not take that liberty, nor did that liberty have any defenders.

2. Objection. The case of a wife’s disposing of goods is unlike that of vows, because vows are voluntary, but disposing of goods, as a work of mercy, is necessary.

Answer. Though it was a voluntary thing to make or not to make a vow, yet once a vow was made, it was not in the power of the person who made it not to perform it: it was a678 necessary duty to perform a vow, even expressly commanded. As for the alleged work of mercy, I will679 show hereafter that a wife is not necessarily bound to it.

§. 26. Of human laws which restrain wives from disposing of goods without or against their husbands’ consent.

A fourth reason is taken from the laws of men, to which we are subject, and which we must obey even for conscience’ sake, so far as they do not thwart God’s law; and in this case they do not, as the reasons gathered before out of God’s word show.

Now our law says that680 every gift, grant or disposal of goods, lands or anything else whatever made by a married681 woman, and each and every bond and conveyance of land made by her, and recovery allowed by her, are void if they are done without her husband’s consent. Yes,682 if she does wrong to another, she has nothing with which to make satisfaction while she is married: either her husband must make it, or it must be made by the imprisonment of her person. And683 though she has an inheritance of her own, yet she cannot grant any annuity out of it while she is married, without her husband; if any deed is made to that purpose without his consent, or in her name alone, it is void in law. Yes,684 if there is a dispute between the husband and his wife, by which certain lands of the husband’s are assigned to the wife with his consent, and she grants an annuity to a stranger out of such lands, the grant is void. And685 if he covenants to give her such and such clothing yearly, she cannot dispose of it as she pleases without his consent, but may only use and wear it herself.686 Nor can she lease her own land for years, for life, etc. If she does, it is void, and the lessee who enters by force of it wrongfully dispossesses the husband, and is a trespasser. And687 if she sells anything, the sale is void, unless she is a merchant, where custom enables her to trade. Finally,688 she cannot make executors without the consent of her husband, nor a devise of land, or a will.689 If she makes a will and leaves her own inheritance by it, and her husband dies, and she dies afterward without publishing it anew, it is of no force, because it was void from the first. These and many other such cases which might be cited plainly show that by law a wife does not have power of herself, without her husband, to dispose of the common goods of the family.

§. 27. Of the harms which may follow from a wife’s disposing of goods without or against her husband’s consent.

A fifth reason may be taken from the harms which would690 follow if this liberty were given to women. They are these:

1. The wealth of the family might be wasted before any remedy could be thought of. For if the wife may dispose of the goods without her husband’s consent, it must also be granted that she may do it without his knowledge; for it is to be supposed that if he knew of the disposing of what he does not like, he would hinder it. And if it is done without his knowledge, then what he thinks is remaining as a stock for the family may be laid out by the wife, and nothing left; whereas if he knew of the spending of that stock, he might perhaps be more thrifty and sparing in other expenses.

Objection. This liberty is not granted to wives beyond their husbands’ means.

Answer. Wives cannot always know their husbands’ means. For a husband may be deeply in debt, and yet, to maintain his credit, by which he hopes to raise his fortunes, he may allow a liberal provision for his house. If his wife then gathers from this that he is very rich, and is accordingly very bountiful in her gifts, she may soon go beyond his means, and so increase his debt that he will never be able to recover himself.

2. Persons of contrary religions and dispositions who are691 outside the family might be maintained by the goods of the same family. For if the husband were of one religion and the wife of another, he might maintain those of his religion without her knowledge, and she might maintain those of her religion without his knowledge.

Objection. This liberty of disposing of goods given to the wife is limited within the bounds of the household of faith.

Answer. If divines grant wives this liberty, the wives will judge and determine for themselves who are of the household of faith. Popish wives will say (say what we can to the contrary) that Jesuits, priests and friars are of the household of faith, and its principal members.

3. Many quarrels and contentions would arise from it between692 husband and wife. For if a wife persists in doing what her husband will not consent to, surely not one husband in a thousand will bear it well, but will rather seek every way he can to cross her, thinking himself despised if she has her way whether he will or not.

Objection. Wives must use this liberty with all due respect for their husbands’ authority.

Answer. If the husband firmly stands on his authority, and in spite of all the fair means that can be used will not grant this liberty, I do not know what better respect she can show to this authority than to refrain and abstain from doing what she would otherwise most gladly do. But if, when it comes to the last point, she says it is her right, and that if she cannot have his consent she will do it without his consent, she shows no great respect in this.

Many other harms might be listed, but I will not dwell on them any longer. Only, from these let it be well considered whether it would not be better for a family that the husband should be barred from disposing of the goods without his wife’s consent (so that there might be, according to the proverb, only693 one hand in the purse) than that both husband and wife should have liberty to dispose of them without each other’s consent.

§. 28. Of ownership of goods, whether it gives a wife liberty to dispose of them as she will.

To justify a wife’s liberty in disposing of the common goods694 of the family without her husband’s consent, it is said that she has a true right and ownership in those goods.

1. Answer. Even if it were granted that a wife has true ownership of the goods, this conclusion would still not follow from it, that she has power of herself to dispose of the goods without her husband’s consent. For the authority which God has given a husband, and the subjection which he has laid on a wife, restrain her power and liberty in what is her own. For example, suppose695 that a woman at the time of her marriage has a lease for years, or the wardship of the body and lands of a minor, or has it by gift or696 purchase after marriage: she cannot give it away, however extreme the need may be, but her husband may dispose of it at any time during the marriage, and his disposing of it will cut off the wife’s claim. Or suppose that the only child of her father is an heiress of land, and has in herself (her father being dead) the full possession of it; or that a widow has the right to, and possession of, her husband’s estate, and, so possessed, is married to a husband: does she, being a wife, have liberty to dispose of that estate which she brought with her without or against her husband’s consent? I think no one will say so. I am sure that whatever she gives, lends, sells or otherwise disposes of without his consent, he may, if he will, recover again for his lifetime; and yet no man will deny that she has the truest interest and ownership in the lands and inheritance named above.

Objection. May she not dispose of her own inheritance as well as of those goods or revenues which her husband gives her?

Answer. No; for the husband’s gift is a general consent of his for her to dispose of what is given her as she sees fit.

§. 29. Of the reasons against a wife’s ownership of the common goods of the family.

2. Answer. It may safely be denied that a wife has ownership of the common goods of the family, of which she is not an heir. For ownership of goods is a civil matter, and is to be limited according to the law of man under which we live. Where the law or custom of the place makes all the children coheirs, all have an equal right to their separate parts; where the eldest only is made heir, he has a right to all; where the youngest only is made heir, he has a right to all; but neither the law of nations nor the law of the land where we live gives the wife ownership.697 By the common law marriage is a gift of all the goods and personal chattels of the wife to her husband, so that no kind of ownership of them remains in her.698 And all personal goods and chattels given to the wife during marriage are at once, ipso facto, transferred (as to the ownership of them) to the husband. So by our law she is so far from gaining any ownership in her husband’s goods by her marriage that she loses all the ownership she formerly had in her own goods. Yes,699 even her necessary clothing is not hers to own. While she remains a wife she is (to use the law’s phrase) under covert baron, that is, under her husband’s covering.700 She can neither lease, sell, alienate, give, nor otherwise rightfully make anything over, no, nor even make a will to dispose of any goods, while her husband lives, without his consent: which a husband may yet do while his wife lives, and that without or against her consent.

Objection. The law gives a wife a right in a great part of the husband’s goods, providing for her jointure or her widow’s third, which the husband cannot dispose of without her consent.

Answer. This provision is only for the time of her widowhood, in case she outlives him; but for the time that she remains his wife he may dispose of everything, and she can recover none of it till he is dead.

Objection. This restraint of wives holds only in the court of men.

Answer. Since it is not against the law of God, it must also hold good in the court of conscience. More than that, it agrees with the law of God and is grounded on it.

For (to leave out the proofs cited before) what could be the reason that the daughters of Zelophehad, who were heirs to their father, were forbidden to marry outside their father’s tribe, and that a law was made that no daughters who possessed any inheritance should marry outside their father’s tribe, except that all that a woman had before marriage passed to the husband and became his by virtue of marriage? This also is noted for that purpose by some, not unfittingly nor without probability: that it is the common phrase of Scripture to call husbands701 (but not wives) rich, implying by this that riches belong to husbands as their own. Yes, usually in Scripture goods and lands are said to be the husband’s.

Objection. The wives of Jacob call the goods which their husband had theirs, saying, “all the wealth that God has taken away from our father is OURS,” Gen 31:16.

Answer. They use the word ours in opposition to their father’s house, and in relation not to their persons but to their702 husband’s family; and therefore they add “and our children’s.” So by that place no greater right can be proved for wives than for children. When the Holy Spirit speaks of the same goods, he does not say, in relation to both husband and wives, their flocks, their substance, but only in relation to the husband, his flocks, his substance. For as in a mixture of wine and water, though the greater quantity is water, yet we call the whole wine, so in the common goods of the family, though the wife should bring the greater part, we call it all the husband’s.

§. 30. Of answers to the reasons for a wife’s ownership.

To prove a wife’s ownership of the common goods of the family, the following reasons are alleged.

1. Objection. Since marriage gives a wife a right to her husband’s body,703 much more does it give her a right to his goods.

Answer. I deny the consequence. For the use of the body is an act belonging only to the marriage bond, in which the difference between superiority and subjection does not appear: the wife has as great a power over the husband’s body as the husband over the wife’s. That is not so with the goods: not one thing can be named in which the power and authority of the husband consists more than in the goods.

2. Objection. In the form of marriage the man says to his wife, “With all my worldly goods I thee endow.”

Answer. 1. Those words are to be understood of the use of his goods, and not of ownership of them.

2. If a husband intends ownership by them, the ownership which she has by them she has not by virtue of the general law of marriage, but by his particular free gift.

3. Those words are not used in the form of marriage in all countries. If those words give the wife her ownership, then wives who are married without those words being used have no ownership; so this cannot be a general ground of liberty for all wives.

3. Objection. A wife has as good a right in her husband’s goods as the church has in Christ’s blood; but there the church has ownership.

Answer. Neither of those points can be proved. But if a wife’s right in her husband’s goods is like the church’s in Christ’s blood, what is gained by it? The church does not have power to dispose of his blood without or against Christ’s consent: the Church of Rome is counted a proud, usurping harlot for taking it on herself to do so.

§. 31. Of the privileges of wives above children and servants in and about the goods of the family.

Question. Where then is the wife’s preferment above servants and children, if she does not have ownership?

I answer, “Much in every way.”

1. There704 is due to her a freer and more plentiful use of all the goods than to them.

2. By her place she has the ordering and disposing of the goods allotted for the common use of the family, as was705 granted before.

3. Her husband ought to give her a portion to dispose of as she sees good,706 as we will show later, when we come to the husband’s duties.

4. She is a joint governor with her husband over the children and servants, as was shown707 before.

Again I answer that this argument might as well be brought against that fear, subjection and obedience which the Scripture expressly requires of wives; and it might be asked, if wives must fear and obey their husbands and be subject to them, where is their preferment above their children and servants? But708 it has been shown that, though the same things in substance are required of wives as are required of children and servants, yet there is a great difference in the manner of performing them.

§. 32. Of examples and other reasons alleged for the liberty of wives to dispose of goods.

2. Abigail’s example is alleged for a wife’s liberty, and709 the example of the good housewife described by Solomon.

Answer. 1. Abigail’s example was extraordinary. Besides, who can tell whether her husband’s heart did not so trust in her that he committed the whole government of the house to her, so that she had a general consent for what she did?

2. It is clear that the other good wife had her husband’s consent for what she did. For besides its being said that “the heart of her husband trusts in her,” it is also said that “her husband praises her.” Therefore he was neither ignorant of what she did nor unwilling that she should do it: it was neither without nor against his consent.

3. It is alleged that wives take as much care in getting710 goods, or in preserving them for the good of the family; therefore it is just and fair that they should have a like power in disposing of them.

Answer. Though the first part may be questioned, at least for the greater sort and number of wives, yet to answer this reason I need not question it; for the consequence does not follow, even if that is granted. The right of disposing of goods does not arise wholly from the care and pains of getting and preserving them, but from the order which the Lord has been pleased to set down. A wise and industrious child may be a means to raise and increase his father’s estate when his father takes little care and pains about it. Yes, a faithful and wise steward or other servant (as Jacob and Joseph were) may do much more by his pains and care in getting and preserving the goods of the family than his master; yet it will not follow from this that such a child or such a servant has as great a right and power to dispose of such goods as his father or his master.

4. The close union between man and wife is alleged:711 they are said to be yokefellows, and from this it is inferred that they have a like power in disposing of goods.

Answer. They are yokefellows in mutual fellowship, not in equal authority; and in relation to others, such as children and servants, not in opposition to each other. In this respect she is subject, not equal. If therefore he wills one thing and she another, she must not think to have an equal right and power: she must give place and yield.
