A Wife’s Not Going Against Her Husband’s Will (II)

The Third Treatise: Of Wives · §§. 33–42

§. 33. Of the subjection of wives in distributing goods to charitable uses.712

Some who grant that a wife is so subject to her husband in civil matters that she must not dispose of any part of his goods at her pleasure for any civil use deny that this subjection extends to giving alms and other such charitable uses.

Before I come to settle this question, let it be remembered that it was granted before that713 ordinary duty must give way to extraordinary need, so that relief in present necessity is not in dispute. Let it also be remembered that714 a wife may have goods of her own; indeed,715 it will be shown that a husband ought, according to his ability, to commit something to her discretion and disposal. Out of these and such goods she is as much bound as her husband to spend something on charitable uses, and (as God gives occasion) to reach out her hand to the poor and needy.716

Further, let this be laid down first: if a wife is forbidden or restrained by her husband, she ought to use all the good means she can, by herself and her family, to move her husband to grant her some liberty, so that she may have some opportunity to prove her merciful and charitable disposition. If she cannot prevail in this, then she ought to make known to her husband the cases of such persons as she thinks fit to be relieved, and use every argument she can to persuade him to give them some relief.

But suppose a wise, religious, merciful wife is married717 to a covetous worldling who, though he has sense and understanding enough to manage civil affairs and to provide for the outward, temporal condition of the house, yet has no heart to relieve the poor, and is not only unwilling to do good in that way himself, but will not allow his wife to do it. May a wife then secretly take some of the goods he has reserved for his own disposal and, absolutely without any kind of consent, distribute them to charitable uses? Or, though he expressly forbids her, may she dispose of them directly against his consent?

With reverent respect to better judgments, I think she must718 not (except as excepted before). For since it was proved before, in general, that she had no such liberty in disposing of goods, I cannot see how this particular end of giving alms can dispense with her general subjection “in everything,” unless there were some particular warrant for it in God’s word.

§. 34. Of general exhortations to works of mercy. How far they bind wives.

Objection. The many general exhortations to works of mercy, which are directed to all generally, without limitation to any particular persons, give wives sufficient warrant. Such as these: “Give alms,”719 “Let us do good,”720 “Do not neglect … to share with others,” etc.721

Answer. All these are strong motives to provoke wives to be merciful and charitable in such things as they can give by any means with their husbands’ consent, or in such things as their husbands have given them. Indeed, they are also strong motives to provoke husbands to allow them liberty to give alms. But in the case put forward they give wives no liberty. For it is a settled case, laid down by Christ himself, that works of charity must be done, and alms must be given, out of such things722 as we have, or which are in our power to give.723 Now if the husband will not give her that power, she has no power to give, and so she is excused. In this case her true will, and her faithful and earnest desire, will be accepted for the deed, according to what the apostle says: “If the willing mind is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what he does not have.” Many cases may be given in which inferiors are restrained from works of mercy. Suppose, for example, that a son or servant wants to visit someone sick or in prison, but his parent or master (though leave is asked) will not allow him, but charges him not to stir out of doors, or to go with him another way. Shall this son or servant do that work of mercy in spite of that charge?

§. 35. Of obedience to a husband in such things as he sinfully forbids.

Objection. 2. This restraint is not in the Lord, but rather against him and his word; therefore a wife is not bound by it.

Answer. Though the husband sins in restraining his wife, yet she may obey in that restraint, and that in the Lord, because the Lord, who has commanded her to be subject “in everything,” has nowhere given her warrant not to be subject in this particular. It is expressly said in the law concerning a wife’s vows that if her husband “nullifies them after he hears of them, then he will bear her iniquity.”724 Did he not then sin in restraining her, and was she not guiltless, though she yielded to his restraint? The condition between husbands and wives in this case is not unlike the case between other superiors in authority and their inferiors in subjection. Now other inferiors may lawfully abstain from such things as their governors sinfully charge them to abstain from. For suppose a son, grown to be a man, lives in his father’s house at his father’s expense and has no set portion of his own, and his father will not give him leave to spend anything on charitable uses: is he now bound to give alms? Will the curse fall on him if he does not give? I acknowledge indeed that it is a cross, both to such a son and also to a wife, to be so restrained; but not a curse or a sin. The sin and the curse lie on the heads of those who restrain them by virtue of their authority, in which they abuse their authority, as other governors may do and often do; and yet by this neither is liberty granted to subjects, nor authority taken from governors. In this comparison between a son and a wife I do not wish to be misunderstood. For I do not bring it to make the condition of a wife and of a son all one, but to show that those general precepts of giving alms may have their exceptions, as those who handle that point in particular give other examples. There must therefore be some further ground than the general command of almsgiving to prove the liberty of wives just named.

§. 36. Of Zipporah’s case in circumcising her son.

Objection. 3. A wife was made to be a help to her husband. Therefore, in the things in which he fails, she must make up for him, as Zipporah did, who performed a duty that belonged to her725 husband, and not to her.

Answer. She may be a help in many other things, though this is out of her power; indeed, in this too she may be a great help by counsel, persuasion and other such means. The case of Zipporah was extraordinary, and one of urgent, present necessity, even to save her husband’s life. Besides, Moses was unable to do it himself, but was willing that she should do it. Now what is this to ordinary cases, and to such things as husbands are well able to do themselves, but are altogether unwilling that their wives should do?726

But what if Zipporah’s example in this is not warrantable? For it does not appear that it was wholly approved by God. God often removes temporary judgments for the sake of the very work that is done, though it is done sinfully in its manner. Take as an instance the repentance of Ahab, 1 Kgs 21:29.

§. 37. Of the wife of Chuza’s case in ministering to Christ.

4. Objection. Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, ministered to Christ out of her means without her husband’s consent.

Answer. If this could be proved, it would be to some purpose. But this clause, without her husband’s consent (in which the main point of the question lies), is not in the text, nor can it be gathered from it with any good probability. All the show of probability that can be given for it is that Joanna is said there to be “the wife of Herod’s household manager Chuza.” But to show that that amounts to nothing, let it be noted:

1. That phrase does not imply that Chuza was then living. It is said that “David was the father of Solomon by Uriah’s wife,”727 but Uriah was not then living. Therefore the translators, for clarity’s sake, insert these words (her that had been) the wife of Uriah. So likewise Onan is commanded to sleep with his728 “brother’s wife,” yet this does not imply that his brother was then living.

Objection. Why should mention be made of Chuza, Herod’s household manager, if he was not then living?

Answer. To show that Joanna was a woman of high position, so that this fruit of her faith in following Christ was all the more commended. So, in another kind, Matthew is given the title729 “the tax collector” after he had wholly left that office, the more to commend his faith.

I do not here directly affirm that Chuza was then dead; but for anything this phrase implies, he might have been dead.

2. Some gather that this household manager was the royal official whose730 son Christ healed, and who then believed, “he and all his household.” If he was, then there can be no doubt that his wife followed Christ with his goodwill and consent.

3. Chuza, being Herod’s household manager, and so a man of high position and public employment, might, if he was then living, have deputed the managing of all affairs at home to his wife, as the731 husband of the good wife commended by Solomon did; and so she might have had at least a general consent.

I do not determine with certainty that any of these is expressly so; I only note them as probabilities, yet such as sufficiently overthrow the supposed liberty of a wife to give alms without any consent of her husband. For of all the probabilities, this one seems the most improbable. It can never enter my heart to imagine that Christ would give his enemies such an occasion of slander as to say that he carried other men’s wives about with him, without or against their husbands’ consent, and allowed them to spend their husbands’ goods on him. I would much rather think either that the women who followed him had no husbands living, or, if they had, that they did what they did with their husbands’ consent.

§. 38. Of the restraint of wives about allowance for themselves or families without their husbands’ consent.732

What has been said so far concerning a wife’s subjection in disposing of goods may also be applied to other things concerning herself, her children, servants, etc. Of this I will give some examples.

A wife has no power to appoint what she pleases by herself, without or against her husband’s consent, either for her own allowance or for her family; she must rather rest satisfied with what he appoints. For he, being the head, must have the overruling say in it. Besides, he knows better what can be afforded.

Question. What if a husband makes himself poorer than he is, and the allowance he appoints is lower than his means, and unbecoming his position and standing?

Answer. She ought, if she possibly can, by her own earnest persuasion or any other fair means, to move him to what tends to his honor and reputation. But if she can in no way prevail, her subjection requires contentment and patience.

§. 39. Of a wife’s subjection to her husband about children.733

A wife must not, absolutely without, or directly against, her husband’s consent, order and arrange matters for the children in giving them names, clothing their bodies, appointing their callings, their places of upbringing, their marriages or their portions.

1. As for giving names to children: besides that throughout734 Scripture this is for the most part laid on the husband, as on Abraham,735 on Zechariah736 and on others, and that husbands have ordinarily done so accordingly, as Adam,737 Lamech,738 Abraham739 and others, it is to be noted that when there was a difference between the man and his wife in naming a child, he giving one name and she another, the name he gave stood. Though Rachel740 named her youngest son Ben-oni, yet Benjamin (the name Jacob gave) was the child’s name. So also when Elizabeth741 told her relatives that her child’s name must be John, they would not rest in it until Zechariah had confirmed that name. Indeed, though Joseph was only the supposed father of Jesus, yet because he was the husband of Mary, the mother of Jesus,742 he was given this honor, to give the name to her child.

Where Scripture sometimes says that the mothers named their children, as Leah,743 Rachel744 and others, it is to be supposed, on the ground just named, that they had their husbands’ consent.

2. As for appointing place and marriage, it is noted that Rebekah745746 asked her husband’s consent. Though she told her son Jacob that he should go to his uncle Laban in Haran, to be kept safe there from the fury of Esau, yet she would not send him until Isaac747 had given his consent to his staying there and to his taking a wife from there.

3. As for appointing to a calling, it is noted of Hannah748 that,749 though before her child was born she had dedicated him to the Lord by a solemn vow, yet when the child was born750 she asked her husband’s consent about it.751

4. What is noted of Hannah, that she brought her son “a little robe” each year “when she went with her husband,”752 shows that she did not do it without her husband’s consent. Women are for the most part inclined to dress their children up above their husband’s position and calling, and therefore there is good reason that in this they should be governed by their husbands.

Objection. What if husbands are more eager than wives to have their children dressed vainly and unbecomingly?

Answer. A wife must do what she can to hinder it. If she can in no way prevail with him, she, because of her subjection, is much more excused than he could be if he allowed his wife to have her will in this.

5. The law that lays the charge on the husband to give753 such and such portions to his children, and the corresponding practice of husbands from time to time, show that the wife has no power of herself to order them.

§. 40. Of a wife’s subjection to her husband about ordering servants and animals.754

If wives must have their husbands’ consent in ordering and disposing of their children, who come out of their own womb, much more must they have it for their servants.

They must not take in or turn out servants against their husbands’ mind. In this point, as in many others, Sarah showed her wifely obedience, in that755 she would not deal harshly with her maid, though she was provoked, much less756 put her out of doors, until she had made the matter known to her husband. Though she failed in the manner, yet in the thing itself she is a good example. It is further noted and approved in the757 Shunammite that she asked her husband’s consent about sending a servant with her.

My meaning is not that wives who have servants allowed them to attend on them should ask their husbands’ consent whenever they have occasion to use them. For their husbands, by allowing them men to attend them, show their will and consent that they may use them as they see occasion. My meaning is that they should not use and employ their servants in such things as they know their husbands would dislike, unless they can gain their husbands’ consent.

Against these particulars of children and servants it may be objected that wives are parents of their children as well as husbands, and mistresses of servants as well as husbands are masters, and therefore have altogether as great a power over them as their husbands.

Answer. Indeed, if the husband’s authority does not come between, that may be granted in the relation between her and them. But since her power is subordinate to her husband’s, she does not have so great a power in relation to him; and the power of a wife that we are now speaking of is directly in relation to her husband.

The same may be said of their animals and livestock, a particular point also noted in the example of the Shunammite. Having occasion to use an animal, she went to her husband and said, “Please send me … one of the donkeys.”758

§. 41. Of a wife’s subjection in receiving strangers, traveling from home, and making vows.759

If wives must not use the things belonging to the house at their pleasure, much less may they bring strangers into the house and receive them without or against their husbands’ consent. The good Shunammite,760 so often named as a precedent for good wives, first asked her husband’s consent before she lodged a prophet of the Lord.

The same pattern is also commended to wives to move them not to travel from home without their husbands’ consent. For though that good wife had a very weighty and just occasion761 to go to the prophet, yet she would not go before she knew her husband’s mind.

As for a wife’s power to make vows: since the law gives a husband power to annul her vow when he knows of it,762 it implies that she ought to have his consent in making it, at least if she wants it to stand; and she ought to want that, or else she mocks God.

I have thought it good to mention these particular points to illustrate a wife’s subjection, because all of them are grounded on God’s word. Many others might be added to them, but these are sufficient.

§. 42. Of faults contrary to a wife’s subjection in doing things without or against their husbands’ consent.

Now let us consider the usual vices and faults contrary to these duties. The general sum of them all is for a wife to take it on herself to do what she pleases, whether her husband wills it or not, either not wanting him to know what she does, or not caring though it is against his mind and will. Of this sort are

1. Those who secretly take money out of their husbands’ cabinets,763 tills or other such places where he keeps it, never telling him of it, nor wanting him to know it; likewise those who in the same way take wares out of the shop, grain out of the granary, sheep out of the flock, or any other goods, to sell and make money of, or to give away, or to use some other way, so that their husbands will never know, if they can help it. Such wives sin heinously in this, and that in many respects.

First, they disobey the ordinance of God in a main branch of their particular calling, which is subjection.

2. They repay badly the care and pains their husbands take for their good. Many such wives repay evil for good, which is a devilish quality.

3. They are often a means of wasting and impoverishing their husbands’ estate.

4. By this they show themselves no better than764 pilfering thieves. All that can be justly and truly said for their right in the common goods cannot defend them from the guilt of theft. They are the more dangerous the more they are trusted and the less they are suspected; and their deed is the more heinous the dearer their husbands ought to be to them.

5. They are a very bad example to the other inferiors in the house. For a man seldom has a deceitful wife without some of the children or servants being made accessory to it, being made her instruments to take the goods and dispose of them as she orders; and so they are made unfaithful.

6. They make themselves slaves to their own children and servants, whom they dare not displease for fear they should tell what was done.

7. They teach their children and servants to be thieves. For besides that those whom their mistresses use to steal for them are by that made accessory to their sin, they will also steal for themselves when their mistresses will not know. So, what with the wife’s stealing one way and the children’s or servants’ another way, a man’s estate may be wasted like dew before the sun, and he not know which way it went.

2. Those who will have whatever allowance they think best for765 themselves and the family, and scornfully say, They will not live on what their husbands provide: they know best what allowance is fittest for the family, and that it will have. Many will make their husbands’ ears ring with it, and indeed make the whole house (if not the street too) ring with it, if they think their allowance does not match the utmost extent of their husbands’ estate. This impatience and insolence, as it crosses God’s ordinance, so it makes life miserable for them both.

3. Those who pamper, dress or in any way bring up their children766 otherwise than their husbands would, even to their husbands’ grief and dishonor: keeping them at home when their husbands, for their better education, would have them away from home. As these sin in hindering the good of their children, so they also sin in not yielding to their husbands.767

4. Those who will have their own will about servants, taking in and putting out whom they please and when they please; using some servants whom they find suit their own purpose, to the harm of their husbands; and carrying themselves so sharply768 and shrewishly toward others who serve their husbands’ purpose that a good, trusty, faithful servant cannot stay long in the house.

5. Those who secretly lend out their husbands’ horses or other769 such animals, caring more to please a vain friend than to please a good husband. This fault is all the greater when it is done to the husband’s loss and harm.

6. Those who are most merry and festive when their husbands are farthest away and cannot know it. Solomon sets it down as a mark of a harlot,770 to deck out her house and to look for guests when her husband “has gone on a long journey.” Then she ought to be most solitary, and by abstaining from merry gatherings to show that nothing can dampen her mirth more than the absence of her husband.

7. Those who think their houses a prison to them, who cannot771 stay at home long. They think they have power to go when and where they will, and to stay out as long as they please, whatever their husbands think of it.772 The apostle lays this down as a mark of a wanton wife and an idle homemaker: “They … learn to be idle,” he says, “going from house to house.” Therefore in773 another place he exhorts them to be “keepers at home.” The wise man goes further, and makes this another mark of a harlot, that “her feet do not remain at home,”774 which we may see borne out in the Levite’s adulterous wife,775 whose fearful end was a stamp of God’s judgment on such loose wickedness.

8. Those who do not care how or to what they bind themselves776 without their husbands’ consent or knowledge. Those especially offend in this who, being seduced by Jesuits, priests or friars, take the sacrament, and on that bind themselves by solemn vow and oath never to read an English Bible, nor any Protestant books, nor even to go to any of their churches or to hear any of their sermons; and most of all those who enter some popish nunnery and vow never to return to their husbands again.

Objection. Hannah777 vowed her child to God without her husband’s consent; why may they not much more vow themselves to God?

Answer. She was certainly persuaded that her husband would not be against it, and so she had an implicit consent. This may well be gathered, because she afterward made it known to him, as the778 name given to the child, and779 Hannah’s words, “I will take him to appear before the Lord and to stay there permanently,” and her husband’s answer, “May the Lord confirm His word,”780 and781 his going up with her when the child was dedicated to the Lord, all show.

So much for the first branch of a wife’s submission, in abstaining from doing things without her husband’s consent. The second follows: in doing the things he requires.

A Wife’s Active Obedience to Her Husband

The Third Treatise: Of Wives · §§. 43–50

§. 43. Of a wife’s active obedience.

It is a good proof and test of a wife’s obedience to abstain from doing such things as she would otherwise do, if her husband’s contrary will did not restrain her. But that is not enough: an active obedience must be yielded as well as a passive one. That old law mentioned before (“your desire will be subject to your husband, and he will rule over you”) implies as much too. If she refuses to do what he wants her to do, her desire is not subject to him but to herself, nor does he rule over her.

This active part of her obedience concerns

1. His commands: readily doing what he lawfully782 commands.

2. His reproofs: carefully setting right what he justly blames.

As for the first, a wife ought to be so far from scorning to be commanded by her husband that the very knowledge she has, by any means, of her husband’s mind and will ought to have the force of a strict command with her. This readiness to obey is commended in the wives of Jacob. When Jacob had told them what reasons he had to leave their father’s house, and so intimated that he meant to leave and wanted them to go with him, then, even before he had expressed his will in particular, they readily answered, “Do whatever God783 has told you.” By this they gave him to understand that they were ready to yield to whatever he wanted done.

§. 44. Of a wife’s willingness to live where her husband wishes.784

To make this part of a wife’s obedience somewhat clearer, I will illustrate it by two or three particular instances recorded and approved in God’s word.

The first is that a wife ought to be willing to live where her husband wants her to live.

The wives of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob showed their wifely obedience in this. Though their husbands brought them from their own country and from their fathers’ houses, yet they did not refuse to go with them, but lived in a strange country, and that in tents.

Note in particular what Jacob’s wives say to their husband in this case: “Do we have any portion or inheritance left in our father’s785 house?” By this they imply that, since it was their husband’s pleasure to go, they would no longer stay in their father’s house to look for any further portion or inheritance there.

These examples further show that if a husband has just occasion to move from one country to another, and within those countries from place to place, his wife ought to yield to go with him, if he requires it of her. Note what the apostle says: “Have we no power to take along a wife?”786 That question implies a strong assertion. Since the husband, then, has the power to take a wife along from place to place, she ought to submit herself to that power. This clause (“as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas”) shows that this was not only a power that might be used, but one that was used by husbands and yielded to by wives.

Objection. The examples just named are extraordinary, and on extraordinary occasions.

Answer. Yet they may be patterns for ordinary occasions that are lawful and warrantable. Was it not an extraordinary act of Elijah to pray first that there might be no rain,787 and then again that there might be rain? Yet this is set forth as a general pattern to move us to pray for lawful things.

Now in laying down this duty I added the clause and caution of just occasion, to answer both those who, out of discontent or superstition, leave the land where the true gospel is upheld and preached and go into idolatrous places, and also those wandering, giddy heads who, only to satisfy their own whims and to see the fashions, as we say, can never rest in one place, but are continually moving from country to country and from place to place. In such cases I think (to use the words of the apostle) a wife “is not bound.”788

But if a man is sent on an embassy by his prince or country; or if a preacher or professor is called into another country, as Bucer and Peter Martyr were into England in King Edward’s days (which is usual in other countries to this day); or if a man is sentenced to long imprisonment, and on these and other such occasions he requires his wife to be with him, she ought in duty to yield to his demand.

Contrary to this is the mind and practice of many wives who,789 being attached and devoted to one place more than another, such as the place where they were born and brought up, where their greatest, best and most friends live, and where they have good acquaintance, refuse to go and live where their husband’s calling lies, however much he requires and desires it. So many husbands, to their great loss, are forced for peace’s sake to yield to their wives, and so either to give up their calling or to keep two houses. From this it follows that sometimes they must neglect their servants and calling, and sometimes be absent from their wives, if not from their children also. Some wives claim that they cannot endure the smoke of the city, others that they cannot endure the air of the country; whereas in truth their own whims and fancies stifle them more than either city smoke or country air. I cannot call such the daughters of Sarah in this.790 They are not like those “holy women” named before, who “put their hope in God and were subject to their husbands,” but rather like that loose wife of the Levite, who would not live in her husband’s791 house in the hill country of Ephraim, but at her father’s house in Bethlehem in Judah. Such wives as I speak of may be more chaste in marriage, but in wifely subjection they are little more dutiful. Let this be taken for a fault, and it will be amended all the sooner.

§. 45. Of a wife’s readiness to come to her husband when he requires it.792

Another particular instance of a wife’s readiness to yield to her husband’s command is to come to her husband when her husband requires it, either by calling her or by sending for her. The793 wives of Jacob named before, being sent for to come to their husband in the field where he was, made no excuse, but came at once. Wives ought to subject their wills to their husbands so far in this that, though it may seem to them somewhat beneath them to come, yet if their husbands want it so, they must yield; otherwise they seem even to “despise their husbands.”794

Contrary to this is Vashti-like defiance, when wives think and795 say that it is a servant’s part to come when called or sent for, and that they will never yield to be their husbands’ servants, to come at their command. By the same reasoning all duties of subjection may be rejected. But as for this particular, let such proud796 dames note the outcome of Vashti’s stubbornness. As many excuses might be made for her, I think, as for anyone. For first, she was797 of royal descent, being the daughter of a king. Secondly, she was then among the honorable women of the kingdom. Thirdly, the king was drunk when he sent for her. Fourthly, he sent for her to show her beauty before crowds of men, which was not seemly. But all these were not enough to excuse her fault and free her from blame. First, though she was of royal parentage, yet she was a wife, and her husband sent for her. Secondly, being among the noble women of the kingdom, she should all the more have shown herself a pattern of subjection in this respect. Thirdly, though he was drunk, yet he remained a husband, and what he commanded was something she could have done without sin. Fourthly, if she thought the thing unseemly, she should first have used all the fair means she could to be spared; but if she could not prevail by any of them, then (since the thing was not absolutely unlawful and a sin) she should have yielded.

Objection. Her fault was not that as a wife she did not come to her husband, but that as a subject she did not come to her sovereign.

Answer. Her fault was in both; and in the judgment passed against her the former was urged most, namely that by her798 example all women might learn to “despise their husbands.”

2. Objection. Her deed is censured so only by heathen men, who had no understanding of God’s word.

Answer. 1. Holy Scripture, by the separate circumstances it notes so distinctly, intimates that her rebellious deed was a notorious fault; and accordingly both799 judicious commentators and preachers charge her with sinful disobedience to her husband.

2. Though they were heathen, yet by the very light of nature they showed what subjection is required of wives to their husbands; and this makes the sin all the worse.

3. Abimelech was only a heathen man; yet his sentence concerning a woman’s subjection, in these words, “he is to you a800 covering of the eyes,” is taken to be judicious, and, since it is approved by the Holy Spirit, to be a good proof. As for that particular case of Vashti, why is it recorded at such length in Scripture, if not for the instruction and admonition of wives?

§. 46. Of a wife’s readiness to do what her husband requires.801

A third particular instance of a wife’s readiness to yield to her husband’s command is to do whatever business he requires of her. When three men suddenly came to Abram, and he wanted to receive them, he told his wife, “Quick! Prepare three measures of fine flour,” etc.802 And she did it accordingly. Jeroboam, having a weighty occasion to send to Ahijah the prophet, thought it fitting to send by his803 wife; and she accordingly went (though a queen). She did as her husband wanted.

Contrary to this is the disposition of many wives, who will not do804 anything on command. If such a wife’s husband, wanting to receive a friend on short notice, uses Abram’s phrase, “Quick! Prepare,” etc., she will say, “Let him come and do it himself, if he wants it done so quickly; I will not be his drudge.” Or if, having a matter of importance and secrecy, he wants his wife to do it herself, she will reply, “I am none of your servants. Can you not give it to one of them, or do it yourself?” Yet such wives will be ready to command their husbands to do every trifle, and if he does not do it, they can reply, “Is this such a great matter? And may a wife not speak to her husband?” If the point of obedience were well learned, it would cast such wives in another mold.

These few particulars may serve for direction in many hundreds. I proceed to the other part of a wife’s active obedience, which concerns her husband’s reproofs.

§. 47. Of a wife’s meekly taking a reproof.805

The husband, having authority over his wife, has power by virtue of it (indeed, it is his duty) to rebuke her when there is needful cause. It therefore follows by just consequence806 that it is her duty to yield obedience to it. This ought to be done all the more because the chief test of sound obedience lies here. For nothing is so hard to stomach as reproof: she who yields when she is rebuked will yield much more when she is entreated. This point of obedience is shown in two ways.

1. By meekness in taking a reproof.

2. By striving to set right what is justly reproved. The very point of obedience lies especially in this latter; the former is a good preparation for it, without which it will hardly be done, at least not done well.

Meekness in this case is one of the chief fruits of807 that “meek and quiet spirit” which Saint Peter commends to wives. However justly Rachel deserved blame for coming in a fuming temper and with an imperious command to her husband, yet because she meekly took his sharp reproof (for she did not answer back against it, but meekly gave a direction for better accomplishing her desire), her example is commendable. Commendable, I say, not in the matter of her direction, but in her patient bearing of reproof.

Much wisdom may be learned from this. For when808 any meekly take a reproof, by this they hold down their anger and keep it from rising like a cloud before their understanding and darkening it; and so they can better judge whether the matter reproved is just or not, and whether it needs setting right or not. Those who are impatient of reproof, and fret and fume against it, cannot judge this so well. The virgin Mary made good use of Christ’s reproving her,809 and by it learned and taught a good point of wisdom: namely, so to refer our affairs to Christ that we wait for his pleasure, and do not prescribe to him time, means, manner or any other such circumstances.

Question. What if the husband’s reproof is bitter?810

Answer. He forgets his place in this, yet she must not forget her duty because of it. If Jacob’s reproof is well noted, we will find it very sharp. For it is expressly said that “Jacob became angry with Rachel” (Gen 30:2), so that he spoke in anger. The manner and form of his words, being a question, and the811 matter too, “Am I in the place of God,” etc., show sharpness. Yet (as was shown before) she showed meekness.

Question. What if his reproof is unjust?

2. Answer. Even so, meekness must not be forgotten. In such a case a wife may make a just defense to clear her own innocence and show her husband’s error. But if he refuses to hear her, or will not believe her, then (as Saint Peter speaks in another812 case) she must, being “conscious of God,” “endure the pain of unjust suffering.”

The two reasons he gives there in that other case may fittingly be applied to this one.

1. In general, this is “to be commended”: it is a grace, a glory to813 her, a matter that deserves praise and commendation.

2. In particular, it is “commendable before God”: however roughly and perversely their husbands814 may deal with them, yet God will graciously regard them, if in obedience to his ordinance they patiently bear their husbands’ unjust reproofs.

3. I may add this reason too: that in this way they will show themselves good Christians indeed, in that they are not “overcome815 by evil.”

Contrary to this is the mind of those who will by no means tolerate a rebuke from their husbands. It makes no difference whether it is just or unjust: if their husbands reprove them, they are sure to have the reproof thrown back in their faces, and that with greater violence than it ever came from them. There are some who seem to be very good wives until they are tried by the touchstone of reproof. But then, though the reproof is most just in matter, most mild in manner, and given in private between their husbands and themselves, yet they grow so impatient, or rather mad, that they do not refrain from giving their husbands the most scornful speeches they can invent, using bitter curses and execrations besides, and threatening to drown or hang themselves if they are crossed in their wills. Indeed, further, if wise husbands bear with them in their anger, and after it has subsided tell them how unbecomingly they behaved for their place, they will seek to justify themselves and lay all the blame on their husbands for crossing them in their will. Or if they cannot help seeing their fault, yet they will only say, “It is my infirmity,” and yet they always continue in that infirmity; and though they make a show of fearing God, yet they do not labor to purge this corrupt disposition out of their hearts. This for the most part is where contentions between man and wife come from. If wives would learn to be subject in this point, many quarrels that arise between them from time to time would be calmed, if not prevented. Michal816 the wife of David, and Job’s wife (though they gave just occasion to be most sharply reproved, yet) will rise up in judgment against these wives, because they were silent after they were reproved, and did not answer back. Solomon often calls those who cannot bear rebuke “scorners,”817 so that by this wives show that they are very scornful.

§. 48. Of a wife’s readiness to set right what her husband justly reproves in her.818

A further degree of obedience in bearing reproof is that819 a wife should readily set right what is justly reproved by her husband. I say justly, because where there is no fault, no amendment is needed. Patience may be needed (as was shown before), but no repentance for what is not amiss. But where anything is amiss, it must be set right. Rachel did amiss in820 bringing idols into her husband’s house. Her husband, in821 telling her among others to “get rid of the foreign gods,” reproved them all. On this she, with all the rest, “gave Jacob all their foreign gods.” This was a good amendment.

A reproof may justly be given either for a good duty omitted or for an evil thing committed, and the setting right, or amendment, must answer to it. A duty formerly omitted must, after the reproof, be more carefully observed and performed, if it is a continual duty and can be performed again; otherwise the amendment is a testimony of true sorrow for that fault. When an evil has been committed, if any means can be used to make up the hurt and repair the injury that followed from it, it must be done; if not, sorrow must be shown, as before, and care taken that the same, or the like, is not committed again.

As a good conscience requires as much of all Christians, whoever reproves them, so the respect a wife owes to a husband requires it in a special manner. Otherwise her fault is doubled: 1. by continuing in her sin; 2. by disobedience to her husband.

Contrary to this is the spirit of those who grow worse for reproof,822 being like those “scorners” (of whom Solomon speaks) who “hate” those who reprove them. It is the saying of some wives that if their husbands would let them alone they would do better, but that on rebuke they will never amend: the more their husbands find fault, the more they will go on doing what they do. What other judgment can be given of such than the one the wise man gives, that there is “more hope823 for a fool” than for them? So much for submission.

§. 49. Of a wife’s contentment with her husband’s present condition.824

Contentment is also a part of obedience. It concerns a man’s outward condition and means, in and with which a wife must rest satisfied and content, whether it is high or low, great or lowly, wealthy or needy, above, equal to, or below the condition she was in before marriage. Indeed, though a man has once been great in wealth, yet if he declines in it and is brought to a lowly condition, she ought to rest content. Job implies as much in his reply to his wife, saying, “Should we receive825 good from the hand of God, and not receive evil?” The evil he speaks of was the loss of his goods, servants and children, together with other miseries that Satan, by God’s permission, inflicted on him. The receiving of evil he speaks of was a resting content with it and a patient bearing of it. Evil may be laid on anyone, and so they may be forced to bear it; but only those who are content with it receive it. Now since he uses the plural number (WE), and, speaking to his wife, says (should we not receive evil), he shows that his wife ought, as well as he, to rest content in that poor and miserable condition. For

1. Man and wife being one flesh by virtue of their marriage union, both his advancement and his abasement are hers: as she rises with him, so she falls with him. Therefore, as she is willing to be advanced with him, so she must be content to be brought low with him.

2. If at the time of marriage her husband was of lower condition than she, she voluntarily put herself into that lowly condition. For a wife takes her husband (as he takes her) for better, for worse, for richer, for poorer. And will she not be content with her own act? If after marriage his condition declines and grows lower than it was, she is to be persuaded that God ordered it so, and that God aimed at her humbling as well as his. On that ground she ought, in dutiful submission to God’s overruling providence, to be patient and content. Job implies this in the phrase should we not receive evil from the hand of God? and in this one, “the Lord has taken away.”

3. A wife’s contentment is a great ease to her husband when he lies under a cross, and it makes the burden seem much lighter than it otherwise would, at least if he is a kind husband and moved by his wife’s distress, as he ought to be. For a loving husband in every distress is more troubled for his wife than for himself.

§. 50. Of wives’ discontent at their husbands’ condition.

Contrary to this is the impatience and discontent of wives at826 the lowliness and (as they think) the inferiority of their husbands’ condition, which is shown in many ways.

1. Some, when they are married, finding their husbands’ means827 weaker than they imagined, repent of their marriage, and do not hesitate to tell their husbands that if they had known before that they were no better men than they find them to be, they would never have taken them for husbands. In this, first, they betray their foolish indiscretion by saying, when it is too late, if I had828 thought this; and besides, they show their own rashness and thoughtlessness, in that they gave their hands and pledged their faith to those whom they did not know. If they say they were deceived by their relatives, whom they trusted, I answer that marriage is too weighty a matter to be left wholly to the trust of relatives. Everyone who agrees to be married ought to know well the person to whom in this case they yield; and above all they ought to seek direction, help and blessing from God. If, in spite of all the means they could possibly use, they are deceived, they are to look to God and see his providence in it, and to weigh duly whether the Lord has crossed their desire for their humbling, or to test their patience, wisdom and other such graces, or else to wean them from some vain and worldly delights to which they were too much addicted.

2. Others, seeing that their husbands’ means are decayed829 and wasted, never inquire into the cause, but lay all the blame on their husbands, and with their discontented looks, angry words and impatient behavior so vex their hearts that they make the cross much heavier than it otherwise could be. Even if the estate should be ruined by a husband’s wastefulness, a wife ought still to look to God’s providence in it, as was noted before.

3. Others, scorning to stoop and come down to their830 husbands’ present condition, through their pride and vainglory are a great means of making his condition much worse. For as long as they can get it by any means, they will not cut back anything of their fine clothing, delicate food, rich furnishings and other such things, which cause their husbands great expense. By this it also often happens that husbands are thought to be wealthier than they really are, and so greater taxes and charges than they can bear are laid on them for king, country, church, poor and the like.

4. Others, through discontent, lie lazing long in their beds,831 or sit idle when they are up, and will not take the least bit more pains to raise up and increase their husbands’ means. By this God is provoked more and more to weaken their means, so that he may punish such pride and laziness in wives all the more.
