A Wife’s Submission to Christ First

The Third Treatise: Of Wives · §§. 51–74

§. 51. Of cases in which a wife ought not to refrain from what her husband forbids.832

So much for the distinct branches of a wife’s subjection. The limitation and manner of performing it follow next.

To know the limitation of a wife’s obedience, and the manner in which she ought to yield subjection to her husband, two things must be considered:

  1. The place of a husband.
  2. The place of a wife.

The husband’s place is noted in this phrase, as to the Lord:833 by which it is shown that the husband, even by virtue of his place, stands to his wife in Christ’s place. This is laid down still more plainly in the words that follow, “the husband is834 the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the church.”

The wife’s place is indicated in these words, “as the church835 is subject to Christ, so let wives be to their own husbands.” From these it is clear that the obedience which a wife performs to her husband must be such an obedience as the church performs to Christ.

From the place of a husband I gather this general ground concerning a wife’s subjection, that

Subjection must be yielded to the husband as to Christ. From this two conclusions will follow. One is negative, which is this:

The wife must yield no other subjection to her husband than what is consistent with her subjection to Christ.

The other is affirmative, which is this:

The wife must subject herself to her husband in the manner in which she would or should subject herself to Christ.

The former is a necessary condition required of all inferiors in their subjection and obedience (as I showed836 before), and much more in a wife’s subjection to her husband, because of all who are unequal837 there is the least disparity between husbands and wives.

From this, for our present purpose, I gather these two other, more particular conclusions. The first of them is this:

1. If God expressly commands the wife some duty, and her husband will not by any means consent that she should do it, but forbids her, she may and ought to do it without his consent, or against it.

Two cautions are to be carefully observed about this conclusion:838

1. That the wife be sure that God has commanded her what she does without or against her husband’s consent. If she is in doubt, then she must wait, and refrain until she gains his consent. When two opposite cases meet together, and the one is doubtful, the other plain and express, the doubtful case must give way to the more evident. Now the law of subjection is unqualified: “your desire will be subject to your husband.”839 Its extent is general, in everything. The only reservation and exception is in the Lord. Therefore, if the wife is not sure that what her husband forbids her is against the Lord, she must refrain from doing it.

The second caution is that she use all the good means she can to gain her husband’s consent before she does, against his consent, even what is commanded. In this way she will testify to her subjection both to God and to her husband. To God, in that nothing can keep her from doing his express commandment: she will rather offend her husband than God, when one of them must be offended. To her husband, in that she pushes it to the utmost, and uses all the means she can to avoid offending him, so much so that he himself might see (if the god of this world did not blind his eyes) that the offense is in no way given on her part, but merely taken on his.

For proof of this, it is true beyond all contradiction that the wife is not bound to greater subjection to her husband than the subject is to the magistrate. But a subject ought not to refrain from a binding duty commanded by God because his governor forbids him. Take the example of Daniel,840 who prayed to God daily, though the king had made a solemn decree that no one should make any petition to God or man for thirty days except to the king. Take also the apostles,841 who preached the gospel, though they were expressly forbidden.

Though the Scripture is plentiful in giving examples of wives’ subjection, yet it is very sparing in recording examples of those who refused to be subject in such justifiable cases, so that wives would not take too great a liberty from them.

Some are recorded, but they are either extraordinary or not in every way justifiable. Abigail’s example842 was extraordinary, and therefore not to be imitated except in similar extraordinary cases.

The example of Rebekah,843 which may seem somewhat more to the point, is not in every way to be justified. For though what she intended was in substance very good, and ought to have been done, namely the blessing of Jacob (for God foretold that the blessing belonged to Jacob when he said, “The older will serve the younger”),844 yet because she did not remind her husband of God’s word, nor labor to persuade him to fulfill it, but went about the matter deceitfully, she cannot be justified in it. But in general this example shows that God’s word must be yielded to rather than a husband’s will.

For a better application of this point, I will lay down some particular instances agreeable to God’s word. Suppose a wife well instructed in the true religion is married to an idolatrous or profane husband, and he, without any just cause, forbids her to go to church, especially on the Lord’s Day, to pray in English, to read the word, to teach her children the principles of religion, to restore what she has gotten unjustly and fraudulently, and the like: she may and must do these things all the same.

Objection. Why should the giving of alms not be counted among these?

Answer. 1. Because the husband has a greater power over the goods than over these things.

2. Because almsgiving is not absolutely commanded to all, but to those who have the means to give; but these things are absolutely commanded to all.

§. 52. Of cases in which a wife ought to refrain from what her husband requires.

The other particular conclusion is this, that

If a husband requires his wife to do what God has forbidden, she ought not to do it.

Two cautions like the former are likewise to be observed845 about this point.

First, that she be sure (being truly informed by God’s word) that what she refuses to do at her husband’s command is forbidden by God.

Secondly, that she first labor with all meekness, and by all the good means she can, to dissuade her husband from urging and pressing on her what she cannot do with a good conscience.

A like proof may be brought for this as was brought for the former. For we know that a wife is not bound to greater subjection to her husband than a son is to a father; but a son may, in the case put forward, refrain from doing what his father requires and commands him to do. Take the approved example of Jonathan, who refused to bring David846 to Saul to be killed, though his father commanded him to do so. I might also show the same in Saul’s subjects and847 servants, who refused to kill the priests of the Lord at his command. Though a husband is not named in particular among those to whom we are forbidden to listen if they848 entice us to idolatry, yet by the rule of relation he is implied, and is gathered by just consequence from this clause, “your friend who is as your own soul”; for who is so dear as a husband?

To illustrate this in some particulars, as I did the former: if a husband commands his wife to go to Mass, to a stage play, to play at dice, to prostitute her body to impurity, to go about garishly and whorishly dressed, to sell by scant weights, short measures, or the like, she ought not to do it.

§. 53. Of wives’ faults in showing more respect to their husbands than to God.

Contrary to this limitation is, on the one side, a fawning, flattering disposition in those wives who seek to please their husbands so much that they do not care if they displease God (Jezebel was such a one; to please her husband she most wickedly849 plotted Naboth’s death); and on the other side, a fainting, timid heart, which makes them fear their husbands more than they fear God. Good Sarah,850 that worthy example of good wives in other things, failed somewhat in this. If wives duly considered, and always remembered, that they have a husband (namely Christ) in heaven as well as on earth, and that there is a greater difference between that husband and this than between heaven and earth, and that in giving reward and in taking revenge there is no comparison between them, then their care to please their husband in heaven, or their fear of offending him, would be much greater than their care to please, or fear to offend, their husband on earth. If anything were commanded or forbidden them by their husbands on earth against Christ, they would say, “If I do this, or refrain from that, I would be dealing falsely against my own soul; for nothing can be hidden from my husband in heaven. Yes, in this I would be obeying Satan rather than God.”

§. 54. Of the manner of a wife’s subjection to her husband.

The second general conclusion, concerning the manner of a wife’s subjection, which was gathered from the place of a husband, was this, that

The wife must subject herself to her husband in the manner in which she would or should subject herself to Christ. The particle As in this clause (as to the Lord) implies as much.

This very conclusion is also inferred from the place of a wife. In the same place that the church is to Christ, a wife is to a husband; therefore such subjection as the church yields to Christ, a wife must yield to her husband. The very words of the apostle expressly affirm this.851 Now we know that every Christian wife in her own person ought to yield that obedience to Christ which the church in general does; therefore she also must yield such subjection to her husband as she should to Christ.

Question.852 What if a husband is an enemy of Christ? Must such subjection be yielded to an enemy of Christ as to Christ himself?

Answer. Yes, because in his office he stands in Christ’s place, though in his heart he is an enemy. In this case the wisdom, patience and obedience of a wife will be best tested. It is said of the church that she is a lily among thorns.853 She remains lily-like, white, soft, pleasant and lovely, though she is joined with thorns, which are rough, prickly and sharp. So a wife must be mild, meek, gentle and obedient, though she is married to a crooked, perverse, profane, wicked husband. In this way her virtue and grace will shine out the more clearly, just as the stars shine most brightly in the darkest night. Among wives Abigail deserves great praise, who did not forget her duty, though she was married to a churlish, covetous, drunken sot, a very Nabal in name and deed. As for those who take occasion from the wickedness of their husbands to neglect their duty, they add a curse to their cross. For it is a cross to have a bad husband, but to be a bad wife is a sin, which brings down a curse. Therefore let wives turn their eyes from the disposition of their husband’s person to the condition of his place; and, by virtue of that place, seeing that he bears Christ’s image, be subject to him as to Christ.

This general conclusion might be applied to the matter of subjection as well as to the manner. For the church acknowledges Christ as her superior, fears him inwardly, reverences him outwardly, and obeys him both by refraining from what he forbids and by doing what he commands. Since these points have been distinctly and fully handled before, and applied to wives, I will not repeat them again. Therefore, to dwell now on the manner only, there are four854 virtues which are especially needed for this, with which the church seasons her subjection to Christ, and with which wives also may and must season their subjection to their husbands.

These are the four:

1. Humility, 2. Sincerity, 3. Cheerfulness, 4. Constancy.

§. 55. Of wives’ humility in every duty.855

Humility is that grace which keeps one from thinking of himself more highly than is fitting, and, because of the lowly opinion he has of himself, makes him think reverently and highly of others. So if humility is placed in a wife’s heart, it will make her think better of her husband than of herself, and so make her the more willing to yield him all subjection. The apostle requires it of all856 Christians as a general sauce to season all other duties; but in a special way it is needed by inferiors, and most of all by wives, because there are857 many privileges belonging to their place, which may soon make them think they ought not to be subject, unless they are humbly minded. That the church seasons her subjection with it is clear from the Song of Songs, where she often acknowledges her own lowliness and the excellence of her spouse.

Therefore as the church is humbly subject to Christ, so let wives be to their husbands.

§. 56. Of wives’ pride.

Contrary to this is pride, which puffs wives up and makes them think there is no reason why they should be subject to husbands: they can rule themselves well enough, yes, and rule their husbands too, as well as their husbands rule them. There is no more pestilent vice in an inferior than this. It is the cause of all rebellion, disobedience and disloyalty: “Strife comes only from pride.”858

§. 57. Of wives’ sincerity in every duty.859

II. Sincerity is that grace which makes one inwardly, in truth, what he appears outwardly to be in show. This is that “sincerity of heart”860 which is expressly required of servants, and it may be applied to wives, for indeed it belongs to all kinds of people. Because it is discerned only by the Lord, who “knows everyone’s heart,”861 it will move a wife to keep her eye on him in all she does, and to endeavor to approve herself to him above all. That is why uprightness and walking before God are often joined together: he who is upright will surely walk before God, that is, endeavor to approve himself to God, as Noah862 did, and as863 God commanded Abraham to do.

Though there were no other motive in the world to move her to subjection, yet for the sake of conscience toward Christ she should yield it. Peter864 testifies of holy women that they “put their hope in God and were subject to their husbands,” implying by this that their conscience toward God made them subject to their husbands. Was not Sarah’s subjection seasoned with sincerity when within herself,865 in her heart, she called her husband lord?

There is great reason why wives should subject866 themselves in sincerity. For

1. In their subjection even to their husbands they have to867 deal with Christ, in whose place their husbands stand. So, though their husbands, who are but men, see only the face and outward behavior, yet Christ sees their heart and inward disposition. Though their husbands see only the things they do before their faces, and can hear only of such things as are done before others, yet Christ sees and knows the things that are done in the most secret places there can be, when no creature besides themselves knows of it. Now let it be granted that in their outward conduct they give their husbands very good satisfaction and please them in every way; yet if sincerity has been lacking, with what face can they appear before Christ? He will take a very different kind of account of them. Before Christ all their outward show will be of no use to them at all.

2. In this lies a main difference between true, Christian,868 religious wives and merely natural women. These may be subject for self-interested reasons: namely, so that their husbands may love them the more, or live the more quietly and peaceably with them; or so that they may the more readily obtain what they desire from their husbands; or for fear of their husband’s displeasure and wrath, knowing him to be an angry, furious man, so that otherwise it might go worse with them: they might lack many needful things, or receive many hard blows, if they were not subject. But the other have regard to Christ’s ordinance, by which their husbands are made their head, and to his word and will, by which subjection is commanded them. In this way869 holy women subjected themselves. They cannot be holy who do not subject themselves in this way; for this is a sweet perfume that sends up a pleasing fragrance into Christ’s nostrils, and makes the things we do pleasant and acceptable to him.

3. The benefit of this virtue, once planted in a wife’s heart,870 is very great, both to her husband and to herself.

To her husband, in that it will make her show her respect for him before others, behind his back, as well as before himself in his presence. It will also make her faithful to him, and careful to do his will wherever he is, whether with her or away from her.

To herself, in that it will give her sweet inward comfort, though her husband should take no notice of her subjection, or misinterpret it, or repay it badly. For she might say as Hezekiah did, “Remember, O Lord, how I have walked before You in truth and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what was good in Your sight.”871

That the church seasons all her subjection with sincerity is clear from the fact that she is said to be “all glorious within”872 (there is no glory within without sincerity), and that she is often said to seek the one her soul loved.873 If her soul loved him, she was subject to him in sincerity of heart. Therefore as the church is sincerely subject to Christ, so let wives be to their husbands.

§. 58. Of wives’ merely outward subjection.

Contrary to sincerity is pretense, and a merely outward subjection, for show: when a wife even despises her husband in her heart, as Michal did David,874 and yet puts on a fair face before him, like that adulterous woman who “eats and wipes her mouth and says, ‘I have done nothing wrong.’” Solomon makes it a mark of a wicked wife to flatter with her words.875 Though such a wife should perform all the duties named before, yet they would all be nothing to God if they were done with a double heart and not in singleness of heart. For as many outward imperfections are pardoned by God where sincerity is, so no outward actions are accepted by him, however fair they seem, where there is no sincerity.

§. 59. Of wives’ cheerfulness in every duty.876

III. Cheerfulness is more visible than sincerity, and makes subjection the more pleasing not only to God but also to man, who may easily discern it by its effects.

As for God, just as he himself does all things willingly and cheerfully, so he expects his children to follow him in this, and so to show themselves his children. “God loves a877 cheerful giver”: not only a cheerful giver of alms, but of every duty to God and man.

As for men, it also makes them accept any duty much better when they observe that it is done cheerfully. It even enraptured David with joy to see his people offer their gifts willingly878 to the Lord. When a husband sees his wife perform her duty willingly and cheerfully, it cannot but stir up love in him. This cheerfulness is shown by a ready, quick and speedy performance of her duty. Sarah’s readiness to obey879 shows that what she did, she did willingly.

That the church subjects herself to Christ in this way is evident from what David says, “Your people shall be willing in the day880 of Your power.” Therefore as the church is cheerfully subject to Christ, so let wives be to their husbands.

§. 60. Of wives’ sullen and forced obedience.

Contrary to this cheerfulness is the sullen disposition of some wives, who will indeed be subject to their husbands and obey, but with such a scowling and sour face, with such pouting and muttering, that their husbands are grieved more by the manner than they can be pleased with the thing itself that their wives do. In this they show themselves like a bad-tempered cow, which, having given a good yield of milk, kicks it all over with her heel; and so they prove the proverb true, As good not to do it at all as to be never the better for it. Such subjection is in truth no subjection. It can be neither acceptable to God, nor profitable to their husbands, nor comforting to their own souls.

§. 61. Of wives’ constancy in doing their duty.881

IIII. Constancy is a virtue which makes all the rest perfect and sets the crown on them; without it they are all nothing. It is found in those who, after they have begun well, continue to do well to the end, and so reap the fruit of all. It concerns both continuance without interruption and perseverance without revolting and giving up altogether. So it is not enough to be subject by starts and fits, at one time yielding all good obedience, at another stubborn and rebellious. Nor is it enough to have been a good wife in former times and afterward prove bad. There must be daily going forward and holding on, continually, as long as husband and wife live together. This grace was in her of whom it is said, “She brings him good and not harm all the days of her life.” Such were all the holy wives commended in Scripture. Among other particulars, mention is made of the wife of Phinehas,882 who on her deathbed showed the reverent, good respect she had for her husband, though he was a wicked and vile man. This grace the church adds to all her other virtues: in all parts of her subjection she remains constant and faithful to death. By this it comes about that at length she receives the reward of her holy obedience, which is full and perfect communion and fellowship with her spouse Christ Jesus in heaven. Because of her immovable constancy it is said that “the gates of Hades will never prevail against883 her.” Therefore as the church is constantly subject to Christ, so let wives be to their husbands.

§. 62. Of wives’ repenting of their former goodness.884

Contrary to this constancy is, first, interruption of duty, a returning to it and a leaving off by turns, like one who is sick with a recurring fever: sometimes well, sometimes ill, now hot, now cold. That sometimes ceasing takes away all the worth, grace and glory from the sometimes doing. Besides, it is twenty to one that, through the corruption of nature, that changing and alternation of fits will at length cease and end in the worse. It is very likely that Michal was such a one. For at one time she showed herself so full of respect for David that885 for his sake she incurred the displeasure of the king, her father; at another time she despised him in her heart, and with her tongue886 taunted him.

Contrary also to the constancy named above is apostasy,887 that is, a complete abandoning of the former good course, as if a wife repented of her former good beginning. Such a one is she who is said to “abandon the guide of her youth and forget the888 covenant of her God.” For all we read to the contrary, Job’s wife was such a one. And such are many who in their younger years, while their religious parents lived (as Joash889 did while good old Jehoiada lived), behaved themselves very well, like good, dutiful wives; but having grown older, have also grown so stubborn and rebellious that it is as if they altogether repented of their former good beginning. This revolt arises sometimes from the evil counsel of wicked companions, and sometimes from their own proud disposition. I may say of these wives’ subjection, as the prophet says of the righteousness of those who turn away,890 their subjection will not be remembered, but in their rebellion they will die. Therefore as the church is subject to Christ, let wives be to their husbands.

§. 63. Of the extent of a wife’s obedience.891

The extent of a wife’s subjection (which now remains to be handled) is set down in these general terms (in everything),892 which are not to be taken so generally as if they admitted no restraint or limitation; for then they would contradict such cautions as these, in the fear of the Lord, as to the Lord, in the Lord. For man is so corrupt by nature, and of so perverse a disposition, that he often wills and commands what is contrary to God’s will and commandment. When he does so, that Christian principle laid down by the apostle as a settled case must prevail, “We must obey God rather than men.”893

Question. Why then is this extent laid down in such general terms?

Answer. 1. To teach wives that it is not enough for them to obey their husbands in some things, as they themselves think fitting, but in all things whatever in which the husband, by virtue of his superiority and authority, has power to command his wife. So this general extent excludes not God’s will, but the wife’s will. She may do nothing against God’s will; but she must do many things against her own will if her husband requires it of her.

2. To show that the husband’s authority and power is very large: it has no restraint but God’s contrary command, and if a wife is not sure of that, she must yield to her husband’s will.

§. 64. Of a wife’s striving to bring her judgment into line with her husband’s.894

From that extent I gather these two conclusions:

1. A wife must strive to bring her judgment and will into line with her husband’s.

2. Though in her judgment she cannot think what her husband requires to be the most fitting, yet she must yield to it in practice.

In the former of these, I do not say absolutely that a wife is bound to bring her judgment into line with her husband’s. For he may be deceived in his judgment, and she may see his error; and then, unless her understanding were blinded, she cannot hold to be true what he judges to be so. But I speak of an endeavor (when she has no sure and undeniable grounds to the contrary) to suspect her own judgment when it is contrary to her husband’s, and to think that she may be in error, and so not to be too peremptory and resolute in contradicting her husband’s opinion. This submission, even of her judgment, concerns not only necessary things, for which her husband has an express, definite warrant from Scripture, but also things doubtful, and things neither commanded nor forbidden; for this clause (in everything) extends even so far. And the subjection of a wife concerns not her practice only, but her judgment and opinion also. If she can bring her judgment to the lawfulness and fitness of what her husband requires, she will perform it much more cheerfully. To this purpose (as I take it) may be applied that exhortation of the apostle to women, that they “learn in quietness and full subjection.”895 Though this is meant chiefly of learning in the church, yet it does not exclude her learning at home from her husband: for in the next words he adds, “I do not permit a woman … to usurp authority over a man, but to be in silence.”

§. 65. Of wives’ overweening opinion of their own wisdom.

Contrary to this is the presumption of those wives who think themselves wiser than their husbands, and better able to judge matters than they are. I do not deny that a wife may have more understanding than her husband. For some men are very ignorant and dull; and on the other side, some women are well instructed, and have by this attained a great measure of knowledge and discretion. But many, though they have husbands of sufficient and good understanding, wise and discreet men, yet think that what they have once conceived to be true must be so. And such is their obstinacy that they will not be brought to think that they may err, but say that they will never be brought to think otherwise than they do, though all the husbands in the world were of another opinion. They are not much unlike the wise man’s fool, who thinks himself wiser than seven men896 who can give a reason.

§. 66. Of a wife’s yielding to her husband in things she thinks are not the most fitting.897

The latter conclusion, concerning a wife’s yielding in practice to what her husband requires, though she cannot bring her judgment to think as he does about its fitness,898 concerns things left free, namely, such as are in their particulars neither commanded nor forbidden by God: as the outward affairs of the house, ordering it, disposing of goods, receiving guests, etc.

Question. May she not reason with her husband about such matters as she thinks unfitting, and labor to persuade her husband not to persist in pressing them? Indeed, may she not endeavor to bring her husband to see the unfitness (as she thinks) of what she sees?

Answer. With modesty, humility and reverence she may do so, and he ought to listen to her, as the husband of the Shunammite did, 2 Kgs 4:23, 24. But yet, if despite all she can say he persists in his resolution and will have it done, she must yield.

First, her subjection is shown most of all in such cases. In them she plainly shows that what she does, she does out of respect for her husband’s place and power: were it not for that, she would not do it. Other things are not such evident proofs of her subjection to her husband. For if he commands her to do what God has expressly commanded, so that she ought to do it whether her husband commanded it or not, it may be thought that she does it at God’s command, and not at her husband’s. If her husband commands her to do what God has expressly forbidden, then she ought by no means to yield to it. If she does, it may rather be called a joint conspiracy of husband and wife together against God’s will (as Peter said to Sapphira, the wife of Ananias, “How could you+ agree together to test the899 Spirit of the Lord?”) than subjection to the image of God in her husband.

Secondly, her yielding in things neither commanded nor forbidden tends greatly to the peace of the family, as subjects’ yielding to their magistrates in such cases makes greatly for the peace of the commonwealth. For in differences and dissensions one side must yield, or else great injury is likely to follow; and of the two, who should yield but the inferior?

§. 67. Of wives’ making their own will their law.

Contrary to this is the custom of many wives, who will never do more than they themselves think fitting, however much their husbands require it. Surely they come far short of the apostle’s extent (in everything), though in their own eyes they may seem to be very subject. But when wives will be subject no further than their own judgments, wills and desires agree with their husbands’, what can be thought but that they are subject to their own wills rather than to the will of their husbands? Many such wives, from the least difference in judgment and opinion, even in the smallest matters, take occasion to refuse subjection, and think they have warrant enough to do so. From this much contention often arises, the fault of which lies especially on the wife’s neck, though the occasion may arise from the husband. And I think that wives themselves would judge so of similar cases between them and their children.

§. 68. Of care in choosing husbands to whom wives may be subject without grief.900

Objection. If the case is so between man and wife, it is not good to marry.

Answer. This is no good inference. For all the seeming hardness of a wife’s case lies in the wickedness of a husband who abuses his place and power, and not in the subjection which is required by God. For if a husband carries himself toward his wife as901 God requires, she will find her yoke easy, and her subjection a great benefit even to herself. Therefore I would urge those who are unmarried, whether maidens or widows, to be very careful in their choice of husbands; and in their choice to regard above all their good qualities and character, in which they bear the image of Christ as well as in their office and authority, so that their wives may be subject to them with joy and comfort, not with grief and anguish. Subjection will prove a vexation when the husband is an ignorant, profane, idolatrous, worldly, wicked man: the wives of such husbands are often brought into many straits. You+ widows and maidens who are free, do not be too free and eager in giving your+ consent to someone you+ do not know. Among other motives, think often of this point of subjection, to which all wives are bound: I say this both of its separate branches and of its extent. After you+ are married, it is vain to think of freedom from subjection. By taking husbands, and giving yourselves+ to be wives, you+ bind yourselves+ to the law of the man as long as he lives. Then, as you+ desire to be accepted by God and to find mercy and comfort from him, you+ must bear this yoke, however heavy and grievous it may seem to be.

§. 69. Of the reasons to move wives to do their duties.

So much for wives’ duties. The reasons noted by the apostle to urge those duties now follow. They are laid down in these words.

Eph 5:22. —As to the Lord.

v. 23. For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the church; and He is the Savior of the body.

v. 24. Therefore, as the church is subject, etc.

The main ground of all the reasons which the apostle suggests here is taken from the place in which God has set a husband. This is first implied by consequence in these words, as to the Lord, and then more plainly and directly expressed in these, the husband is the head of the wife. The particle set before these words (for), being a causal conjunction, shows that they are set down here as a reason. This reason is first set forth under a metaphor (head), and then amplified by the resemblance which a husband has in this to Christ (as Christ, etc.). This resemblance is further commended by the power and benefit that proceed from the headship of Christ in the strict sense, and of a husband also by consequence, in these words (and He is the Savior of the body). From a husband’s resemblance to Christ he infers that a wife should resemble the church, and so concludes, Therefore, as the church is subject to Christ, so let wives be to their husbands.

From the ground named above for a wife’s subjection, its separate amplifications, and the inference drawn from it, five separate and distinct reasons may be gathered to urge a wife’s subjection to her husband.

The first is taken from a husband’s place: he stands in the Lord’s place to his wife (as to the Lord).

The second from his office: he is a head to his wife.

The third from the image he bears, or from the resemblance between him and Christ (as Christ, etc.)

The fourth from the benefit that his wife receives from him (He is the Savior, etc.)

The fifth from the example and pattern of the church (as the church is subject, etc.)

§. 70. Of a husband’s place.

The place in which God has set a husband, as it serves902 to direct a wife in the manner of her subjection, of which I have spoken903 before, so it also serves to move a wife to yield such subjection as is required. This will clearly appear from these two conclusions which follow from it.

1. A wife, by subjecting herself to her husband, is in this subject to Christ.

2. A wife, by refusing to be subject to her husband, in this refuses to be subject to Christ.

That these two conclusions are rightly and justly gathered from the ground named above, I prove by like conclusions which the Holy Spirit infers from a like ground. It is evident that Christ Jesus, even incarnate and made flesh, was in the place of his Father. That is why Christ said to Philip, who desired to see the Father, “Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father.”904 Now mark what Christ infers from this, both on the one side (“he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me”) and on the other (“whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him”). It is also evident that ministers of the gospel stand in the place of Christ: for so the apostle says of himself and other ministers, “We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you+ in Christ’s place, etc.” Now mark again the conclusions Christ infers from this: on the one side, “Whoever listens to905 you+ listens to Me,” and on the other, “whoever rejects you+ rejects Me.” It was on this ground that God said to Samuel, concerning the people who rejected his government, “It is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me.”906

To apply this reason: I hope such wives as live under the gospel have so much religion and piety in them as to acknowledge that it well becomes them to be subject to the Lord Christ Jesus. Here, then, learn one special and principal part of subjection to Christ, which is to be subject to your+ husbands. In this way you+ will show yourselves+ to be the wives of the Lord Christ, as the apostle says of obedient servants that they are “servants of God.”907

Again, I hope none are so void of all religion and piety as to refuse to be subject to Christ. Here, then, take notice that if you+ willfully refuse to be subject to your+ husbands, you+ willfully refuse to be subject to Christ. On this ground I may fitly apply to wives what the apostle says of subjects: whoever resists the power and authority of a husband908 resists the ordinance of God, and those who resist will bring judgment on themselves.

This first motive is a strong motive. If wives duly considered it, they would be subject more readily and cheerfully than many are. They would not think so lightly of their husband’s place, nor speak so reproachfully against God’s ministers, who plainly declare their duty to them, as many do.

§. 71. Of a husband’s office.

The second reason, like this one, is taken from a husband’s909 office: he is the wife’s head. This is also urged for this very purpose in other places.

This metaphor shows that he is to his wife as the head of a natural body, both more eminent in place and more excellent in dignity; and by virtue of both he is a ruler and governor of his wife. Nature teaches us that this is true of the head of a natural body; and the apostle, by calling a husband a head, teaches us that it is as true of a husband. From this it follows that it agrees with common equity and with the light of nature that the wife should be subject to her husband. The apostle urges this argument in plain terms in another place, saying, “Does not nature itself teach you+, etc.?”910

Go therefore, O wives, to the school of nature; look at the outward parts and members of your+ bodies. Do they desire to be above the head? Are they reluctant to be subject to the head? Then let your+ soul learn from your+ body. Would it not be monstrous for the side to be raised above the head? If the body were not subject to the head, would not destruction fall on head, body and all its parts? Just as monstrous, and much more monstrous, is it for a wife to be above her husband; and as great, yes, and greater, disturbance and ruin would fall on that family. The order which God has set in it would be completely overthrown by this, and those who overthrow it would show themselves opponents of God’s wisdom in establishing order. This reason drawn from nature has force to move even pagans and savages to yield subjection; how much more Christian wives, since it also agrees with God’s word and is confirmed by it!

§. 72. Of the resemblance between Christ and a husband.

The third reason, taken from a husband’s resemblance to911 Christ in this, adds an edge to the former reason: in being a head, he is like Christ. So there is a kind of fellowship and partnership between Christ and a husband: they are brethren in office, like two kings of separate realms.

Objection. There is no equality between Christ, the Lord from heaven, and an earthly husband: the disparity between them is infinite.

Answer. Yet there may be likeness, resemblance and fellowship: inequality is no hindrance to these. Two kings may be more different in rank than a subject and a king, and yet those two kings are brethren and fellows in office. There may be a resemblance where there is no parity, and a likeness where there is no equality. The glorious, bright sun in the sky and a dim candle in a house have a kind of fellowship and the same office, which is to give light; yet there is no equality between them. So, then, a husband resembles not only the head of a natural body, but also the glorious image of Christ, and is that to his wife which Christ is to his church.

To apply this point, mark how two positions (worth noting) arise from it.

1. Subjection is due to a husband as well as to Christ.912

I do not say as great, because of the difference in glory, but as well, because of the likeness in office. A constable (though a poor, lowly man) must be obeyed as well as a high sheriff; a beggar’s child must obey his father as well as a king’s child. Therefore wives who are not subject wrong their husbands, just as those who are not subject to Christ wrong him.

2. Those who by their subjection maintain the honor of their husband’s place maintain by this the honor of Christ’s place; and again, by the rule of contraries, those who by refusing to be subject impair the honor of their husband’s place impair by this the honor of Christ’s place.

The obedience of a poor man’s child or servant vindicates the obedience which kings’ children and servants owe their father and sovereign; and so, on the contrary, disobedience in lowly persons dishonors the place of great ones.

The argument of Memucan, drawn from the greater to the913 less (in these words, “Queen Vashti has wronged not only the king, but all the princes and the peoples”), may be applied from the less to the greater. Disobedient wives wrong not only their own particular husbands, but also all heads, even Christ the head of the church.

If a natural body and the church were pliable, and could be seduced and drawn to act presumptuously and rebel against their heads, the bad example of wives would be enough to move them to it; for, as far as lies in them, they seduce them by their example.

From the last positions named above (namely, that the obedience of a good wife maintains the honor of Christ’s place, and on the contrary side that the disobedience of a bad wife impairs its honor) I may justly infer two other conclusions.

1. That Christ will surely reward the good subjection of914 good wives: for he has said (and what he has said he can and will perform), “I will honor those who honor Me.”

2. That he will severely avenge the rebellion of evil wives: for again he has said, “Those who despise Me will be despised.”

We know that fellows in office are ready to stand up for the915 good name of one another’s place, and to maintain its honor; and that not without good reason, for by this they maintain their own honor and good name.

Therefore, as good wives may well expect a reward at Christ’s hands, however their husbands regard their obedience, whether well or badly (a great encouragement for wives to perform their duties, however bad their husbands are), so evil wives have just cause to fear vengeance at Christ’s hand, however their husbands bear with them.

Those who duly weigh this reason, taken from the resemblance between Christ and the church, cannot but hold it to be a motive of great importance.

§. 73. Of the benefit which a wife has from a husband.

The fourth reason, taken from the benefit which a wife receives916 from her husband, presses the point in hand still further. Though Christ is in the strict sense the Savior of the body, yet even in this a husband bears a resemblance to Christ, and is in a manner a savior. For by virtue of his place and office he is, on the one side, her protector, to defend her from harm and preserve her from danger; and on the other side, a provider of all needful and necessary things for her. In this respect she is taken from her parents and relatives and wholly committed917 to him (as Jacob’s wives said, “Do we have any portion or inheritance left in our father’s house?”). Yes, she herself and all she has are given to him; and he in turn imparts whatever he has for her good and for her use. David compares a wife to918 a vine in relation to her husband, suggesting by this that she is raised by him to the height of honor she has, as a vine is raised by the tree or frame near which it is planted. By his honor she is dignified; by his wealth she is enriched. Under God he is all in all to her. In the family he is a king to govern and aid her, a priest to pray with her and for her, a prophet to teach and instruct her. As the head is placed in the highest place over the body, and understanding is placed in it, to govern, direct, protect and in every way seek the good of the body; and as Christ is united to the church as a spouse, and made her head, so that she might be saved, maintained and provided for by him: so for this end a husband was placed in his place of superiority, and his authority was committed to him, to be a savior of his wife. Therefore, if none of the former motives prevails with wives and moves them to be subject to their husbands, yet this one ought to.

For from this reason flow these two conclusions.

  1. The subjection required of a wife is for her own good.
  2. In refusing to obey, she shows herself both ungrateful to her husband and injurious to herself.

That her subjection is for her own good is evident from this919 end for which a husband is made a head: to be a savior, not to puff him up, or to make him domineer and tyrannize over his wife. So if she is subject to him, she may reap much good from him. As the church is wisely governed and safely protected by subjecting herself to her head, Christ Jesus, and as the body shares in much good and is preserved from much evil by subjecting itself to the head, so if a wife is subject to her husband she will fare much the better for it: all the ease, profit and benefit of it will be hers. If, therefore, she cares for her own good, this is a way and means ordained by God for this end; let her seek it in this.

If, despite this, she refuses to be subject to her husband, does she not (as we say) stand in her own light? Being by her sex the weaker, and the less able to help herself, if she rejects this good help which God has provided for her, is she not most injurious to her own self? And considering920 the care and pains her husband undergoes for her sake, is it not most unnatural and monstrous ingratitude inwardly to despise, or outwardly to scorn, such a head? No better proof of a grateful heart can be given by a wife to her husband than cheerful and ready subjection, and no greater ingratitude can be shown than rebellion and disdain. Now among vices ingratitude is one of the most odious to God and man: so, both to avoid the black spot of ingratitude and to win the name of gratefulness, wives ought to be subject.

§. 74. Of the example of the church set before wives.

The last reason, taken from the example of the church, is also921 of good force to persuade wives to subjection. Example prevails more with many than precept. If any example may have force, then this one most of all. For it is not the example of one only, but of many; not of many ignorant and wicked persons, but of understanding, wise, holy and righteous persons, even all the saints that ever were, are, or will be. For the church includes all under it, even that whole society of saints who are chosen by God in his eternal counsel, redeemed by Christ with his precious blood, and effectually called by the gospel of salvation, God’s Spirit working inwardly and powerfully on them; not excepting those very souls of just and perfect men now triumphing in heaven. Note how this church is described in vv. 26 and 27. Let this example therefore be thought of often: no one will ever regret following it. For it treads the only right path to eternal glory, to which those who follow it will surely come.

But to show the force of this reason a little more distinctly, note these two conclusions that follow from it.

1. Wives are as much bound to be subject to their husbands as the church is to Christ. Otherwise why should this example be set before them in this way and pressed on them? Why are husbands set in Christ’s place and likened to him?

2. A wife’s subjection to her husband, corresponding to the church’s subjection to Christ, is evidence that she is of the church, guided by the same Spirit that the church is. For it cannot be performed by the power of nature; it is a supernatural work, and so an evidence of the Spirit.

Therefore, O Christian wives, as your+ husbands resemble Christ by their place, so you+ resemble the church by your+ practice. Of the two, this is the more commendable: for that is a dignity, this a virtue; but true virtue is much more glorious than any dignity can be.

When these reasons are well weighed, and the force of them all joined together, they cannot but work on the most stubborn stomach there is. Therefore, if this point of subjection seems too bitter a pill to be well digested, let it be sweetened with the syrup of these reasons, and it will be swallowed much better, and work to all the better effect.

The Fourth Treatise: Of Husbands

A Husband’s Affectionate Authority over His Wife

The Fourth Treatise: Of Husbands · §§. 1–12

§. 1. Of the General Heads of this Treatise.

Eph 5:25, etc.

Husbands, love your+ own wives, just as Christ loved the church, etc.

As the wife is to know her duty, so the husband922 much more his, because he is to be a guide and a good example to his wife. He is to dwell with her according to knowledge (1 Pet 3:7), and the more eminent his place is, the more knowledge he ought to have of how to walk worthy of it. Neglect of duty in him is more dishonoring to God, because by virtue of his place he is “the image and glory of God”;923 and it is more harmful, not to his wife only, but also to the whole family, because of the power and authority he has. He may abuse it to support his wickedness, having no superior power in the house to restrain his fury; whereas the wife, however wicked she is, may be kept under by the power of her husband, and restrained from outrage.

Therefore, to go on in order, in setting out the husband’s924 duties (as we have the wife’s) we are to consider:

  1. The duties themselves.
  2. The reasons to enforce them.

In setting down the duties we must note

  1. The matter in which they consist.
  2. The manner in which they are to be performed.

The apostle comprises the whole matter of them all under love, which is the sum and head of all.

This we will handle first, and then go on to other particulars.

§. 2. Of that love which husbands owe their wives.925

This head of all the rest, love, is expressly set down, and is the only one mentioned, in this and in many other places of Scripture; by this it is evident that all other duties are comprised under it.

To pass over other places where this duty is urged, in926 this place love is named four times, besides being implied under many other terms and phrases.

Whoever takes a wife, therefore, must love her for this very reason, that she is his wife. So it is noted of Isaac (the best pattern of husbands noted in Scripture) that he “took Rebekah as his wife. And Isaac loved her.”927

Many good reasons for this may be given.928

1. Because no duty on the husband’s part can be rightly performed unless it is seasoned with love. The apostle exhorts all Christians to “do everything in love”;929 much more ought husbands to do so. Though in place they are above their wives, yet love must not be forgotten.

2. Because of all persons on earth a wife is the most fitting930 object of love. Neither friend, nor child, nor parent ought to be loved as a wife is. She is called “the wife of his bosom,” to show that she ought to be like his heart in his bosom.

3. Because his eminent place and power of authority931 may soon puff him up, and make him lord it over his wife and trample her under his feet, if an entire love for her is not planted in his heart. It is to keep him from abusing his authority that love is pressed on him so much.

4. Because wives, through the weakness of their sex (for932 they are the weaker vessels), are very prone to provoke their husbands. So if love does not prevail in the husband, there is likely to be little peace between man and wife. “Love covers a multitude of imperfections.”

5. Because as Christ, by the love he showed first, provokes the church to love him, so a husband, by loving his wife, should provoke her to love him in return. He should show himself like the sun, which is the fountain of light, and from which the moon receives what light she has: so he should be the fountain of love to his wife.

Objection. Love was laid down before as a common duty belonging to both man and wife. How then is it required here as a particular and distinctive duty of a husband?

Answer. With respect to the general extent of love, it is indeed a common duty belonging to the one as much as to the other; indeed,933 belonging to all Christians, to all men. For it is the very nature of love, and a special property of it, “not to seek its own,” but the good of others. All are bound to do this by virtue of the bond of nature; Christians more than others, by virtue of the bond of the Spirit; among Christians, wives and husbands especially, by virtue of the marriage bond; and of married couples, husbands most of all, by virtue of their place and charge. Their place is a place of authority, which without love will soon turn into tyranny. Their charge is, especially and above all, to seek the good of their wives. As wives are the chief and greatest charge of husbands, so their chief and greatest care must be for them. The parents and relatives of wives, as they hand over all their authority to the husbands, so they cast all their care on them. Therefore, so that husbands may take the more care of their wives and the better seek their good, they ought to love them in a special way. Husbands are most of all bound to love, and bound to love their wives most of all.

So this affection of love is a distinct duty in itself, belonging934 especially to a husband; and it is also a common condition which must be attached to every other duty of a husband, to season and sweeten it. His look, his speech, his bearing, and all his actions in which he has to do with his wife must be seasoned with love. Love must show itself in his commands, in his reproofs, in his instructions, in his admonitions, in his authority, in his familiarity, when they are alone together, when they are in company before others, in worldly affairs, in religious matters, at all times, in all things. As salt must be first and last on the table, and eaten with every bite of food, so love must be first in a husband’s heart and last out of it, and mixed with everything in which he has to do with his wife.

§. 3. Of a husband’s hatred and lack of love.

Contrary to this is hatred of heart. As this vice is935 very odious and detestable in itself, so it is much more so when the wife is made its object. As love moves a husband to do his wife what good he can, so hatred moves him to do her what harm he can. Moses notes a man’s hatred of his936 wife to be a cause of much harm: for the nearer and dearer any persons are, the more violent will be the hatred that is fastened on them.

That is why a divorce was allowed between937 a man and his wife in case he hated her. This law was without question made for the relief of the wife, so that the hatred her husband had conceived against her should not do her some harm if he were forced to keep her as his wife. Christ seems to imply this in these words: “Moses permitted you+ to divorce your+ wives because of your+938 hardness of heart.” Since this is so deadly a poison, then, let husbands take heed that they do not allow it to soak into them.

Nor is it enough for a husband not to hate his wife;939 for even the lack of love, though it is only a privation, is yet a great vice, and also contrary to the duty of love named before. Where this lack of love is, no duty can be well performed, just as when the great wheel of a clock, the first mover of all the rest, is out of order, not one wheel can be in good order. Those who think lightly of this plainly reveal that there is little or no love of God in them at all. For if the apostle’s inference holds good, drawn from a man’s neighbor or brother, whom940 he has seen, it will hold much more when it concerns a wife: for “how can he who does not love his wife” (whom God has given him as a token of his favor, and as a suitable helper for him, to be in his bosom and always in his sight, indeed to be no longer two, but one flesh) “love God, whom he has not seen? If any man says he loves God, and hates his wife, he is a liar.” Let husbands therefore give evidence that they love God by loving their wives.

§. 4. Of a husband’s wise maintaining of his authority.941

All the branches which grow out of this root of love, as they concern husbands’ duties, may be drawn under two heads:

  1. A wise maintaining of his authority.
  2. A right managing of it.

That these two are branches of a husband’s love is evident from the place in which God has set him, which is a place of authority. For the best good that anyone can do, and so the best fruits of love that he can show to anyone, are those done in his own place and by virtue of it. If, then, a husband gives up his authority, he disables himself from doing that good, and from showing those fruits of love, which otherwise he might. If he abuses his authority, he turns the edge and point of his sword the wrong way: instead of holding it over his wife for her protection, he turns it into her belly to her destruction, and so shows more hatred than love by it.

Now, then, to handle these two separately and distinctly:

I. That a husband ought wisely to maintain his authority942 is implied in this apostolic precept, “husbands, dwell with your+ wives according to knowledge,” that is, as men well able to maintain the honor of the place in which God943 has set you+, not as dolts and fools without understanding. The same is also implied in the titles of preeminence which Scripture gives to husbands, such as lord, master,944 head, guide, image and glory of God, etc.

The honor and authority of God, and of his Son Christ945 Jesus, are maintained in and by the honor and authority of a husband, as the king’s authority is maintained by the authority of his Privy Council and the other magistrates under him; indeed, as a husband’s authority is maintained in the family by the authority of his wife (for as the man is “the glory of God,” so946 “the woman is the glory of man”).

The good of the wife herself is also much furthered in this way,947 just as the good of the body is furthered by the head’s keeping its place. Should the head be put under any of the parts of the body, the body and all its parts could not fail to suffer much damage by it. In the same way the wife and the whole family would feel the damage of the husband’s loss of his authority.

1. Question. Is it in the husband’s power to maintain his own authority?

Answer. Yes, in his more than in anyone else’s. For note the948 counsel of the apostle to Timothy (though in another case, yet very much to this purpose): “Let no one despise your youth.” It was therefore in Timothy’s power to maintain his honor, and not to allow it to be despised; and so it is in a husband’s power.

2. Question. How may a husband best maintain his authority?

Answer. The direction which the apostle gives to Timothy949 for maintaining his authority may fitly be applied to a husband for this purpose: “Be an example … in conduct, in love, in spirit, in faith, and in purity.” It is as if he had said, If you walk before them worthy of your place and calling, and worthy of the honor and respect due to it, showing the fruits of love, faith, and other such graces, they will surely reverence your youth; but if instead you carry yourself basely, in a way unbecoming a minister, you give them just occasion to despise you. In just this way husbands may best maintain their authority, by being an example in love, gravity, piety, uprightness, etc. The fruits of these and other such graces, shown by husbands before their wives and family, cannot fail to work a reverent and dutiful respect toward them in their wives and their whole house: for by this means they will see the image of God shining more clearly in their faces.

Objection. Goodness and grace itself is hated by wicked and ungodly wives: it was an act of piety that made Michal despise David.

Answer. 1. Grant that it is so: yet this may be a good direction for husbands who do not have such wicked wives.

2. It does not always turn out so, no, nor even for the most part, among those who are wicked; true virtue and integrity often cause admiration in those who do not love it.

3. Though some are of so crooked and perverse a disposition as to take occasion for contempt where none is given, yet the husband who carries himself worthy of his place will clear himself before God and man.

§. 5. Of husbands losing their authority.

Contrary is the practice of those who by their profaneness, wild living,950 drunkenness, wickedness, flightiness, wastefulness, and other such base conduct make themselves contemptible, and so lose their authority. Though a wife ought not to take these occasions to despise her husband, yet it is a just judgment on him to be despised, since he makes himself contemptible.

Contrary also to the directions given above is the stern,951 rough, and cruel conduct of husbands who try to maintain their authority by violence and tyranny. Force may indeed cause fear, but a slavish fear, a fear that breeds more hatred than love, more inward contempt than outward respect.

And contrary is the servile disposition of those who, against their952 own judgment, yield to the bent of their wives’ minds in things that are unlawful. They will lose their authority rather than displease their wives. This is a fault expressly forbidden by the953 law; and yet it is a fault into which not only wicked Ahab954 but also wise Solomon fell.955 How heinous a fault, and how grievous a fall, this was in Solomon, its fearful outcome shows. Like him, not in wisdom but in this point of gross folly, are those who at their wives’ urging allow priests and Jesuits to lurk and celebrate Masses in their houses, and consent to be present at them themselves. Like Ahab are those magistrates who allow their wives to overrule them in the course of justice. That is how it comes about that more petitions and suits are made to the wives of magistrates in cases of justice than to the magistrates themselves, and the favor of their wives is more valued than their own. So the power of governing, and the main stroke in deciding matters, comes from their wives; they are only the mouths and instruments of their wives, so much so that among the common people the titles of their places and offices are given to their wives. Some husbands allow this because of their timid and foolish disposition, lacking the courage and wisdom to maintain the honor of their places against the insolence of their wives; others from a subtle, covetous, wicked mind, so that by means of their wives there may be more freedom for receiving bribes. Among these I may count those who, against their own mind, to satisfy their wives’ minds, allow both wives and children to follow the fashion, to dress in a way unbecoming their station, to keep frivolous company, and the like; and also those who at their wives’ pleading are moved (as Samson was) to reveal secrets956 that are not fit to be known. Husbands may listen to their wives when they urge good things, but they must not obey them in evil things. If they do, their fault is double: 1. in doing evil; 2. in losing their authority.

Let husbands therefore be very watchful against their wives’ evil urgings. Satan labored to overthrow Job by his wife, and by this he overthrows many in these days.

§. 6. Of husbands’ high regard for wives.957

As authority must be well maintained, so it must be well managed: and for this purpose two things are needful:

  1. That a husband respect his wife tenderly.
  2. That he care for her providently.

A husband’s tender respect for his wife is

  • Inward.
  • Outward.

Inward, with respect to his

  • Opinion of her.
  • Affection for her.

Outward, with respect to his conduct toward her.

As for a husband’s opinion of his wife, two things are to be weighed:

  • Her place.
  • Her person.

1. Her place is indeed a place of inferiority and subjection, yet the nearest to equality that can be: a place of common958 equity in many respects, in which man and wife are in a way equal fellows and partners. From this, then, it follows that

The husband must regard his wife as a yokefellow and companion. This is one point of giving honor to the wife; and it is implied in the phrase by which the end of making a wife is noted,959 which our English translates “suitable for him,” word for word as before him, that is, like himself, one in whom he might960 see himself, or even (to use our apostle’s word) himself. These phrases imply a kind of fellowship, as do the many privileges common to both, which have been noted961 before.

As a wife’s acknowledgment of her husband’s superiority is the groundwork of all her duties, so a husband’s acknowledgment of the fellowship between him and his wife will make him carry himself toward her much more amiably, familiarly, lovingly, and in every way as becomes a good husband.

§. 7. Of that fellowship which is between man and wife, in spite of a wife’s inferiority.

Objection. Fellowship between man and wife cannot stand together with a wife’s inferiority and subjection.

Answer. Those who cannot see how these may stand together are of very small understanding. Is there not a fellowship between superior and inferior magistrates in relation to their subjects? Indeed, Scripture mentions a fellowship between Christ the head and the other saints in relation to the glory962 of which all are made partakers (for it calls us “co-heirs with Christ”), and, in relation to God’s people, a fellowship between God and his ministers (for it calls them “God’s fellow963 workers”). Yet no one can deny that the saints and ministers are inferior and in subjection to Christ and to God. But to answer the objection point by point:

1. There may be not only a fellowship but also an equality in some things between two of whom one is, in other things, inferior and subject: as between man and wife in the power over each other’s bodies. For the wife (as well as the husband)964 is in this “both a servant and a ruler: a servant to yield her body, a ruler to have power over his.”

2. There may be fellowship in the very same things in which there is inferiority. For fellowship concerns the thing itself, inferiority the measure and manner. So in giving light the sun and moon have a fellowship, but in the measure and manner the moon is inferior: the moon does not have as much light as the sun, and what light it has, it has from the sun. And so in governing, the king and the other magistrates have a fellowship, but in the measure and manner of government they are inferior to him. Even so it is between man and wife: in many things in which there is a fellowship, the wife is nevertheless inferior. So inferiority may stand together with fellowship.

3. There are no unequals between whom there is so close a parity as between man and wife. If, therefore, there may be a fellowship between any who are superior and inferior to one another, much more between man and wife.

As965 the soul, therefore, rules over the body by a mutual and loving consent and agreement, so must a man rule over his wife.

§. 8. Of husbands’ too low regard for wives.

Contrary is the notion of many who think there is no966 difference between a wife and a servant except in familiarity, and that wives were made to be servants to their husbands, because subjection, fear and obedience are required of them. This is why wives are often treated little better than servants. It is a notion and a practice that smacks too much of heathenish and senseless arrogance. Did God at first take the wife out of man’s side so that man should tread her under his feet? Or rather so that he should set her at his side, next to him, above all children, servants, or anyone else in the family, however near or dear to him? For none can be nearer than a wife, and none ought to be dearer.

§. 9. Of husbands’ good esteem of their own wives.967

2. As for the person of a wife: A husband ought to esteem that particular person to whom he is joined in marriage by God’s providence to be the fittest and best for him. This is implied in that word of restriction (OWN) which the apostle notes where he says, “Husbands, love your+968 OWN wives,” and he presses it again with a comparison of the body, (“as your+969 OWN bodies”). Everyone thinks his own body the best and fittest for him. A man might perhaps wish some defects or deformities in his own body amended, and desire that his were like another’s, straighter, stronger, and more attractive than his own; yet he would not want his head to be on that other man’s body. A man who would love his wife ought to have the same opinion of her.

There is good reason for him to do so: for the proverb is true,970 if it is rightly taken, “marriages are first made in heaven,” that is, God has an overruling hand in ordering them. Solomon971 implies this by the contrast he makes between wealth and a wife: that is from our fathers, this from the Lord. In this respect he says, “he who finds a wife … obtains favor from the Lord.”972 If therefore you are loved by God, and love him, he will make your wife turn out a good thing to you.

Objection. A wife may be a very depraved and wicked woman: how then can she be counted the best wife?

Answer. 1. It may be that she was good enough when she was first brought to you, but you, by your evil example, or negligent government, or harsh treatment, have made her as bad as she is. If that is so, then she is to be considered not as you have marred her, but as you married her.

2. Though she is not the best in condition compared with other wives, yet in relation to you she may be the best in outcome: if not for your ease and quiet, yet for the testing of your wisdom and patience; and so973 she may be a school of virtue to you. As974 a skillful pilot’s competence is tested and known by stormy seas, so a man’s wisdom is by a troublesome wife. Indeed, she may be given to you as a punishment for some former sins, such as seeking a beautiful, honorable, rich, good-looking wife rather than a religious and chaste one; or seeking her without first seeking any direction or help from God, or otherwise than you have warrant from God, as by stealth and without parents’ consent; or some other sins of another kind, to bring you to repentance. Or she may be given as a means to restrain and wean you from some future sins to which you are prone, and so be a blessed cross to keep you from a fearful curse.

§. 10. Of husbands’ perverse opinion of their own wives.

Contrary is the corrupt and perverse opinion which many have of their own wives, thinking them the worst and least fit of all, even though they are such as deserve all good respect and esteem in every way, both in gifts and qualities of mind and in grace and beauty of body. Where others (who look with a clear eye) commend their good qualities, they misinterpret and misjudge everything: if their wives are religious, they think them hypocrites; if serious, sober and modest, melancholy; if cheerful, wanton; if they keep at home, idle drones; if they take occasion (however just) to go out, gadabouts, and flighty. This bad opinion of their wives causes their hearts to be wholly removed from their own wives and set on forbidden flesh. By this the devil gains what he desires: to separate those whom God has joined together, and to join those whom God has separated.

§. 11. Of husbands’ entire affection for their wives.975

A husband’s affection for his wife must correspond to his opinion of her. He ought therefore to delight in his wife entirely, that is, so to delight in her as to delight wholly and only in her. In this respect the prophet’s wife is called the976 “desire,” or delight, or pleasure, “of his eyes”: that in which he delighted most of all, and therefore fittingly so called.

Isaac took such delight in his wife that it drove out a strong contrary passion, namely the grief he felt at the departure of his mother: for it is noted that “he loved her and was comforted after his mother’s death.”977

The wise man elegantly sets out this kind of affection in these words: “Rejoice in the wife of your youth. Let her978 be as the loving doe and pleasant roe, and be enraptured always with her love.” Note here both the metaphors and the hyperbole used to set out a husband’s delight in his wife. In the metaphors, again, note both the creatures to which a wife is likened and the attributes given to them. The creatures are two, a doe and a roe, which are the females of a stag and a roebuck. Now it is noted of the stag and the roebuck that of all beasts they are the most enamored (if I may so speak) with their mates, and even mad in their heat and desire for them.

Solomon has used these metaphors to set out that unfeigned and earnest, entire and ardent affection which a husband ought to bear toward his wife. Taken in a good sense and rightly applied, so that they do not exceed the bounds of Christian modesty and decency, they are very fitting and to the purpose. If we stretch them beyond modesty, we wrong their writer, or rather the Holy Spirit who directed him, and set a harmful pattern before husbands.

The attributes given to these creatures amplify the point greatly. The first is called a loving doe, the second979 a pleasant roe; word for word, a doe of loves, a roe of favor, that is, exceedingly loved and favored (for, to set out the extent of God’s love for his Son, Christ is called “the Son of His love”).

These comparisons, applied to a wife, vividly set out the delight a husband ought to take in her; and yet it is amplified much further by the hyperbole used in this phrase, “be enraptured with her love,” word for word err in her love,980 by which no sinful error or foolish doting is meant, but a lawful, earnest affection. It implies two things especially. First, to go so far as to make a man overlook some blemishes in his wife which others would soon spot and dislike, or else to count them no blemishes, delighting in her not one bit the less for them. For example, if a man has a wife who is not very beautiful or well-formed, but has some deformity in her body, some imperfection in her speech, sight, bearing, or any part of her body, yet he is to love her and delight in her as much as if she were the fairest and in every way the most perfect woman in the world. Secondly, to esteem her so highly, to love her so ardently, to respect her so tenderly, that others may think he even dotes on her. A husband’s affection for his wife cannot be too great if it is kept within the bounds of decency, sobriety and seemliness. The wife’s affection for her husband ought to be as great; yet because of the husband’s place of authority, he must especially take every occasion to show this inward affection of his. Read the Song of Songs, and in it you+ will see such affection shown by Christ to his spouse as would make one think that he (to use the phrase with reverence, in a holy manner) even erred in his love and doted on her. A good pattern and precedent for husbands. For nothing is more lovely than a981 good wife.

§. 12. Of the Stoical disposition of husbands toward their wives.

Contrary is the disposition of husbands who have no heat or heart of affection in them, but, like Stoics, delight no more in their own wives than in any other women, and count them no dearer than others. It is a disposition in no way warranted by the word. The faithful saints of God mentioned before, and many others like them, were no Stoics without all affection; nor did they think it unbecoming to delight in their wives in a special way (witness Isaac “caressing” his wife),982 for this is a privilege belonging to the state of marriage. But so that I am not misunderstood in this, let it be noted that the affection I speak of is not a carnal, sensual, beastly affection, but such as may stand with Christian gravity and sobriety: having relation to the soul of a man’s wife as well as to her body, and grounded both on the close union of marriage and on the inward qualities of his wife.

So much for a husband’s inward respect for his wife. Next we are to speak of his outward conduct toward her.
