A Husband’s Humble Gentleness to His Wife

The Fourth Treatise: Of Husbands · §§. 13–23

§. 13. Of a husband’s kind acceptance of the things his wife does.983

Saint Peter gives a general rule for a husband’s outward conduct toward his wife: that he dwell with her according to knowledge, that is, as a man able to order his conduct wisely, to his own honor and his wife’s good, so that she may have just cause to bless God that she was ever joined to such a husband.

Out of this general rule these two branches sprout.

  1. That a husband give no just offense to his wife.
  2. That he wisely deal with any offense given by her.

To avoid giving offense he must have regard

  1. To what she does as duty to him.
  2. To what he does as duty to her.

With regard to the former, two things are required:

  1. That he kindly accept what she is willing and able to do.
  2. That he wisely commend and reward what she does well.

Having thus laid down these heads for order’s sake, I will handle the separate points one by one.

The first particular in which a husband shows himself984 to be a man of knowledge in walking before his wife is a kind and respectful acceptance of every good duty his wife performs. Abraham, as a testimony of his kind acceptance of Sarah’s pains in nursing her child, held a great feast when the child was weaned; and Elkanah, with a like regard, gave his wife liberty985 to do what seemed best to her.

This must be a great encouragement to wives to be subject to their husbands in all things, when they see that no part of their subjection is carelessly neglected, but rather graciously accepted. It puts life into a wife’s spirit to think that her care and pains in pleasing her husband will not be in vain.

§. 14. Of husbands’ slighting and rejecting their wives’ goodness.

Contrary is the practice of those who, thinking all that a wife986 does to be only her duty, take little or no notice of it; or, if they cannot help noticing it, yet regard it lightly and pass over it carelessly. This often makes a wife even regret the good she has done, as David regretted the service987 he had done for Nabal. The truth is that wives ought to look to God for his acceptance rather than to their husbands; and though their husbands will take no notice of the good things they do, or not regard them, yet they ought to do their duty for conscience’ sake and for the Lord’s sake. But even so, considering our weakness and reluctance toward every duty, it cannot be denied that a husband’s slight regard for his wife’s goodness gives her occasion to grow weary of it, and that he does as much as lies in him to make her regret it.

But what may we say of those who scornfully reject their wives’988 duty, and indeed like them the worse for making conscience of it, and so (quite contrary to the rule of Christianity) “overcome good with evil”?989 Surely they show a very diabolical spirit in themselves, and cannot help causing their wives much grief and offense, and making what their wives do very irksome and tedious. Fathers ought not to provoke their990 children, much less husbands their wives.

§. 15. Of husbands’ courteous acceptance of their wives’ reverent bearing.991

For a better understanding of so needful a point, I will992 apply it somewhat more particularly and distinctly to the separate duties of a wife, which were drawn under two heads:

Reverence.

Obedience.

For the first: if a wife shows her dutiful respect for her993 husband by any reverent behavior, gesture, or speech, he ought to meet her (as we say) halfway, and show his gracious acceptance of it by some like courteous behavior, gesture, and speech, seemly, not foolish.

Objection. In this way a husband will abase himself and disgrace his place.

Answer. The courtesy I speak of, as it comes from a superior, being a purely voluntary matter and a token994 of kindness and favor, is no abasement of himself, but an advancement of his inferior: a great grace to her, no disgrace to him. Abram was counted by the Hittites “a prince of995 God,” yet in speaking with them “he bowed down” to them. It is noted as a commendable thing in Esau that, though he was at that time his brother’s superior (at least he took himself to be so), yet, seeing how Jacob reverenced him, bowing seven times to the ground, he “ran to him and embraced996 him, threw his arms around his neck.” Most to the point is the example of King Ahasuerus, who, seeing Esther standing reverently997 before him, held out his scepter to her, which in a king is great courtesy.

But to put the matter beyond all question, let the example of Christ noted in Solomon’s Song be observed, and we will find his courtesy in every way answering the reverence of his spouse.

§. 15. Of husbands’ too great loftiness.

Contrary is a lofty bearing of husbands toward their wives, who pay no regard to all the reverence their wives show, regarding their wives in this no more than children or servants, or no more than kings regard the reverence of their subjects.

I have often noted that there is a great difference between a wife and all other inferiors, and in that respect every sign of her reverence should be much better regarded. Yet we know that kings and queens will put out their hands to be kissed by their subjects when they kneel before them, which is a token of courtesy: how much more ought husbands to show courtesy! They are unworthy to be reverenced by their wives who, too much like lords, look down on them.

§. 16. Of husbands’ ready yielding to their wives’ humble requests.998

Again, since it is a token of reverence in a wife humbly to999 make her desire known to her husband, he ought to show so much courtesy as to grant her desire readily. This courtesy Ahasuerus, named before,1000 showed to Esther; David1001 to Bathsheba; Isaac1002 to Rebekah; Abraham1003 to Sarah; and many other husbands to their wives. Abraham1004 showed such respect for his wife in this that, though the thing she desired was grievous to him, yet he yielded to his wife.

Objection. God first commanded him to do so.

Answer. This adds the more force to the argument, showing that it is God’s express will that a husband should show this kind of courtesy to his wife. A man ought to do much more at his wife’s request than at anyone else’s, whether friend, child, or parent; indeed, he ought to show himself much more free, eager and cheerful in granting his wife’s request than anyone else’s: provided, however, that what she desires is something that may lawfully be granted. To yield in unlawful things is to lose his authority, as was shown1005 before.

§. 17. Of husbands’ harshness to their wives.

Contrary is the harshness of the disposition of those who yield to their wives’ request as a hard-milking cow lets down her milk, not without much ado; and by this all the grace of their yielding is taken away. There can be no courtesy in yielding when it is forced from them against their mind and will. Their wives must ask and plead again and again, indeed be forced to use the mediation of others to persuade their husbands to yield to their request, before they will yield, if they yield at all. What is this but to proclaim to all the world that they have no affection for their wives? If a wife’s breath is alien to her husband, surely his heart is first estranged from her; and that is the ready way to make him set his heart on forbidden women.

§. 18. Of husbands’ forbearing to demand all that they may.1006

As a wife’s reverence, so also her obedience must be answered with her husband’s courtesy. As evidence of this, a husband1007 must be ready to accept that in which his wife shows herself willing to obey him. He ought to be sparing in demanding too much of her. In this he ought so to frame his conduct toward her that the obedience she performs may come from her own voluntary disposition, from a free conscience toward God (even because God has placed her in a place of subjection), and from a wifely love, rather than from any demand on her husband’s part, and as it were by force.

Husbands ought not to demand of their wives everything1008 that wives ought to yield to if it is demanded. They must consider what is lawful, needful, fitting, advisable and suitable for their wives to do, indeed, what they are most willing to do, before they are too peremptory in demanding it. For example:

1. Though the wife ought to go with her husband and1009 live where he thinks fit, yet he ought not (unless he is forced to it by some urgent calling) to move her from place to place, and carry her away from a place where she is well settled, without her approval. Jacob1010 consulted his wives and found out whether they were willing before he carried them away from their father’s house.

2. Though she ought cheerfully to receive whatever guests1011 he brings into the house, yet he ought not to be grievous and burdensome to her in this. The greatest care and pains in receiving guests fall on the wife; she ought therefore to be treated tenderly in it.

If he sees that she is conscientious and wise, well able to manage1012 and order matters about the house, yet unwilling to do anything without his consent, he ought to be ready and free in giving his consent and satisfying her desire, as Elkanah was;1013 and if she is shy and reluctant to ask consent, he ought to offer it of his own accord. Indeed, he ought to give her a general consent to order and arrange matters as in her wisdom she sees fit, as the same Elkanah did (“Do,” he says to his wife, “what you think is best”), and as1014 the husband of that good housewife whom Solomon describes did.

A general consent is especially needed for ordering household affairs. For it is a charge laid on wives to1015 “govern their households”; by which it appears that the business of the house belongs to the wife, and is most especially hers. In this respect she is called the1016 housewife. So in these matters husbands ought to leave things to their ordering, and not restrain them in every particular from doing anything without special leave and direction. To illustrate this in1017 some particulars, it belongs particularly to a wife:

  1. To1018 order the decorating and adorning of the house.
  2. To1019 arrange the ordinary provisions for the family.
  3. To1020 rule and govern the maidservants.
  4. To1021 bring up the children while they are young, and the like.

He ought therefore, with a general consent, to leave these to her discretion, limited only by these two1022 cautions.

1. That she has in some measure sufficient discretion,1023 understanding and wisdom, and is not too ignorant, foolish, simple, wasteful, etc.

2. That he keeps a general oversight of all, and so interposes his authority that he allows nothing unlawful or unseemly to be done by his wife about the house, children, servants, or other things: for

  1. The general charge of all lies principally on him.
  2. He will give an account to God for all things that are wrong in his house.
  3. The blame for all will also lie on him before men.

But with those two cautions provided, he ought, together with his general consent, to put trust1024 in his wife (as Potiphar1025 did in Joseph), making in this a difference between a wife and all others, whether grown children, friends, or servants, whom he employs in his affairs. He may direct them in every particular, for matter and manner, and take a strict account of them for expenses laid out or other things done, because what they do is wholly and only for another. To his wife (who is a joint parent of his children and governor of his house, to whose good the husband’s wealth comes, and who in that respect does for herself what she does for her husband) greater liberty and freedom must be given.

§. 19. Of husbands’ too great strictness toward their wives.

Contrary is the harshness and severity of many husbands who stand on the utmost step of their authority and yield no more to a wife than to any other inferior. Such are those

1. Who are never content or satisfied with any duty the1026 wife performs, but are always demanding more and more.

2. Who do not care how grievous and burdensome they are to their wives: grievous, by bringing into the house guests they know cannot be welcome to them; burdensome, by too frequent and unseasonable invitations of guests, or by imposing other such extraordinary business, over and above the ordinary affairs of the house. Too frequent imposing of such things cannot help breeding much weariness. Unseasonable imposing (as when the wife is weak through sickness, childbearing, nursing, or other such causes, and so not able to give the satisfaction she otherwise would) cannot help greatly disquieting her and giving her great offense.

3. Who hold their wives under as if they were children or servants, restraining them from doing anything without their knowledge and particular, express consent.

4. Who are overbusy in prying into every business of the house, and will have their hand in everything. Besides giving their wives no opportunity to show the understanding, intelligence, wisdom, care, and other gifts with which God has endowed them, such husbands take away the main end for which a wife was given to a man, namely, to be “a helper.”1027 Such husbands cannot help neglecting other weightier matters which belong more properly to them. For observe it and you+ will find that the husbands who are busiest about the private affairs of the house that belong to their wives are the most negligent of the affairs that belong to themselves. They think they walk in integrity, but they are not just or wise in this. For “the just man walks in HIS integrity,”1028 and “the wisdom of the prudent is to discern HIS way”: that is, the integrity which belongs to his own particular place, and his own way. But “every fool will be meddling,” namely, with things not belonging to his place.1029

5. Who are oversuspicious of their wives, and therefore overstrict in calling them to account. Saint Paul calls suspicions1030 “evil,” and not without just cause: for they are evil in their nature, and evil in their effects, being the occasion of much harm; but in none are they so evil as in husbands toward their wives. If a wife’s faithfulness is suspected without just cause (and the welfare of the family and the increase of its wealth come to her good as well as to the husband’s), who shall be trusted? It is the ruin of many families that servants are trusted, and not wives.

So much for a husband’s kind acceptance of what his wife is willing and able to do.

§. 20. Of husbands’ encouraging their wives in good things.

The love which a husband owes to his wife further requires1031 that he wisely commend and reward what she has done well. What the apostle says of the magistrate’s authority may fitly be applied to a husband’s, in relation to his wife: “Do what is good, and you will have his praise.”1032 It is expressly noted in the description of a good husband that “he praises” his wife;1033 and when it says, “Give her1034 the fruit of her hands,” it is implied also that he rewards her.

This is an undoubted evidence of his kind acceptance of her duty, and a further encouragement to stir her up to go on and continue in well-doing. Indeed, it is also an evidence of his joy and delight both in her person and in her well-doing. If there is no delight in someone’s person, his well-doing will stir up envy rather than joy; and those who envy a man’s well-doing will never commend or reward him for it.

In a husband’s commending of his wife this caveat must be added: that he so orders his praise that it does not smack of flattery or foolish doting, nor1035 stir up lust or envy in others.

§. 21. Of husbands’ ungrateful discouraging of their wives.

Contrary is the ungrateful, if not envious, disposition of husbands1036 who pass by many good things that their wives ordinarily do every day, without any approval, commendation or reward, yet are ready to find fault with the least slip or neglect in them; and that in such general terms, as if they never did anything well, so that their wives may well complain and say, as it is in the proverb,

Oft did I well, and that hear I never:

Once did I ill, and that hear I ever.

Yet such men will be ready to praise other men’s wives, and to reproach their own wives with the examples of those others, when their own far excel them in every kind of goodness. What does this show but that either they take no notice of their own wives’ goodness, or else regard it little because it is so common? If their wives do not have the more grace in them, this disposition is enough not only to discourage them from doing any good duty, but also to breed jealousy in them, and to turn their hearts away from their husbands.

§. 22. Of a husband’s mildness.1037

So much for the regard a husband is to have for the duty his wife performs to him.

To avoid giving just offense, a husband must further have good regard for what he does as duty to his wife. As he must accept duty kindly at his wife’s hands, so he must mildly perform the1038 duty he owes to her.

This mildness is a special fruit and evidence of love, and a notable means of taking away all the offense that might otherwise be taken at many things he does. Sugar and honey are not more pleasant to the tongue than mildness is to the heart. It causes things that are otherwise irksome and grievous to the soul to be well received and taken in, just as bitter pills dipped in sweet syrup, or rolled up in the soft pulp of an apple, are soon swallowed down and well digested. If a husband desires to be counted a servant of the Lord, he must learn this lesson: for “the servant of the Lord must … be gentle to all men.”1039 If any other servant of the Lord must, much more husbands; if to all men, most of all to their wives; and that in many respects.

  1. Because of the close union between man and wife.
  2. Because of the joint authority she has with him over others: so that in this he may be a precedent and example to her.
  3. Because of her weakness: glasses are handled tenderly; a small knock soon breaks them.

§. 23. Of husbands’ bitterness.

Contrary is bitterness, a vice expressly forbidden, and that to husbands in particular. It is a vice that cannot stand with a husbandly love; and so the apostle, commanding the one, forbids the other: “Love,” he says, “and do not be bitter.”1040 Nothing more blunts the edge of his authority, perverts the use of his government, provokes his wife’s resentment, or makes his words and deeds less regarded, than bitterness. It is like gall and wormwood mixed with sweet and wholesome foods, which keeps them from being well digested, so that they are violently spat out again as soon as ever they are tasted. Men in authority are very prone to this; and therefore, husbands, be all the more watchful against it: “love your+ wives and do not be bitter toward them.”

A Husband’s Patient Correcting of His Wife

The Fourth Treatise: Of Husbands · §§. 24–39

§. 24. Of the titles which a husband gives to his wife.1041

The mildness of a husband named above must be shown in his

  • Speech.
  • Conduct.

For as far as reverence extends in the duties of wives, so far must mildness be extended in the duties of husbands.

Whether a husband’s speech is to his wife before her face, or about her1042 behind her back, it must be sweetened with mildness.

1. As for his speech to her: 1. the titles by which he calls her, 2. the instructions which he gives her, 3. the commandments which he lays on her, 4. the reproofs with which he checks her, must all be mixed with mildness.

Among other titles, the most ordinary and usual title, “wife,”1043 is a mild and kind title, and the least offensive of all. If a husband gives his wife any other title, it must be one that shows kindness, familiarity, love and delight. Such are all the titles which Christ gives to the church, as “Spouse,” “love,” “Dove,” and the like. I do not deny that in the Song of Solomon, and in other places of Scripture, many titles are given and words used by Christ to the church which are not fitting for husbands to use to their wives, because they are metaphorical and hyperbolical. But yet in them all we may observe tokens of amiability, kindness and mildness, which is the end for which I have cited his example.

Contrary to these are such titles as, on the one side, set the wife1044 in too high a place over her husband, as “Lady,” “mistress,” “Dame,” “mother,” etc. And on the other side, such as set her in too low a rank, as “woman,” “wench,” etc. And their Christian names shortened, as “Sal,” “Mal,” “Bess,” “Nan,” etc. And names of kindred, as “sister” and “Cousin.” And insulting names, as “slut,” “drab,” “quean.” And names more fitting for beasts than for wives, as “Cole,” “Browne,” “Muggle,” etc.

Objection. These are titles of mildness, kindness and great familiarity. For husbands call their wives by these names, not when they are angry and displeased with them, but ordinarily and usually, even when they are best pleased.

Answer. The mildness and familiarity required of a husband must be such as may stand with his authority and place of eminence (as some of those names do not), and with that close union which is between man and wife above all others (as others do not), and with Christian gravity and discretion (as others do not). Christians therefore must take care that they do not justify corrupt customs by their practice.

§. 25. Of a husband’s manner of instructing his wife.

2. To instruction the apostle expressly joins meekness:1045 “Instruct with meekness” (he says) “those who oppose themselves.” If ministers must use meekness when they instruct their people, much more must husbands when they instruct their wives. If1046 meekness must not be laid aside in a case of opposition, then it must be laid aside in no case and at no time.

To show meekness in this case, let these rules be observed.1047

1. Note the understanding and capacity of your wife, and fit your instructions to them. If she is of limited capacity, give “precept on precept, line on line, a little here, a little there.” A little at a time, often given (that is, something every day), will grow in time to a great measure; and it will so grow that, together with knowledge of the thing taught, love for the person who teaches will increase.

2. Instruct her in private, between yourself and her, so that her ignorance may not be spread abroad. Private actions passing between man and wife are tokens of much kindness and familiarity.

3. In the family, instruct the children and servants when she is present in such a way that she may learn knowledge by it. There can be no meeker or gentler manner of instructing than to instruct one person by instructing another.

4. Together with your precepts, mix sweet and pithy persuasions,1048 which are proofs of great love.

Contrary to this is a harsh and rough manner of instructing: when husbands try to thrust into their wives’ heads, as it were by force, deep mysteries which they are not able to grasp; and yet if the wives do not grasp them, the husbands will be angry with them, and in anger give them abusive words, and proclaim their ignorance before children, servants and strangers. This harshness is ordinarily so fruitless, and besides so exasperates a woman’s spirit, that I think a husband would do better to leave out the duty altogether than to do it in such a manner.

§. 26. Of a husband’s manner of commanding his wife anything.1049

3. The commandments which a husband gives to his wife, whether they are affirmative (bidding her to do something) or negative (forbidding her to do this or that), must all be seasoned with mildness. To this end, regard must be had to the matter and the manner of his commandments.

With respect to the matter, the things which he commands1050 his wife to do must be

  1. Such as are truly lawful and honorable.
  2. Such as she is persuaded are so.
  3. Such as become her place.
  4. Such as are of weight and importance.

And on the other hand, the things which he forbids must be

  1. Such as are truly unlawful to be done.1051
  2. Such as he can clearly prove to her to be unlawful.
  3. Such as are unbecoming her place.
  4. Such as will have some evil and harmful effect if they are done.

1. To command a thing unlawful, or to forbid a thing which ought to be done, is to set his own authority against God’s. In that case he brings his wife into this strait: she must reject either God’s commandment or his. How then can she think that her husband loves her, when he brings her into such snares and straits that she must either fall into the gulf of God’s displeasure or dash against the rock of offending her husband? Mildness is far from such commandments.

2. The same may be said of such things as to a wife’s conscience1052 seem sinful, if they are enjoined on her, or seem her bounden duty, if they are forbidden; especially if she has any ground for her conscience out of God’s word. The conscience is subject to God alone. If it is forced, it will be a fearful horror, and a very hell, in the person whose conscience is forced: “She who has doubts is condemned” if she does what1053 she has doubts about.

1. Objection. In doubtful matters the commanding power1054 of a governor is a sufficient warrant and ground to settle the conscience of those who are under authority.

Answer. 1. In things purely doubtful, about which the party in subjection has no warrant out of God’s word one way or the other, it may be so. But when the conscience does not doubt and hang in suspense, but is persuaded on some ground taken from God’s word that what is commanded is unlawful, or that what is forbidden is a bounden duty, then to do the one, or to leave the other undone, is a sin to the party so persuaded. And this is the doubting (of which the apostle speaks) that condemns a man. In this case, to urge a wife to do this, or not to do that, is to urge her to sin, which a mild spirit and a loving heart will not do.

2. Though the husband’s command is a sufficient warrant to the wife, and she ought to yield if he peremptorily presses her to this or that, yet the love and mildness required of a husband should make him so tender toward her as to forgo something of his power. When he sees her conscience troubled about his command, he should relieve her conscience by forbearing to press what seems so burdensome to her. A husband may sin in pressing that too much on his wife which she, at his pressing, may yield to without sin.

§. 27. Of a husband’s wise conduct when his wife is erroneously scrupulous.1055

2. Objection. What if a husband, from his own knowledge, observes that his wife is erroneously scrupulous, and that she misinterprets and misapplies the word of God which she makes the ground of her scruple?

Answer. He must first labor to settle her conscience by plainly showing her error, which is a true and a great token of love. If, despite all that he can do in that way, she cannot be brought to yield to what he would have, then he must carefully observe these two things.

  1. Whether her refusal to yield is obstinacy or weakness.
  2. Whether it concerns a slight or a weighty matter.

By the reasons which she gives, and her manner of pressing1056 them, he may discern whether weakness or obstinacy makes her hold out against him. If the reason she rests on, taken from God’s word, is doubtful, and may seem to support her somewhat to one who does not have a good, sound judgment and a sharp, discerning understanding, it is to be presumed that there is more weakness than stubbornness in her. But if she can give no good reason, but only seizes on every appearance that seems in any way to lean toward her words, and peremptorily holds to her conclusion, and stiffly stands on her own resolution, though the emptiness of her pretexts is clearly exposed to her, so that she has nothing further to object; or if she gives no reason at all but her own thought, notion and will, and yet refuses to yield, surely obstinacy possesses her heart. In a case of obstinacy it is very advisable that a husband stand on his power to maintain his authority, and by the best wisdom he can (using only such means as are lawful) bring her to yield from her stubbornness to what he requires; especially if the matter is weighty: as in the case where a religious man has married a popish wife, and she will not be moved by any reason to stop going to Mass, or to yield to going to the preaching of the gospel. But if through weakness she cannot be persuaded of the lawfulness of what her husband requires, and the matter required is of no great consequence, and the weakness of her conscience causes no great error, a husband ought to show his mildness so far as to forbear pressing her conscience.

§. 28. Of a husband’s forbearing to press things unbecoming a wife’s place.1057

3. Things unbecoming the place of a wife are dishonorable to her. For a husband to urge his wife by strict charge to do them shows more harshness than mildness. Had the spirit of that proud monarch Ahasuerus been milder toward his wife, he would not have pressed his wife so far to so unseemly a thing as he did, namely, to come before all his princes and people to make a show of her beauty. It is true indeed (as we showed1058 before) that she did wrong in refusing to yield to it when he peremptorily required it. But that offense on her part does not justify his deed and free him from all blame. It is noted that he was “merry with wine” when he gave that commandment,1059 by which it is implied that his practice was more fitting for a drunken man than a sober one. Such is the practice of those who demand of their wives that they do such tasks as become maidservants rather than wives, or harlots rather than chaste women; such as going to taverns, alehouses, playhouses and such places where loose companions are.

§. 29. Of a husband’s pressing his authority in weighty matters.

4. To use a man’s authority about weighty matters, matters of importance, gives it such weight that it will be much better regarded. For in this way a wife will either be brought to yield to what is commanded, or to condemn herself for not yielding. Yes, in this way a wife may see that it is not so much his own will that makes him use his authority in commanding, as the necessity of the thing itself, which tends especially to the good of her who does it. For the performance of a duty is for the most part most advantageous to the one who performs it, so that by this a husband shows love to his wife in pressing what he presses.

So that this token of love may appear more clearly, it is needful1060 that a husband add just and weighty reasons to his commandment, so that by them his wife may better discern the fitness, lawfulness, expediency and necessity of the things commanded. We know that all the things which God commands are weighty and necessary. Yes, his will (being the very rule and ground of all goodness) makes things absolutely necessary; yet to his commandments he is accustomed to add weighty reasons, showing on the one side the benefit and blessedness that will come to those who obey his commandments, and on the other side the harm and misery that will fall on the heads of those who refuse to obey. By this he shows the great and good regard which he bears toward us, and the earnest desire he has for our good. So a husband may show much love and kindness even in his commandments.

§. 30. Of husbands’ too great pride in commanding.

Contrary to this is the peremptory pride of husbands, when they will have their own will done. It makes no difference whether the thing commanded is lawful or unlawful, whether their wives’ consciences can yield to it or not, whether it is consistent with the honor of their places or not, and whether it is weighty or light: it is their will that it should be done, and done it shall be; that is all the reason they will give. Some think it a glory to command whatever they please, and think that there is no proof of their authority, and of their wives’ subjection, except in such things as they command by their own will, without any further ground or reason. If such husbands meet with defiance, if, though they command much, they do not find a corresponding performance, they may thank themselves, for they take the ready course to have their authority despised and even trodden underfoot.

§. 31. Of husbands’ rare and mild use of their commanding power.

Husbands must have regard to the manner of using their authority in commanding, as well as to the matter.

With respect to the manner, his commandments must be

  1. Rare, not too frequent.
  2. By way of entreating, not too peremptory.

Authority is like a sword, which with overmuch use will1061 be blunted, and so fail to do the service which it otherwise might when there is most need. A wise, grave, peaceable man may always have his sword in readiness, and that also very bright, keen and sharp; but he will not be very ready to pluck it out of its scabbard. He rather keeps it for a time of need, when it will be of most use to him. So husbands who are too frequent in their commands show themselves neither grave, nor wise, nor lovers of peace.

As the use of a husband’s authority in commanding must be1062 rare, so when there is occasion to use it, it must be tempered with such mildness and moderation that (following Saint Paul’s example), though he has power to command what is fitting, yet he would rather entreat it “on the basis of love.” Note how mildly Abram frames his words to his wife: “Please say”1063 (he says) “you are my sister.” Though the thing he required smacked of too much weakness, yet his manner of requiring it well became a kind husband.

§. 32. Of husbands’ insolence and peremptoriness.

Contrary to this is the insolence of many, who cannot speak to their wives except by way of command. Their authority is like a swaggerer’s sword, which cannot rest long in the sheath, but is drawn out on every small occasion. This frequent use of commanding makes their commandments disregarded. The same may be said of those who are too peremptory in commanding. There must be no saying no to what they say; they will have their mind done by command, and no other way. No persuasion, no entreaty may be used; they would rather not have their will done at all than have it done other than by absolute command. Indeed, they will not allow others, in case of any refusal, to entreat or persuade, but will try what they can do absolutely by authority. So, just as steel often breaks when one tries how far it will bend, so by putting their authority to the utmost trial they often lose all their authority. In that case “the remedy” (as we say) “is in their own hands.”

§. 33. Of a husband’s reproving his wife.1064

4. The authority and charge which God has given a husband over his wife require that, as good and just occasion is offered, he should reprove her. For this is a special means to draw her from those sins in which she might otherwise live and lie, yes, and die also; and so live, lie and die under God’s wrath. To free a wife from that misery and wretchedness is as great a token of love as to pull her out of the water when she is in danger of drowning, or out of the fire when she is in danger of burning. Solomon calls reproofs “life-giving,”1065 and expressly notes that “reproofs”1066 are “the way to life”: a means to breed and preserve spiritual life, and to bring one to eternal life, and so to escape death and damnation. In these respects rebukes are called “a precious balm,” or “excellent oil,” which may heal a wound but makes none: it “does not break the head,”1067 as the psalmist says. On this ground, no doubt, it is noted of many good husbands, who were beyond all question loving, kind, meek and mild husbands, that they reproved their wives: as Jacob,1068 Job,1069 David,1070 and others.

§. 34. Of neglecting reproof.

Contrary to this is the servile and timid spirit of many husbands, who are reluctant to offend and (as they think) to provoke their wives, and so choose rather to let them continue in sin than to tell them of it. In this they both dishonor their place, and the image of God which they bear by virtue of their place, and also in effect and in truth hate their wives. The law implies this where it says, “You must not hate your brother in your heart,1071 but you must directly rebuke your neighbor, and not allow sin to rest on him.”

§. 35. Of ordering reproof well in its matter.1072

That a husband may clearly demonstrate that his reproving of his wife is truly a fruit of his love, he must take special care to sweeten it, especially with mildness: for it is the bitterest pill that a husband can give to a wife. It is a verbal correction, and in that respect a middle means (if I may so speak) between admonition and correction, partaking somewhat of both. It goes no further than words, and so is an admonition; the words of a reproof are sharp, and so it is a correction. Though it is only a mild correction, yet it is a sharp admonition, and all the correction which a husband can give his wife by himself: for we will1073 show later that he must not proceed to blows and strokes.

To sweeten reproof with mildness, regard must be had (as was noted before about commanding) both to its matter and to its manner.

The matter of reproof must be1074

  1. Just.
  2. Weighty.

Justice requires that what he reproves his wife for be a truth, and a known truth, indeed a thing of which he is certain. Christ, in giving direction for reproving rightly, lays this down as a ground: “If your brother trespasses, etc.”1075 A trespass therefore must go before reproof: where there is no trespass, reproof is unjust.

Again, the apostle advises that an accusation should not1076 be received “except on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” By this he implies that an idle report must not be received; rather, where blame is laid, there must be two or three witnesses to confirm it, so that he who censures may have good and sure ground for what he does. Indeed, that advice was given in particular about an elder, but from the less to the greater it will follow that it is good advice concerning wives: for no kind of person must be more wary in laying blame on another, and reproving them for it, than a husband with his wife.

Equity further requires that the matter for which a husband1077 reproves his wife be weighty: namely, some fault that is dangerous to her soul, harmful to their worldly condition, or contagious through its bad example to children and others in the family; but most of all, sin against God, which provokes his wrath and pulls down his heavy curse on him, her and the whole family.

When what a wife is reproved for is a truth, a known truth and a weighty truth, the husband in performing this duty justifies his deed and shows that there was need of it, and so gives evidence of his love. He makes his reproof pierce more deeply, and so makes her more ashamed of her fault. From this it will follow that she will either amend her fault or at least have her mouth stopped, so that she will have nothing to object against it. The reproofs of the three saints mentioned before, Jacob,1078 Job1079 and David,1080 corresponded to these points of justice and wisdom; and their effects corresponded to those which we have noted in this reason, as the silence of the three wives implies: for none of them answered back.

§. 36. Of undue reproof.

Contrary to the justice and equity named above are overready1081 credulity and undue suspicion. Credulity is when belief is given to every idle report, and blame is then laid on the wife before any just proof is made of what she is blamed for. By this it often comes to pass that she is wrongfully and unjustly blamed; and if she is, what good fruit can come from such reproofs? Indeed, what evil fruits are not likely to come from them, such as secret discontent (if not malice and hatred) and open contentions and quarrels?

The same may be said of light and causeless suspicion, which1082 is the mother of jealousy and the very bane of marriage. The devil takes great advantage from it against them both, seeking by it to untie the knot which God has so firmly tied between them. Suspicion is to the mind what a colored glass is to the eye: it shows things to the sight not as they truly are in their own true color, but as the color of the glass is. Suspicion will make a man twist everything that his wife does, and blame her many times for things that are praiseworthy. In that case, what can be thought but that a husband is seeking an advantage against his wife, rather than any good for her?

If to those two vices named above (credulity and suspicion) he1083 adds rashness and hastiness in reproving, and makes every small and light matter which he in any way dislikes a matter for reproof, does he not proclaim to all who come to know it that he loves scolding more than he loves his wife? Indeed, is this not the ready way to make all his reproofs (if not scorned) lightly regarded? What then will be the profit of them?

§. 37. Whether a husband may reprove his wife for such things as he is guilty of.

To the matter of reproof some add that a husband ought not to reprove his wife for a fault of which he himself is guilty. But I doubt this direction. I do not deny that he ought to take special care that he is not guilty of the crime for which he blames his wife. Otherwise, 1. He blunts the edge of his reproof, so that it cannot readily pierce into her heart. 2. He makes it rebound back on himself with these reproaches: “Physician, heal1084 yourself!” “You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye.” “You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?” 3. He is a heavy witness against himself; for in judging another he condemns himself. But to infer from this that, because he is guilty of the same vices as are in his wife, he ought not to reprove her, though she deserves to be reproved, is hardly sound and good divinity. For in this way he makes himself guilty of a double fault: one, of committing the sin himself; the other, of allowing his wife to lie in it. Whereas if he reproved his wife, he might by it reclaim both her and himself: for I do not doubt that his reproving of his wife would strike deeper into his own conscience than if a third person reproved them both. How Judah and David1085 were struck to the heart after they had given sentence against the very crimes of which they themselves were guilty! It is good advice that no man be guilty of what he reproves in his wife; but it is no good rule to say that no man ought to reprove his wife for what he is guilty of.

§. 38. Of ordering reproof well in its manner.

Directions like those which were given for the manner1086 of commanding must be observed in the manner of reproving.

Reproofs therefore must be

  • Rare.
  • Meek.

When reproofs are seldom used, and only on urgent and1087 necessary occasion, 1. It shows that a husband takes no delight in rebuking his wife, but is even forced to it. 2. It makes his wife regard it much more. 3. It is likely to work a more perfect cure, for seldom and rare reproofs commonly pierce most deeply.

Contrary to this is continual scolding and finding fault with a1088 wife for everything amiss. If not only the wife herself, but a child, or a servant, or anyone else in the house does wrong, the wife will be blamed for it. This is too common a fault in husbands, by which they greatly provoke their wives; yes, and many times make them regard a reproof no more than any other word. For as birds which always live in belfries where there is much ringing are not frightened at all by the loud sound, so wives who have their ears filled from time to time with their husbands’ rebukes are brought by habit not to be moved by them at all.

2. That a reproof must be given in meekness is clear from1089 the apostle’s general precept to restore one “with a spirit of meekness”: for a right manner of reproving is particularly intended by it. Now of all with whom we have to do, there is no fitter object for meekness than a wife, who in a more special manner than any other is “your own flesh.”

Meekness concerns both secrecy of place and softness of words.

When a husband is alone with his wife, then is the fittest1090 time for reproof. In this way reproof will correspond to Christ’s direction: “tell him his fault between you and him alone” (Christ says this of a brother); but no brother must be treated more tenderly than a wife. In this way also it will soak better into her soul, when no thought of dishonor and discredit arises to hinder its work; such thoughts will readily arise when a reproof is given in public before others. In this way, likewise, occasion to despise her will be taken away from children and servants, which they would otherwise quickly take if she were rebuked before them, concluding from it that she is kept under as much as they are. Now because she is a joint governor of them with him, he ought by all means to maintain her reputation before them.

1. Question. What if she does not regard a rebuke in secret?1091

Answer. He may follow Christ’s direction, “take one or two others along”: namely, wise, grave, faithful friends, if possible of her own kindred, such as her parents (if she has any living), or those who are next to parents in the course of nature (if they are not partial on her side); and he may rebuke her before them, but by no means before any of the household under her government.

2. Question. What if her fault is public, one that1092 may be a bad example to those of the household, since it was committed in their sight or brought to their knowledge some other way?

Answer. He must wisely show his dislike of her fault in such a way that he in no way impairs her honor. He may therefore declare that such a thing was not well done, and warn his household beforehand against committing the like; indeed, sharply threaten them that if any of them does the like they will dearly regret it. And if any who are under correction offend in it, he may correct them all the more surely and severely, for the very reason that they have followed her example. In this way he will show great and good respect for his wife, and also a thorough dislike and hatred of her sin.

2. “A soft tongue” (as Solomon notes) “breaks a bone,”1093 that is, softens a hard heart and beats down a stubborn pride. How then will it work on a soft heart and a gentle disposition? If therefore a husband looks to do good by reproving his wife, his reproof must be so ordered that it may seem rather a gentle admonition than a sharp rebuke. He may and ought to declare her fault to her plainly, but in mild and meek terms, without reviling, insulting and degrading words.

Question. What if her fault is a heinous, notorious sin?

Answer. In an extraordinary case some sharpness may be1094 used, as the reproofs of Jacob, Job and David show, for every one of them was sharp. But yet this sharpness must not be made bitter by any abusive language. A woman’s wickedness must not move a husband to be perverse and1095 violent, but rather to be all the more watchful over himself, that he keeps himself within the bounds of discretion and moderation. To this end it is fitting that husbands lay it down as a rule never to rebuke their wives when they are angry. Anger raises a dark mist before the eyes of reason, which, while it remains, keeps reason from giving any good direction. Indeed, anger is like a fire, and it so inflames a man and unsettles him that in his disorder he can keep no moderation or measure. However unable a man may be to rule himself when anger is stirred up, yet if beforehand, while “his eye is good,1096 and his whole body full of light,” while he is “in tune” (as we say) and well tempered, he resolutely determines with himself not to do this or that thing in his anger, that earlier resolution will be a special means to make him forbear doing in anger what, if he did it, he could not well order and moderate in anger. For once he begins to do a thing in anger, the least provocation possible will be like bellows to blow that fire up into a flame.

Because of the violence of anger (in which women, because1097 of the weakness of their judgment, are for the most part most violent), it is also the part of a wise man to forbear this duty of reproving his wife even while she is angry. For as it is needful that he should be in a fit state to give a reproof, so it is just as needful that she should be in a fit state to take a rebuke. Anger both fills and festers one’s heart. The heart, then, being full of anger, what room is left for good advice? Will a man pour wine into a vessel full of water, or wait till all the water is drained out?

The heart also being so festered that it tastes of nothing but anger, what good can good advice do then?

It is therefore a special point of wisdom, and shows the good regard that a man bears for his wife, indeed it savors of much meekness and moderation, for a husband to weigh well both his own and his wife’s state of mind when he reproves her, and to forbear doing it while either he or she is angry.

§. 39. Of reproving a wife indiscreetly.

Contrary to this is the indiscretion of husbands who regard neither place, nor persons, nor time, nor the state of mind of themselves or their wives, nor any other circumstance in reproving. Like Saul (who, at a table where there was a great feast, in the presence of his nobles and captains, when he was enraged with anger, not only rebuked but also reviled his son with most virulent and bitter words, and with such words that he did not spare his own wife; for in his rage he called his son “son1098 of a perverse and rebellious woman”), like this foolish and furious Saul, I say, they take the most open place in the family, before children, servants and the whole house, to reprove their wives; and that with such bitter and disgraceful terms that either they provoke their wives to answer back to maintain (as they think) their own credit and reputation (so Jonathan1099 was provoked to answer his father back), or else they give those of the house who see her trampled underfoot like this an occasion to set their feet on her too.

Most husbands are eager enough to reprove, but few do it with meekness and moderation. They cannot do it except in company, nor without bitter words. Many, in rebuking their wives, do not hesitate to use all the evil names they can think of, even such as tend not only to their wives’ dishonor but also to their own and their children’s disgrace. The reason for this is that they never rebuke except when they are angry, and so hardly know what they are doing. By this they also stir up anger in their wives, and yet for all that they do not hold back one bit more, but rather grow more violent: as when the heat of two fires meets together, the flame must be all the greater. Since this is the wrongheaded practice of many husbands, is it any wonder that ordinarily so little good and so much harm is done by reproving? Indeed, would it not be a wonder if any good and no harm were done by it? Therefore, though this is a duty, yet it is a duty to be used rarely and with great moderation.

So much for a husband’s mildness in his speech to his wife.

A Husband’s Kind Conduct toward His Wife

The Fourth Treatise: Of Husbands · §§. 40–46

§. 40. Of a husband’s amiable countenance toward his wife.1100

A husband’s conduct toward his wife must correspond1101 to his speech, or else all its mildness will seem mere compliment.

A man’s conduct includes his countenance, gesture, actions; and mildness must be seated in all of them.

1. His countenance in his wife’s presence, and toward his1102 wife, must be composed to an amiable pleasantness. His authority over her and his eminence above her must not make him forget the close bond and union between them.

Under the face and countenance I include the head, brow, eyes, lips and such other parts as are, according to how they are set, signs of amiability or of discontent. Now among and above the other parts of the body, the outward composition of the countenance soonest and best declares the inward disposition of the heart. By Esau’s pleasant countenance Jacob perceived that Esau was reconciled to him in his heart, and so he said, “I have seen your face, and it is like1103 seeing the face of God,” that is, an amiable, gracious countenance. On this ground David asked God “to shine the light of His1104 countenance upon him,” so that by it he might know the favor and love of God toward him. On the other side, by a frowning and scowling face, by hanging down the head, pouting the lips and the like, anger, malice, grief and other such feelings of the heart are shown. By Cain’s downcast1105 countenance God discerned that anger and envy were in his heart; by Laban’s countenance1106 Jacob observed that Laban’s affection had turned from him. A wife, then, seeing mildness and amiability in her husband’s face, sees it as the face of God, and in it, as in a looking glass, sees the kindness and love of his heart. And so her heart is all the more firmly knit to him by it, and she is moved all the more to respect him.

§. 41. Of husbands’ too great austerity.

Contrary to this is 1. A lofty, proud countenance, like that of an imperious1107 lord over his vassals.

2. A grim, stern countenance, like that of a judge over poor prisoners.1108

3. A scowling, frowning countenance, like that of a discontented1109 creditor over a desperate debtor.

4. A fierce, fiery countenance, like that of an angry king over a1110 subject who has displeased him.

As these and similar countenances show a proud, stubborn, furious, discontented disposition of heart, so they cannot but give a wife great discontent, indeed greatly frighten her, since she is only a weak vessel, and turn her heart and love away from him.

§. 42. Of a husband’s affectionate gesture with his wife.

II. A husband’s gesture ought to be so affectionate and amiable1111 toward his wife that others may see that he is her husband, and his wife may be moved to be affectionate toward him. Those who are ready to show themselves kind and mild husbands in this way are prone to go too far, and so to fall into an extreme on the right hand. For some are never content except when they have their wives in their laps, always hugging, kissing and fondling them, no matter in what company. In this they show more flightiness, foolishness and doting than true kindness and love, which does not forget a husbandly gravity, sobriety, modesty and decency.

Some do not hesitate to cite Isaac’s caressing of Rebekah1112 to1113 justify their lasciviousness.

But they forget that what Isaac did was done when he and his1114 wife were alone: he was seen through a window. Much greater liberty is granted to man and wife when they are alone than in company. Besides, there are many other ways to show kindness and familiarity than by flightiness and wantonness.

§. 43. Of a husband’s aloofness toward his wife.

Contrary to the familiarity I speak of is (as we say) aloofness, when a husband carries himself toward his wife as if she were a stranger to him. If he comes into company where his wife is, of all the women there he will not turn to her or take notice of her. This fault is all the greater if such a man is of a free, pleasant manner, and is accustomed to be merry and friendly with other women. Though his mirth and familiarity are such as are not unbecoming to a Christian, yet since his manner toward his wife is of another kind, it may be a means of breeding jealousy in her. Many think that outward kind gestures toward a wife are foolish doting; but if they knew what a means it is to stir up, increase and preserve love in a wife’s heart toward her husband, they would think otherwise.

§. 43. Of a husband’s giving favors to his wife.

III. Actions are, of all things, the most real demonstrations of true kindness, and a husband must not fail in them if he would have his kind speech, countenance and gesture taken in good part. Kindness and mildness in action consist in giving favors (as we say) to his wife. This is expressly noted of Elkanah, who every year gave favors to1115 his wives. As a husband shows his love to his wife by this, so he will greatly move her to do every duty to him. A small gift, given freely as an act of kindness, not as a debt but in testimony of love, works more on the heart of her to whom it is given than much more given by contract, or for a work done, so that it may seem to be earned.

In giving favors to a wife, a husband ought to be more bountiful and generous than to others, so that she may see by it that he loves her above all; as it is noted that Elkanah gave “Hannah a double portion, for he loved her.”1116 And in giving favors it is best to give them with his own hands, unless he is away from her.

§. 44. Of husbands beating their wives.

Contrary to this are the furious and spiteful actions of many unkind husbands (heads too heady), whose favors are cuffs,1117 blows, strokes and lashes. In this they are worse than the venomous viper. For the viper casts out its poison for its mate’s sake; and will you not, O husband, out of regard for that close union between you and your wife, lay aside your fierceness and cruelty? Many wives, because of their husbands’ fury, are worse off than servants: for

1. Those who will not give a servant a blow do not care what load they lay on their wives.

2. Whereas servants are under the tyranny of such furious men only for a set time and term, poor wives are tied to them all their life long.

3. Wives cannot have as good a remedy by the help of the law against cruel husbands as servants may have against cruel masters.

4. Masters do not have such opportunity to exercise their cruelty on servants as husbands have on wives, who are to be continually at table and in bed with their husbands.

5. The nearer wives are to their husbands, and the dearer they ought to be to them, the more grievous blows must be when they are given by a husband’s hand,1118 than by a master’s.

6. The less power and authority a husband has to strike his wife than a master has to strike a servant, the heavier his blows seem, and the worse a wife’s case seems in that respect than a servant’s. Not unfitly, therefore, is such a man (if he may be thought a man rather than a beast) said to be like a father-killer and a mother-killer.

Question. Is a husband, then, not allowed to beat his wife?1119

Answer. With submission to better judgments, I think he must not. My reasons are these.

1. There is no warrant anywhere in Scripture1120 for it, by precept or example. Though this argument is negative, yet for the point in hand it is a forcible argument in two respects. 1. Because Scripture has so plentifully and particularly set out the distinct duties of husbands and wives, and yet has said nothing about a husband’s striking and beating his wife. 2. Because it has also spoken plentifully and particularly of all who are to correct others, of their manner of correcting, of the bearing of correction by those who are to be corrected, and of the use they are to make of it; and yet it says nothing at all about a husband’s punishing, or a wife’s bearing punishment, in this way. Since Scripture is so silent on this point, we may well infer that God has not ranked wives among those in the family who are to be corrected.

2. That small disparity which (as I have1121 shown before) is1122 between man and wife does not permit so high a power in a husband, and so low a servitude in a wife, that he should beat her. Can it be thought reasonable that she who is the man’s lifelong bedfellow, who has power over his body, who1123 is a joint parent of the children and a joint governor of the family, should be beaten by his hands? What if children or servants should know of it? (as they surely will: for how can such a thing be done in the house without those of the house knowing it?) Can they respect her as a mother or a mistress, when she is under correction as well as they?

3. The close bond, and the very union, that is between1124 man and wife does not allow such dealing to pass between them. The wife is as a man’s self: “The two will be one flesh.”1125 No man but a frenzied, furious, desperate wretch will beat himself. Two sorts of men are noted in Scripture as cutting and gashing their own flesh: idolaters, like the1126 prophets of Baal, and demoniacs, like1127 the man who was possessed with a legion of devils. Such are those who beat their wives: either blinded in their understanding, or possessed with a devil.

Objection. He who is soundest in his wits will allow his body to be pinched, pricked, lanced and otherwise pained, if it is needful and beneficial.

Answer. 1. A man’s heart will not allow him to do any of these things himself. There are surgeons whose work it is to do such things, and if the surgeon himself needs any such remedy for his own body, he will use the help of another surgeon. If the case is such that a wife must be beaten, it is more fitting for a husband to refer the matter to a public magistrate (who is like an approved and licensed surgeon) and not to do it with his own hands.

2. Though some parts of the body may be treated so, not every part may, such as the heart, which the wife is to the man.

3. The comparison does not hold. For the pinching, lancing, etc. named above is no punishment for any fault, as the beating of a wife in question is. There is no question that a man who has the skill may, if need be, open a vein, lance a boil, splint a broken bone or set a dislocated joint in his wife’s body, which may be more painful than correction; and in this the comparison holds, but not in the other.

2. Objection. There is as close a union between Christ and his church as between man and wife; yet Christ does not refrain from correcting and punishing his church.

Answer. There is a twofold relation between Christ and the church. He is a husband to it, having made it “of His flesh, and of His bones,” and he is a supreme Lord over it, having “all authority1128 in heaven and on earth” given to him. He punishes in this latter respect, not in the former. A husband is not such a supreme lord over his wife; therefore Christ’s example is no warrant for him.

4. There is no hope of any good coming from a husband’s1129 beating of his wife. For where the one who is corrected is persuaded that the one who corrects has no authority or right to do so, that one will not be brought to take it patiently, but will resist and strive, if possible, to get the mastery. Let a stranger strike a grown child or a servant who will patiently bear many blows at a parent’s or master’s hand, and they will turn on that stranger and try to give him as good as he brings. Now since a wife has no ground to be persuaded that her husband has authority to1130 beat her, what hope is there that she will patiently bear it and be bettered by it? Or rather, is it not likely that she will, if she can, rise against him, get the mastery over him (as many do), and never do any duty rightly? A fault in a wife is not taken away but increased by blows.

Objection. Smart and pain may make her dread her husband, stand in awe of him, and do her duty the better.

Answer. Such dread and awe befit neither a husband’s place, to demand them, nor a wife’s place, to give them. Though she may be brought by force to yield some outward subjection, yet inward hatred of her husband’s person may be joined with it, which is as bad as outward disobedience, if not worse.

Objection. She may be of so outrageous a disposition that she will not be kept within any bounds except by1131 force.

1. Answer. It was answered long ago that “no fault should be so great as to compel a husband to beat his wife.”

2. Answer. Other forcible means may be used besides beating by her husband’s hands. She may be restrained in her liberty, denied the things she most desires, and kept shut up, as it were, under guard; and, if no other means will serve, she may be handed over to the magistrate. Then, if she is of so servile a disposition that she will be kept under by no other means than by fear and force, by smart and pain, she may fear the magistrate and feel his hand rather than her husband’s.

Objection. If a wife grows so mannish, or rather mad, as to try to strike and beat her husband, may he not beat her in that case to make her stop her outrage?

Answer. I do not doubt that the good provision the law makes to preserve a man’s life may be applied to this purpose. The law absolutely condemns all murder; yet if a man is so assaulted that there is no way to preserve his own life but by taking the life of the one who assaults him, it does not condemn him as a murderer, because he did it in defense of himself. So if a husband1132 is set on by his wife, it is lawful and advisable that he defend himself; and if he can do it no other way but by striking her, that is not to be counted an unlawful beating of her.

§. 45. Of a husband’s bearing with his wife’s infirmities.

So much for the husband’s avoiding of offense; now a word about his bearing with offense.

It is a general duty, common to all people of every sort, to “bear one1133 another’s burdens.” In this wide sense even a wife is to bear her husband’s burden, because he, like everyone else, is liable to slip and fall, and so needs to be supported. Yet this duty belongs to a husband in a more special and distinctive way, and that in two respects.

1. Of the two, he is more bound than his wife, because in relation to his wife he is the stronger: for she is “the weaker vessel,”1134 1 Pet 3:7. But the strong are most bound “to bear with the infirmities of the weak,” Rom 15:1.

2. He is bound to bear with his wife more than with anyone else, because of the close union between them: he who cannot bear with his wife, his flesh, can bear with nobody. The reason the apostle gives to move a man to dwell with his wife according to knowledge, and to give honor to her, implied in this phrase, “as to the weaker vessel,”1135 shows that this is a duty belonging distinctively to a husband, in and by which he may both show his knowledge and wisdom and also do honor to his wife. For why is he reminded of her weakness, but to show that he should bear with her?

As that phrase implies the duty, so it also implies a good reason to enforce it. For precious things that we value highly are handled the more tenderly and carefully the weaker they are, such as china dishes and crystal glasses; and of all parts of the body, the eye is handled most tenderly. Now what things, what persons, are more dear and precious than a wife? Yet she is also a weak vessel; therefore she is much to be borne with.

For a husband’s better direction in this, a distinction must be1136 made between infirmities: some are natural imperfections, others are actual transgressions. Natural imperfections are inward (such as slowness of mind, dullness of understanding, shortness of memory, quickness of temper, etc.) or outward (such as lameness, blindness, deafness, or any other defect and deformity of body). These infirmities should breed pity, compassion, sympathy, yes, and greater tenderness and respect, but no offense. Note Abraham’s example in this case: his wife was barren, yet he did not despise1137 her for it, nor reproach her with any such thing.

Actual transgressions are breaches of God’s law. Those meant here are such as tend most directly to his own disquiet and disadvantage, such as shrewishness, waywardness, fussiness, stubbornness, etc. In bearing with these a husband must especially show his wisdom, and that in various ways.

1. By using the best and mildest means he can to remedy them, such as meek admonition, timely advice, gentle entreaty and compassionate affection. Elkanah, thinking that his wife was at fault in her distress, dealt with her in this way and supported her.

2. By removing the stone she stumbles over, taking away the occasion (as far as he fittingly can) that makes her offend. So Abram, and that by God’s direction, put Hagar and her son out of the house, because they were an offense to Sarah.

3. By turning his eyes away (if the matter is not great, but1138 such as may be tolerated) and taking no notice of the offense, but rather passing it by, as if he did not perceive it. Solomon says that “it is to a man’s glory to overlook an offense,”1139 and he urges a man “not to pay attention to every word that is spoken.”

4. By forgiving and forgetting it (if notice has been taken of it). Jacob took notice of Rachel’s rash and perverse demand, for he1140 rebuked her for it; yet since he readily yielded to what she afterward urged on him, it appears that he forgave the offense, if he did not forget it.

The best test of a man’s love for his wife, and of his wisdom1141 in ordering it, lies in this point of bearing with offenses. Not to be offended with a wife who gives no offense is not praiseworthy: heathen men may go that far. Note what Christ says of this case: “If you+ love those who love you+, and do good to1142 those who do good to you+, what credit and reward is that to you+? For tax collectors and sinners do the same.” But gently to forbear, and wisely to pass over offenses when they are given, and not to be provoked when cause of provocation is given, is a true Christian virtue, a virtue that becomes husbands better than any other kind of men.

§. 46. Of husbands’ testiness.

Contrary to this is testiness and irritability, when husbands are moved by the least provocation, like tinder catching fire at the least spark that falls on it. Indeed, many are like gunpowder, which not only catches fire but also breaks out into a violent flame at the least touch of fire. As gunpowder is dangerous to keep in a house, so such husbands are dangerous to be joined as closely to wives as marriage joins them. If it is said that, as gunpowder does no harm if fire does not come near it, so they are good and kind if they are not provoked and displeased, I answer that we have a proverb that says, “The devil is good while he is pleased,” yet it is not safe to have the devil too near. It is as impossible (considering man’s weakness) for a man to live and keep company with anyone and not give offense, as for flint stones to beat and dash against one another for long and no spark of fire to come from them. How then can it be thought possible for a wife, who is so continually in her husband’s company, and is the weaker vessel, to live without giving him offense? It is not a very kind saying that husbands use, especially when they are told of their unkindness: “Let my wife deserve favor, and she will have it.” How little favor would such husbands have from Christ their husband, if he were of that mind toward them!

Thus far the first part of a husband’s good management of his authority has been handled: a tender respect for his wife.

The second is a provident care for her.
