A Husband’s Providing for His Wife

The Fourth Treatise: Of Husbands · §§. 46–60

§. 46. Of a husband’s provident care for his wife.

A husband who tenderly respects his wife but has no provident care for her shows more affection than discretion: he may have a kind heart, but he lacks a wise head. How then can he be a good head to his wife? She may have some present contentment from him, but she can reap little profit and benefit from him. The duties that have been set out must therefore be done, but those that follow must by no means be left undone.

A husband’s provident care is noted in that office of Christ in which a husband resembles him, namely, to be a “Savior of1143 the body,” as has been1144 declared before. It consists

  1. In providing what is needful for his wife.
  2. In protecting her from what is harmful.

1. A careful providing of what is needful is a principal part of1145 the honor that husbands are to give to their wives.1146 For where the apostle says that “elders … are worthy of double honor,” he means maintenance as well as reverence. The apostle counts him “worse than an unbeliever” who “does not provide for his own,1147 and especially his own household.” Who belongs to a husband’s household, if not his wife? In his house, who is more properly his own than his wife? If then a husband does not provide for his wife, what is he1148 to be counted?

There is great reason he should provide for her, because he has taken her from her parents and family, and has received the portion they allotted her, and has authority committed to him over her, and she is put in subjection under him. Her family, having given away her portion and their power over her, and committed all to him, will take no further care for her; and she, being in subjection under him, cannot provide for herself without him. Who then will provide for her if he does not, whose she is wholly and only?

Contrary to this is the mind of those who take a wife only for their own1149 contentment, or delight, or gain, and never think of the charge they take on themselves together with a wife. Their practice matches their mind: for when they have a wife, they neglect her in everything except what may serve their own ends. They have much to answer for, and all the more because a wife is a special pledge of God’s favor.1150

§. 47. Of a husband’s providing means of spiritual edification for his wife.

In this provident care that a husband ought to have for his wife, we will consider its extent and its continuance.

It ought to extend both to herself and to others.

With respect to herself, to her

  • Soul.
  • Body.

For her soul, means of spiritual edification must be provided, both private and public. Private means are1151 holy and religious exercises in the house, such as reading the word, prayer, catechizing and the like. Since these are the spiritual food of the soul, they are to be provided and used every day, as our bodily food is. A husband, as master of a family, must provide these for the good of his whole house; but as a husband, especially for the good of his wife. For to his wife, as well as to the whole house, he is a king, a priest and a prophet.

He ought therefore to perform these things himself for his wife’s good, or to provide that they may be done by someone else. Cornelius himself performed those exercises.1152 Micah hired a Levite (though his idolatry was evil, yet his care to have a Levite in his house was commendable). The1153 Shunammite’s husband provided a room for the prophet, and that especially for his wife’s sake, for it was at her request.

Public means are the holy ordinances of God publicly1154 performed by God’s minister. A husband’s care for his wife in this respect is so to order his dwelling, and provide other needful things, that his wife may share in them. It is expressly noted of Elkanah that he so provided for his1155 wives that they went with him every year to the house of God; the same is implied of Joseph, the husband of the virgin Mary. In those days there was a public place and house of God, to which all God’s people (however far from it they lived) were to go every year. The places where Elkanah and Joseph lived were far away from the house of God, yet they so provided that not only they themselves but their wives also went to the public worship of God. Now there are many houses of God, places for the public worship of God; but even so, through the corruption of our times, the ministry of the word (the chief means of spiritual edification) is not to be had everywhere. Therefore a husband’s care for his wife in this respect ought to be such that he lives where she may have the benefit of the preaching of the word, or else so provides for her that she may go each week where it may be had.

If men of wisdom and means make a purchase, or build a house to live in, they will make sure it is where there are sweet rivers and waters, and good pasture ground, and where all needful provisions may be had. God’s word preached is a spring of the water of life; the place where it is preached is a pleasant, profitable pasture; all needful provision for the soul may be had there. Let this therefore be inquired after most of all, and let no dwelling be settled except where this may be had.

§. 48. Of neglecting their wives’ edification.

Contrary to this is the practice of those who have their calling in places where the word is plentiful, yet for outward reasons of pleasure, delight, ease and profit move their families into remote places where preaching is scarce, if there is any at all. There they leave their wives to govern the family, with no regard for their lack of the word, since they themselves, often coming to London or other such places because of their calling, enjoy the word themselves. Many city tradesmen, lawyers and others are guilty of great neglect of their wives in this respect.

So also are those who banish all religious exercises from their houses, making their houses brothels of the devil rather than churches of God. If, for lack of means, either public or private, a wife lives and dies in ignorance, profaneness, unbelief and impenitence, which bring eternal damnation, her blood will assuredly be required at his hands. For a husband1156 is God’s watchman to his wife.

§. 49. Of a husband’s providing things needful for his wife’s body.

A husband’s provident care for his wife must also extend to her body, and that both in health and in sickness. In health, by providing such things as are needful to preserve health, such as sufficient food, clothing and the like necessities. Where the1157 prophet, to heighten the misery of the people, says, “Seven women will take hold of one man,” saying, “We will eat our own bread and provide our own clothes. Just let us be called by your name,” he implies that it was a husband’s duty to provide bread and clothing, that is, all necessities, for his wife. The1158 law also implies this, where it commands the man who takes one wife on top of another not to diminish the food and clothing of the first. In sickness, such things are to be provided as are needful either to restore her health, or to comfort, cherish and refresh her in her sickness.

This was1159 noted before among the mutual duties common to both; for by virtue of the marriage bond it belongs to both man and wife. But it belongs to the man by virtue of the power and charge he has over his wife, and therefore it was needful to touch on it here.

§. 50. Of a husband’s provident care for his wife in her childbearing.1160

Most fitting to this place is the provident care that husbands ought to have for their wives both before and at the time of their labor and their recovery after childbirth; and that in two things especially.

1. In getting for their wives, to the utmost of their power and ability, such things as may satisfy their cravings, if they do have cravings (as in all ages women have been subject to them at the time of pregnancy and childbearing). For it is well known that it is very dangerous both for mother and child for her to go without what she craves: sometimes the death of the one, sometimes of the other, sometimes of both has followed from it.

2. In providing such things as are needful for their labor and their recovery after childbirth. This time is especially to be provided for, for many reasons.

1. Because it is a time of weakness, in which the woman cannot well provide for herself.

2. Because her weakness is joined with much pain. The1161 pain of a woman in labor is the greatest pain that is ordinarily endured by anyone for its time. None know it so well as those who feel it, and many husbands, because they are not subject to it, think only lightly of it. But if we duly weigh1162 that the Holy Spirit, when he would set out the extremity of any pains and pangs, likens them to the pains of a woman in labor, we may well gather that they are the greatest of all. This is further shown by the shrieks and outcries that not only weak and faint-hearted women utter at the time of their labor, but that are also forced from the strongest and bravest women there are, and that even though they resolve beforehand to the contrary. Nor can we wonder at it; for their body is, as it were, set on a rack (at least if the labor is hard), and all their parts so stretched that it is a wonder they should ever recover their health and strength again, or that they should hold out against the brunt and not die in their labor, as Rachel and the wife of Phinehas1163 and many in all ages have done. Surely among ordinary deliverances I know none so near a miracle, none in which the Almighty so evidently shows his great power and good providence, as in the safe delivery of women. Besides the great pang of labor, women are also subject after their delivery to many after-pains, which are very painful. From all these pains, and the great weakness that befalls women after childbirth, especially if they nurse their children, men are freed because of their sex. Now then, to apply this point: seeing women are brought to such pains and weakness in bringing forth those children who are the man’s as well as hers, and he is freed from all of it, is it not very just and fitting that he should provide all things needful for her welfare, ease and recovery of strength?

3. Because the lack of needful things is very dangerous at that time: dangerous to the health and life of the woman, and of the child also.

§. 51. Of neglecting wives in their weakness.

Contrary to a husband’s provident care in general are those vices that were reproved in the treatise of common duties,1164 such as grudging the expense spent on a wife, covetousness, wastefulness and idleness.

But contrary in particular to a husband’s care for his wife in childbirth is the inhuman and worse than barbarous unkindness of many husbands, who give no thought at all to the weakness of their wives in this case, to help, ease and comfort them, but rather make their burden much heavier. For,

1. Some, through covetousness, refuse beforehand to give their wife the means to provide such things as are needful for herself and her child. And when the time comes, if their wife wants a midwife who costs somewhat more than the nearest one, she will have none if she will not have the nearest. And as for a nurse to tend her, they think their maid will serve well enough: they need not go to the expense of bringing a nurse into the house. As for fitting lodging, some will not hesitate to say, “Can my wife not give birth in a room without a fireplace as well as the virgin Mary? Why should my wife need more things than she did?” Indeed, further, there are many who, when the time of their wife’s delivery draws near, carry her away from all her family to a place where she is not known, so that her family will not by their pleading draw him to spend and lay out more on his wife than he is willing to. While their wife is weak after childbirth, many are unwilling to allow their wives any other food than is provided in the house for themselves and their children, not considering that her appetite cannot be like theirs.

Many other such bitter fruits of unkind husbands, springing from covetousness, might be listed, by which husbands plainly show that they love their wealth better than their wives: they would rather lose them than part with that.

2. Others, through jealous suspicion, do not refrain, even at1165 the time of their wives’ pain and weakness, from reproaching them with looseness and saying that the child is not the husband’s. To lay this to a wife’s charge unjustly is at any time a most shameful and hateful reproach; but at the time of childbirth, whether just or unjust, it is a thing far too spiteful and vengeful. Some wives are so overcome by it (especially at the time of their weakness) that they are not able to bear it, but even faint and die under the reproach; others, of a bolder spirit, vow never to lie with their husbands again. Many such injuries follow from such unkindness.

§. 52. Of a husband’s providing for his wife according to his means and ability.1166

In a husband’s providing for his wife’s body, regard must be had to the measure and to the manner.

The measure must extend as far as his ability. For a husband ought to maintain his wife in as good a condition and style as himself. By marriage she is advanced to as high a standing and dignity in relation to others as he is; and for her own use she is made a partner of all his goods, and accordingly ought to share in them.

As for the manner, he must allow her (at least if he sees that she has sufficient discretion) to order such things as are needful for herself as she likes best; as Elkanah, in another case, said to his wife, “Do what you think is best.”1167

Both in the measure and in the manner of providing, a difference must be made between a wife and servants or children. These may have their portions of food, clothing and like necessities measured out and rationed to them, which is not fitting to be done to a wife. Nor is it needful that so plentiful a provision be made for them as for her.

§. 53. Of a husband’s stinginess toward his wife.

Contrary to this is a husband’s stingy dealing with his wife: when the allowance she has is far below his means, and is also given to her little by little, as if she were a child. Many husbands make their wives drudge at home, eat poorly and dress shabbily, while they themselves are finely dressed, merry at their feasts away from home, and so far outdo their wives that they are ashamed to be seen in company with their wives. Those who marry their maids, or others of lower rank than themselves, often deal with them in this way, regarding them as no more than servants and lowly persons, though they are their wives. But it has been1168 shown before that wives are advanced by marriage to their husbands’ dignity, however lowly they were before.

§. 54. Of husbands’ allowing their wives to give to others, as they see good occasion.1169

A husband’s provident care for his wife ought to extend so far that she may have (besides what is needful for herself) something to give to those to whom it is fitting for her to give: namely, to children and servants in the house, and to others also outside the house. For this much is noted in Solomon’s description1170 of a good wife: “She provides food for her household and portions for her maidservants … all her household is clothed in scarlet” (namely, by her ordering and managing of things). “Her children rise up and call her blessed,” for her general conduct in the family, and also for the particular kindnesses she has shown them. As for1171 others outside the house, it is also noted that “she opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.” She did these things by virtue of the power and liberty her husband gave her, as appears from two points noted there:

1. Before any mention is made of the things1172 she did, it is said, “The heart of her husband trusts in her.”

2. After all her good deeds are listed, it is1173 said, “Her husband praises her.”

It is fitting that other husbands (whose wives are wise and faithful) should deal with their wives after this pattern: so that in the house the wives may have the more honor from children and servants, and outside the house they may give the better proof of their charity.

For when we consider the many excellent promises that are made to works of mercy and charity, and the many terrible threats that are denounced not only against those who practice cruelty, but also against those who show no mercy, and consider also that wives, together with their husbands, are “heirs of the1174 grace of life,” it is very needful, indeed even necessary, that they should show their faith by some work of mercy and charity. Now unless her husband gives her something to bestow on others at her own discretion, no true and thorough proof of her merciful and charitable mind can be made. If she gives from what her husband has kept back for himself, then, as her giving is unlawful, so she may be thought generous not because she is merciful, but because, for all her generosity, she parts with nothing of her own. Indeed, even if she has a general consent to give from the common goods of the family as she sees cause, that is still not so sure and sound a proof of her charity and mercifulness as if she had something of her own, which she might keep or give away as she pleases, and what she does not give away, lay up as her own store, belonging to herself alone. For there is naturally such a self-love in man, and such a desire to keep what is one’s own, that he is very unwilling to part with any of it, unless conscience and grace alter this corruption of nature and so move him readily to lay out something for charitable uses. But otherwise, with what belongs in whole or in part to another (whether that other is a husband, parent, master, friend or anyone else) he is easily moved to be generous and bountiful: a man will gladly cut a wide strap (as we say) out of another man’s leather.

It is known that many children and servants who, when they come to possess their own goods, are very stingy and miserly, have been generous to the poor with their parents’ and masters’ goods. Indeed, partners in a joint stock will be much more eager to give away what they hold in common with another than what belongs to each of them alone. The truest proof of a merciful and charitable heart lies in giving out what is one’s own.

It is therefore fitting, on this very ground, that a husband should, according to his ability, let his wife have some fund and portion of her own, free for her to dispose of as she sees good; letting her know that the chief end for which he provides so plentifully for her is that she may show the fruits of her faith by some works of charity, and urging her to do so. Many religious, wise and kind husbands do this: some give their wives a quarterly allowance in money; others give their wives power to receive a certain portion of rent from certain lands or houses; others settle on their wives full ownership of some heritable property, and allow them to receive its profits and revenues; others give them certain fees from their offices or from their trade; others, who are poor, allow them to work for themselves and dispose of their earnings as they see cause. Some take one way, some another. Every man in his place knows best the means by which to please his wife in this matter; it will be enough for me to have laid down the general rule.

§. 55. Of husbands’ too great tight-fistedness toward their wives.

Contrary to this is the tight-fistedness of those who allow their wives no more than may serve for their own private use. They think it a great matter, and as much as a husband is bound to do, to let her have clothing, food and drink, and such necessities as befit her rank; but anything beyond that they think needless. So their wives are deprived not only of means to gain respect from their children and servants at home, and to reward those who are obedient and ready to serve them, but also of means to perform such works of mercy as opportunity requires and their conscience moves them to do. Indeed, many wives of rich husbands are brought to great shame by it: for being in places where there is just occasion to contribute to some charitable use, and where, because of their rich and costly clothing, they are expected to be generous, they have nothing at all to give. The fault of some husbands in this respect is great in many ways: 1. They bring shame and grief to their wives, whom they ought to regard with all tenderness. 2. They dishonor their own standing: for those who take notice of this tight-fistedness toward their wives will be ready to judge them both covetous and unkind. 3. The leaving undone of the work of mercy that their wives should have done will be laid to their charge. They will hear that dreadful sentence, “Depart, you+ who are cursed, into the eternal fire,” for “I was hungry and you+ gave Me nothing to eat, etc.” And if they answer, “When did we see You hungry, etc.,” it will be replied, “Because you+ did not allow your+ wives to do it, you+ did not do it.”

So much for the extent of a husband’s provident care for the good of his wife. Next we must speak of its continuance.

§. 56. Of a husband’s care to provide for his wife as long as she lives.

The continuance of a husband’s provident care for his wife must last as long as she lives, even if she outlives him. Not that he can actually provide for her when he is dead, but that before his death he may so provide for her that she may have the means to maintain herself, and to live according to the station to which she is advanced by him; at least, that he leave her not only as much as he had with her, but something more also, as a testimony of his love to her and care for her. Husbands have the example of Christ to press this duty on them: for when he went away from his church1175 here on earth, he left his Spirit, who furnished her with gifts as plentifully as if Christ had remained with her, if not more abundantly.

For the better performance of this duty, husbands who die before their wives must observe two things especially, among others.

1. That they declare their mind and1176 will plainly and expressly before they die, so that their wives are not cheated and defrauded of what they intended for them. David did this at the request of Bathsheba: he settled his estate, and had Bathsheba’s son actually crowned before he himself breathed his last. He did this for other weighty reasons, but in particular for his wife’s good, as may be gathered from the reason she put to the king in these1177 words: “Otherwise, when my lord the king rests with his fathers, I will be counted as a criminal.”

2. That he ask some faithful friend to be a helper to her in his place (as Christ commended his mother to his disciple John). This will be needful because of her weakness, by reason of her sex, and her lack of experience in managing affairs, especially those outside the house.

At the time of a man’s departure out of this world from his wife, the truest proof of his love for his wife will be given. For many who keep up a fair show toward their wives while they live with them show at their death that there was no soundness of affection in their heart toward them: it was all a mere show, for some ulterior motives.

§. 57. Of husbands’ neglect of their wives’ future condition.

Contrary to this are various practices of unkind husbands. For1178

1. Some, through lack of foresight, thriftlessness and wastefulness, disable themselves from doing good to their wives after their death; and so they leave their wives nothing, or (what is worse than nothing) in debt, and with many children to provide for. The care husbands ought to have for their wives should make them think beforehand of the time to come, and even for their wives’ sake be somewhat more diligent, thrifty and provident, and cut off many unnecessary expenses; otherwise their sin is doubled: 1. By a needless wasting of their estate. 2. By neglecting their wives.

2. Others, by flattering or forcing means, draw their wives1179 to give up the right they have in money, goods, house or land by jointure, inheritance or any other way, and yet make them no sufficient recompense in another kind; but at their death leave their wives in a far worse condition than they were in before marriage, besides a greater charge than they had before. As this is a great piece of unkindness, so it is also a main point of injustice.

3. Others, grudging against the laws under which they1180 live for providing for a wife by thirds (a third part of the husband’s estate) or otherwise, use every fraudulent means they can to deprive her of what the law would otherwise settle on her. The civil laws of the state where we live ought to be the rule of our civil actions (so far as they are not contrary to God’s word), and we ought, “as a matter of conscience,” to be subject to1181 them. Besides, a husband ought (even if the law did not force him) to leave at least the thirds to his wife, as a testimony of his love to her and care for her. So this also is a double fault: 1. A transgression of the law. 2. A mark of unkindness.

4. Others, having aged and sickly wives, or otherwise1182 thinking that their wives may, or rather hoping that their wives will, die before themselves, put off making their wills on purpose, so that they need not put in their wives’ thirds, but may dispose of them some other way. Besides showing no good affection toward their wives, these husbands provoke God to disappoint them of their hopes; and so he often does. For he takes them away before their wives, and takes them away in such a way, with no time to make their will, that not only do their wives enjoy their thirds (which the husbands so much wanted to avoid), but someone else also (whom of all people they disliked in their lifetime) seizes on the other two parts.

§. 58. Of a husband’s protecting his wife from danger.

Having shown how a husband is to provide what is needful for his wife, it remains to show how he is to protect her from what is harmful.

Because of the protection a husband owes his wife, he is called “the veil of her eyes.”1183 As this phrase implies subjection on the wife’s part, so it also implies protection on the husband’s. To protect someone is, as it were, to cover them, namely, from danger; to be negligent and careless of them is, as it were, to lay them open to danger. The same duty is implied under another similar phrase, of spreading his wing over his wife.1184 The metaphor is taken from birds, which spread their wings over their young to keep them from harm. This phrase and metaphor is also applied to God, to1185 set out his protection.

But most pertinent to this purpose is the title1186 savior, given to a husband in relation to his wife.

For this end the Lord, who made a woman subject to her husband, gave his sex greater strength, courage and boldness than hers, so that he might protect her who is the weaker vessel. In this duty of protection Christ shows himself an excellent pattern and precedent to husbands.

To perform this duty better, a husband must be careful,

1. To guard against, as far as he can, such dangers as his wife is likely to fall into.

2. To recover her from such as she has fallen into.

For this purpose David took his wives into Gath,1187 so that, if they were left in Israel, Saul would not do them any harm; and again, when they were taken by the Amalekites, he recovered1188 them.

A husband’s care in protecting his wife must be shown according to the danger to which wives are subject.

1. If she is in danger of being led astray and enticed, as Eve was,1189 by any evil instruments of the devil, such as Jesuits, priests, friars, or profane, blasphemous, lustful or dissolute persons, his care must be either to keep them away so that they do not come to her, or to put them away from her as soon as he can. He must not allow them to lodge in his house.

2. If by any trick she is drawn from his house, he must1190 seek her and bring her back again, as the Levite did his wife; or have her (if he can) brought home again, as David had Michal brought; especially if they are taken away by force, as Ahinoam and Abigail, David’s wives, were.

3. If she is unjustly slandered, he is to uphold her good name and reputation as much as his own: as Christ counts himself despised when his church is, so must he. He must have this care1191 for his wife’s good name even after her death, as well as while she lives.

4. Whatever other injury is intended or practiced against1192 her, he must be a tower of defense to protect her (as Ahasuerus was to Esther against Haman), and that not only against strangers outside the house, but also against children and servants in the house. Grown children who are proud and stubborn will be ready to rise up against their mother, especially if she is a stepmother, because she is the weaker sex; for the most part, a father’s look keeps them most in awe. Therefore the husband must be a help to his wife and uphold her honor against them, even if they are children of a former wife.

§. 59. Of a husband’s defending his wife against children of a former wife, and servants.

Objection. Stepmothers often prove unkind and unjust, and deal unmercifully with their husbands’ children. Must a husband in such cases support his wife against his children?

Answer. The protection I speak of is for the case where a wife is wronged; then her husband is to do what he can to right her (as we say). But if she is the wrongdoer, he must by no means back her up against his children, and so make their wrong the greater. Yet he ought to respect his wife so far as to labor, by all the fair means he can, to calm her mind and turn her heart toward them. And if he sees that her heart is wholly turned against them, then he is to send them out to be brought up in some other place, and so take away from her the object of her displeasure, so that he and she may live together more quietly. For if a man must “leave his father and mother,” he must also leave his children, and “be joined to his wife.” Peace and unity between man and wife must be kept unbroken above all others. “Though you cast away1193 all, nothing can happen more troublesome to you than not to have a quiet wife at home. You can find no sin more grievous than to have strife with a wife.”

If a wife must be defended against the stubbornness of children, much more against the insolence of servants. For this purpose the example of Abraham is recorded: his servant might have had a privilege above others, because he had taken her to his bed; yet when she grew insolent toward her mistress, he first put her into her mistress’s hand, to do with her as her mistress pleased, and afterward he cast her out of his house.

§. 60. Of neglecting to defend their wives.

Contrary to this is a dissolute carelessness of husbands, who care no more to help and relieve their wives than they would anyone else.

1. Some fear offending their wives more than they care to do1194 them good, and on that account they let any sort of people come to their wives who are welcome to the wives. If magistrates in a commonwealth will answer for allowing deceivers to come into their dominions to lead their people astray, much more will husbands answer for allowing them to come and lead their wives astray.

  1. Because husbands have a greater charge over their wives than magistrates have over their people.
  2. Because wives ought to be dearer to husbands than people to magistrates.
  3. Because husbands can spot such men sooner in their house than magistrates can in the commonwealth.
  4. Because such men can be kept out of a house much more easily than out of a commonwealth or a city.

2. Others do not care where their wives wander; and if their wives1195 do go out of the house, they will never be sought after by their husbands. Though this may be a just punishment on wandering wives, yet it is not just for husbands to deal with them so. If Christ our husband dealt with us so, we would soon be lost: for we often go astray like wandering sheep, but he is that good shepherd who seeks the lost sheep until he1196 finds it.

3. No wonder, then, that many husbands are no more moved1197 by the ill reports and rumors raised against their wives, when they care so little who comes to their wives or where their wives go. Assuredly the discredit of a wife will turn to the man’s dishonor: for as “a wife of noble character is her husband’s crown,”1198 so by the rule of contraries, an infamous wife is a shame to her husband. If therefore not for his wife’s sake, then for his own sake a man ought not to pass over too carelessly the ill reports that are raised against his wife.

4. There are husbands so unkind as to be moved by no ill1199 treatment done to their wives, and they will not hear any complaint the wives make to them. Indeed, if they see their wives mistreated, they will either pretend not to see it, or only smile at it and go their way, and leave their wives to right themselves as well as they can. As it does not become any Christian to allow his neighbor to be wronged (for it is noted as a commendable thing in Moses that1200 when he saw two Hebrews fighting, he took the part of the one who was wronged and reproved the other), so much less does it become a husband, to whose safekeeping his wife is committed. Nature teaches us that the head is as much affected by a wrong done to the body as by one done to itself; so ought a husband to be.1201

5. As the wrong done by those who are in subjection under the wife in the house is greater than that done by strangers, so the husband’s fault in allowing it is the greater; for he has more power over them in his house than over others.1202 What then may we think of those who, either by looking the other way or by taking sides against their wives, allow both children and servants to treat their wives with scorn? Assuredly those husbands will themselves get some taste of its bitter and evil fruit; and that not only through the great discontent their wives must take at it, but also through the contempt that will fall on their own persons, both from their wives (who cannot think them fit heads to govern others) and from their children and servants, who will take occasion from it to grow proud and presumptuous against him. By despising the weaker, men grow little by little to despise the stronger. Men of wisdom and experience know this well; and so in commonwealths and states governed by wise men, the authority of inferior magistrates is upheld and maintained. Superior magistrates will not allow those who are in authority under them to be despised; for it is well known that it serves not only the honor and ease but also the safety of the supreme magistrate to have the power and authority of inferior magistrates respected, and not trampled underfoot. It shows, therefore, a lack both of love and of discretion and understanding in husbands to allow child, servant or anyone else in the house to treat their wives with scorn, who are joint governors with them over the house.

1202. Si illam quae secundum post te locum obtinet contumelia afficis, non parum tui principatus honori derogas. Chrys. loc. cit. [If you treat with insult her who holds the second place after you, you take no little from the honor of your own rule.]

A Husband’s Sincere and Steady Love for His Wife

The Fourth Treatise: Of Husbands · §§. 61–76

§. 61. Of a husband’s first beginning to love his wife.

Now that the general matter, together with the particular kinds, of husbands’ duties has been handled thus far, the manner of performing them must also be set out.

To instruct a husband in the manner of performing his duties to his wife, the apostle lays down two patterns:

  1. Christ, v. 25.
  2. Ourselves, v. 28.

As Christ loves his church, and as we love ourselves, so men must love their wives.

So that we may follow these patterns the better, we must note point by point how Christ loves his church, and how we1203 love ourselves.

The love of Christ for his church is commended to us in six distinct points, which are its order, its truth, its cause, its quality, its quantity, and its continuance.

I. As for the order, Christ began to love his church: he showed his love to her before she loved him. As the air heated by the sun is hot, and a wall that the sunbeams strike gives a reflection of heat back again, so the church, heated as it were and warmed at heart by the sense of Christ’s love, loved him. The apostle expressly notes this (“We love Him1204 because He first loved us”), and the church herself acknowledges it, saying, “Because of the fragrance of your perfume”1205 (by which we are revived and cheered) “the maidens love you.”

There is in us by nature no spark of love at all.1206 If Christ, by loving us first, did not instill love into us, we could no more love him than a living bird could rise out of a cold egg, if it were not kept warm by its mother sitting on it.

So a husband must be the first to begin to love his wife. His place of eminence and authority requires that he should be to his wife a guide, a title expressly given to him by the Holy1207 Spirit, to teach him to go before her, and by his example to instruct her and urge her on to do her duty. What a shame it would be for a man who is “the image and glory of God” and the “head” of his wife, in the same place toward her that Christ is toward his church, to be provoked to love her by his wife’s wifely conduct (she being the weaker vessel, under him, to learn from him)!1208 There are reasons to stir up a wife to endeavor to go before her husband in doing her duty, and if she does, it is the greater glory to her; but this pattern of Christ should stir him much more to strive to go before her.

§. 62. Of husbands repaying unkindness for love.

Contrary to this is the disposition of those who, having loving and dutiful wives, are nevertheless not at all moved to love them in return, but are as unkind and churlish as if they had the most irritable and perverse wives that could be. But what shall we say of those who love their wives the less, indeed hate them, for their eagerness to love and (as a testimony of true love) to perform every good duty? What can we say, but that they are nothing less than devils incarnate? For it is the devil’s way to overcome good with evil. These men make the doctrine of a wife’s subjection seem harsh, and the careful performance of it a heavy burden. They will never share in Christ’s love who in their place show themselves so unlike Christ.

§. 63. Of the truth of husbands’ love.1209

II. The truth of Christ’s love was shown to his church by its fruits: “He gave Himself up for her.” It was therefore not in word only, no, nor only in heart, but in deed also. So his love proved profitable and beneficial to his church, which by it was cleansed and made “a glorious1210 church.” Had he only borne a tender compassion and a pitying affection toward it, or labored only with comforting and sweet words to uphold and help it, it would still have lain polluted with sin, in the power of the devil and under God’s wrath, and so would have received no profit and benefit at all.

So husbands must love their wives in truth and in deed.12111212 Such a love is required of a man toward his brother; much more, therefore, toward his wife, who is not only a sister (as1213 the apostle expressly calls her) but nearer than sister, mother, daughter, friend, or anyone else whatever. This therefore serves to press the practice of all the duties named before that belong to a husband.

§. 64. Of husbands’ pretense.

Contrary to this is the pretense and hypocrisy of those who make a great show of much love, and a pretense of earnest affection, using many outward compliments, but fail when they come to the truest test, the deed. Some, like suitors or wooers, will promise mountains but not perform molehills. Others will hug and kiss their wives much, but trust them with nothing, nor provide them with the things they need. There are some who will weep much when their wives are sick, yet will not pay for medicine and such things for their recovery. Indeed, many will show a fair face toward their wives all their life long, and at their death leave them nothing to live on.

Hence it is that many who are reckoned by others to be very kind husbands are found by their wives to be far otherwise. If husbands’ love is tested by their practice and performance of the duties named before, it will be found that for the most part they come as far short in love as wives do in subjection.

§. 65. Of the freeness of husbands’ love.

III. The cause of Christ’s love was his love, as Moses notes:1214 “The Lord set His love on you+ … because the Lord loved you+.” His love arose only and wholly from himself, and was in every way free. As there was nothing in the church, before Christ loved her, to move him to love her, so there can be nothing that he could hope for afterward but what he himself bestowed. Indeed, he delights in the righteousness with which she is clothed as with a glorious robe, and in the heavenly graces with which she is adorned as with precious jewels. But that righteousness and those graces are his own, and of his free gift: “that He might present her to Himself a glorious church.”1215

In imitation of this, husbands should love their wives, though there were nothing in their wives to move them to do so but only that they are their wives; indeed, though no future benefit could afterward be expected from them. True love has regard to the object that is loved, and the good it may do to it, rather than to the subject that loves, and the good that it may receive. For love “does not seek its own.”1216

Christ’s love in this branch of it should further move husbands to do what lies in their power to make their wives worthy of love. So it will truly be said of them that they “dwell with their wives according to knowledge,”1217 and so their love will appear to be, like Christ’s love, free.

§. 66. Of husbands loving for advantage.

Contrary to this is the love of those who love only for their own satisfaction and advantage. Many can love no further than they have some bait to allure their desires, such as beauty, wealth, honor, or the like ulterior motives; or at least the hope of some inheritance or portion beyond what they have, or of some favor that they expect from their wives’ families. This cannot be a true, sound love: such a man may be thought to love his wife’s beauty, inheritance, and family rather than his wife. This love cannot last.

§. 67. Of the purity of husbands’ love.

IIII. For its quality, Christ’s love is a holy, pure, chaste1218 love. As he himself is, so is his love, as is evident by its effect: for it moved him to “sanctify” and “cleanse” his church, to make it “a glorious church, not having spot.” He therefore in no way polluted or defiled his spouse. And so that his love might the better appear to be a chaste love, set only on one spouse and not on many, he united all his saints together by the1219 bond of his Spirit, and made them all “one body.”

By this husbands must learn to be so disposed toward1220 their wives as is consistent with holiness and chastity. Though much love is required, yet it must not overflow those banks. “Marriage is honorable … and the bed undefiled.” It must therefore be used as an undefiled thing. This indeed belongs to the wife as well as to the husband. But because he is the head and guide of his wife, and ought to be a pattern and example before her, as Christ is before him, it is applied more especially to him. The purity of a husband’s love spoken of here has a double use:

1. It restrains a husband’s love to his own wife. There is a general Christian love, by which every occasion of doing good is taken, with which a husband may and ought to love others; and there is a particular marriage love, by which he is moved to prefer his wife before all, and to have his heart set and fixed on her, so that it is hers and belongs only to her.

2. It orders and moderates his love, so that it does not turn into sinful lust, by which that state (which in itself, by virtue of God’s ordinance, is holy) is polluted.

§. 68. Of husbands’ looseness.

Contrary to this is not only adultery, of which we have spoken1221 before, but also wantonness, looseness, and impurity with his wife. For many intemperate and unchaste husbands, giving the reins to their headstrong lusts, show as much unseemliness and plain filthiness toward their wives in their words, gestures, and actions (to say nothing of their thoughts, which are not seen) as others do toward prostitutes and harlots. This is a most shameless thing, and I am ashamed even to mention it; but because it is mentioned, let such men know that they will be counted among the “sexually immoral1222 and adulterers” whom “God will judge.”

§. 69. Of husbands loving their wives more than themselves.

The quantity of Christ’s love cannot be expressed, for its1223 measure was beyond measure. “He gave Himself up”1224 for his church, and in that respect he calls himself “the good shepherd” who “lays down His life for the sheep.”1225 “Greater love has no one than this.”1226 What will he who gave his life for her not do for his spouse?

This may seem too high a strain and pitch of love for a husband to attain to,1227 a matter in which he must leave his pattern and not follow Christ. But Saint John extends the love of our brethren even this far: “We ought,” he says, “to lay down our lives for our brothers.” Therefore, by just consequence, for our wives. But so that this extent is not stretched too far, and husbands cast into a pit of needless peril, two cautions must be noted:

1. That there must be an absolute necessity to bring us to this1228 extremity of parting with our life: that is, when the good we aim at on behalf of our wives cannot be brought about any other way than by risking our life. There was no other way to redeem the church but by the blood of Christ.

2. That the good we intend for our wives in this case must be of greater value than our temporal life, as the good of her soul is, the saving of it. So the apostle says, “I will most gladly spend and be spent for the sake of your+ souls.”1229 Men must carry this mind much more toward their wives. It was for our salvation that Christ gave himself.

§. 70. Of husbands’ unkindness.

Contrary to this is the unkindness of those who prefer every trifle of their own before the good of their wives: their profit, their pleasure, their promotion draw their hearts and affections wholly away from their wives. If any extraordinary expense must be laid out, or pains taken, for their wives’ good, little love will then appear; by which it is plain that no true and sound love was settled in their hearts toward their wives. As gold and other such metals are tested by the fire, so love is tested by afflictions and crosses.

§. 71. Of combats under pretense of wives’ honor.

Contrary to this, in the other extreme, is the overbold and headstrong pretended manhood of those husbands who, at every jealous suspicion and slight report, are ready to issue challenges to fight, and to enter into single combats and duels, under pretense of defending their wives’ honor. Since this is no justifiable way of righting a wrong, no honor can come to the wife by it, but much dishonor and danger to the husband. If he prevails over his adversary and kills him, he is made guilty of murder by it, and so reproach and shame must come on himself, his wife, and his whole family. If he is overcome and slain, his wife may be thought more guilty than she was before. And it often happens that God in just judgment gives the challenger over into his adversary’s hand, because he has undertaken so crooked a course.

§. 72. Of husbands’1230 constancy in love.

VI.1231 The continuance of Christ’s love was without end: “Having loved His own … He loved them to the very end.”1232 His love was constant (not by fits, now loving, then hating) and everlasting1233 (never repenting of it, never changing or altering his mind). No provocations, no transgressions could ever make him forget to love, and cease to do the good that he intended for his church. Note what he said to her even when she revolted from him: “You have played the harlot with many1234 lovers, yet return to Me”; and again, “My loving devotion will never be removed.”

For his love does not rest on the deserving of his church, but on the unchangeableness of his own will. As this showed Christ’s love to be a true, sound love, so it made it profitable and beneficial to the church, which, despite her many frailties, is glorified by virtue of it.

This last branch must be added to all the former branches1235 of a husband’s love, or else they will all be in vain and to no purpose. This gives the truest test of sound love. Such was the love between David and Jonathan, the soundest love that ever was between one party and another. This brings the greatest glory to the party who loves, and the greatest benefit to the party who is loved. So that a man’s love may remain firm and inviolable in this way:

1. He must be sure to lay a good foundation. He must ground his love on God’s ordinance, and love his wife because of the marriage bond that knits them together, and the close union that arises from it; and so it will last as long as that knot lasts.

2. He must further support and strengthen it with an inviolable resolution to be changed and altered by no provocation, but rather to pass by all infirmities, endeavoring in love to remedy them if he possibly can; if not, to bear with them.

§. 73. Of husbands’ fickleness.

Contrary to this is the fickleness of those whose love is ready to turn like a weathercock with every blast of a contrary wind: now tender-hearted, then hard-hearted again; now smiling, then scowling; now granting this and that favor, then denying everything, even such things as are needful.

Many whose love was as hot as fire while their wives were young, or their wives’ families were living, or while their wives pleased them, prove as cold as ice in their love when those occasions are taken away.

Again, others, after continuing for some time in doing good to their wives, think it a burden, and growing weary, give up their former good course altogether; which plainly shows that they never truly and entirely loved their wives.

By this pattern of Christ set before husbands here, we have on the one side a good direction to teach us how to love our wives, as has been declared in particular; and on the other side, matter for humbling, in that it shows us how far short we come of our bounden duty. Although wives may complain most of their burden, because it is a subjection, to which by nature we are all loath to yield, yet I am sure1236 the heaviest burden is laid on the husband’s shoulders, and it is much easier to perform the part of a good wife than that of a good husband.

§. 74. Of husbands loving their wives as themselves.1237

To the example of Christ the apostle adds the pattern of one’s self, in these words: “So men ought to love their1238 wives as their own bodies.”

Question. Is the former pattern not sufficient? Is this latter one more excellent, or more perfect?

Answer. Christ’s example is a full, complete, perfect, and1239 in every way sufficient pattern, far more excellent than this of a man’s self. This one is not joined to it to add anything to that, or because of this pattern’s own excellence, but only because of our dullness, to make the point somewhat more plain and clear.1240 For this pattern is more easily perceived and better discerned. Everyone knows how he loves his own body, but few or none know how Christ loves his church. Besides,1241 that example of Christ may seem too high and excellent for anyone to attain to, even inimitable. Therefore, to show that he requires no more than a man may perform, if he will set himself with care and conscience to do his duty, he adds the pattern of one’s self: what one does for his body, if he will, he may do for his wife.

No direction can be taken from this latter pattern that1242 might not be referred to the former, as most of the former (though in a far lowlier manner) may be referred to the latter. For the love that a man bears to himself is true and entire, without any pretense. The most dissembling wretch in the world (who in his dealings with other men does nothing uprightly) neither will nor can dissemble with himself. Though other men will never know the depth of his heart, yet “the spirit1243 within him,” even himself, knows it. So this pattern also presses truth and sincerity on husbands in their affection toward their wives. Of all others, they must not dissemble and be double-dealing with their wives, but must let them know the wholeness of their affection toward them, and see that they neither fawn on them nor flatter them. Those who pretend great love to their wives in show only offend against nature itself. As this love of a man for his own self is, for its manner, entire and true, so it is also free, not forced; for its measure, as great as it can possibly be; and for its continuance, constant; and so it is like Christ’s love. But there are two points especially to be considered in the love of one’s self, which above others are most plainly discerned1244 in this pattern: 1. Tenderness. 2. Cheerfulness.

No other man will or can handle a man’s hand, arm, leg, or any other part of his body as tenderly as he himself does: he feels his own pain keenly.

The metaphors that the apostle uses in these words, “nourishes and cherishes it,”1245 vividly set forth this tenderness. For they are taken from fowls and birds, which very carefully and tenderly hover over their young, covering them all over with their wings and feathers, but so bearing up their own bodies that no weight lies on them.

So husbands ought, with all tenderness and mildness,1246 to deal with their wives, as we have noted before in many particulars. Only, I thought it good to set this example of a man’s self before husbands as a vivid pattern, in which they might see an example without exception going before them, and by which they might receive excellent direction for the better performing of the particulars noted before.

Again, no friend, no parent, no other party will or can so1247 willingly and cheerfully do any kindness for someone as a man does for himself. This, among others, is one special point that the law aims at when it commands a man, “Love your1248 neighbor as yourself”: namely, as willingly and readily as he does for himself. Whatever a man does for himself, he does much more cheerfully than for another. No other proof is needed than experience. Let men take notice of their own mind and disposition when they do things for themselves, and this will be as clear as the light when the sun shines out at noonday.

Husbands ought to have such an affection toward their wives:1249 they ought to do anything for their wives more willingly and cheerfully than for parents, children, friends, or anyone else. Though this cheerfulness is an inward disposition of the heart, yet it may be shown by a man’s eagerness and readiness to do his wife good: when his wife no sooner desires a kindness than he is ready to grant it, as Boaz says to Ruth, “I will do for you whatever you request.”1250 Indeed, if by any means he may know that this or that will be needful for her, though she does not desire it, he will yet bring it about for her. This was the mind of the same Boaz toward Ruth, as the history shows in many particulars.

Contrary to this is the disposition of those husbands who do what they do on their wives’ behalf so grudgingly, so complainingly, and so discontentedly that their wives would rather it were not done at all. The manner of doing these things causes more grief to tender-hearted wives than the things themselves can do good.

So much for the manner that husbands ought to observe in performing their duties. The reasons to enforce it remain to be handled.

§. 75. Of Christ’s example, a motive to provoke husbands to love their wives.

The examples named before, of Christ and of ourselves, as1251 they are patterns for our direction, so they are general motives to provoke and stir us up the more to perform all the duties named before in the manner prescribed.

No greater and stronger motive can be offered than the1252 example of Christ. Example in itself has great force to provoke us to do anything, especially if it is the example of some great one, a man of rank and renown.

But who is greater than Christ? What pattern is more worthy? If (as was1253 shown) the example of the church has great force to move wives to be subject to their husbands, the example of Christ must have much greater force to move husbands to love their wives. It is a great honor to be like Christ, and his example is a perfect pattern.

There are two things in Christ’s example that are especially1254 to be noted to move husbands to love their wives:

1. The great inequality that is between him and his spouse.

2. The small benefit that he reaps by loving her.

For the better discerning of that inequality, the greatness of1255 Christ on the one side, and the lowliness of the church on the other, must be duly weighed.

Christ’s greatness is set forth in Scripture by comparing him with created things and with the Creator. Compared with created things, he is far more excellent than the most excellent, as the apostle proves by many arguments in the first chapter of Hebrews; that whole chapter is spent in proof of this point. And in another place it is said that he is set “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in the present age but also in the one to come.”1256

Compared with the Creator, he is in no way inferior to him, but equal:1257 “the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature,”1258 and that Word1259 of whom it is said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. … Through Him all things were made,” etc. So he is the very Creator himself, eternal, infinite, incomprehensible. So Christ’s greatness is beyond expression.

The lowliness of the church on the other side is as deep. She is a created being, fashioned out of the earth, proceeding from the loins of corrupt Adam; not only finite, but in herself vile and base. The prophet Ezekiel1260 sets her forth in her true colors, as she is in herself. Compared to Christ, therefore, she is “nothing, less than nothing.”1261 What equality, what proportion can there then be between Christ and her?

But if man and woman are compared together, we will find a near equality, and that both in the points of their humbling and in those of their exaltation. As to the former, they are both of the same mold, of the same corrupt nature, subject to the same infirmities, and at length brought to the same end. As to the latter, the best and greatest privileges are common to both of them: they are both made after the same image, redeemed by the same price, partakers of the same grace, and heirs together of the same inheritance.

Question. What, then, is the preferment of the male sex? What is the excellence of a husband?

Answer. Only outward and temporary. Outward, in the things of this world only, for “in Christ Jesus” they are both “one.”1262 Temporary, for the time of this life only, for “in the resurrection, people will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.”1263 Then all subjection of wives to husbands ceases.

To conclude this point: since the inequality between Christ and the church, and the equality between man and wife, are as has been declared, and since Christ stoops to love his church, ought not a man to be moved by this to love his wife?

The other point, concerning the small benefit that Christ1264 reaps by his church, will enforce the point yet further. To illustrate it, we will note the great benefit that a man reaps by his wife.

The benefit that Christ reaps from the church is, in one word, nothing. For Christ is in himself all-sufficient: he neither needs anything nor can receive anything. “If you are righteous, what do you give Him, or what does He receive from your hand?”1265 Yet he abundantly bestows all manner of gifts, temporal and spiritual, earthly and heavenly. It was not, therefore, his own good that he had regard to in loving the church, but her good. For he, being God,1266 became man; being Lord of heaven and earth, he took on himself “the form of a servant”;1267 being rich,1268 he became poor; holding “the keys of Death and of Hades,”1269 and being1270 the Lord of life, he “humbled Himself and became obedient to death.”1271 So, to show love to his church, he left much for her sake, but received nothing from her.

But the benefit that a man reaps from a wife is very great. For “it is not good for the man to be alone,”1272 so much so that “he who finds a wife finds a good thing,”1273 and that in all the points of goodness: a profitable thing, a comforting thing, a delightful thing. They do not know the benefit of the married state who1274 prefer single life to it, especially if the married state is ordered by God’s word, and man and wife are careful to perform their own duty to each other.

To apply this point also, and bring it to its conclusion:1275 if Christ, who can receive nothing from the church, nevertheless loves her, ought not men much more to love their wives, since they receive much good from their wives in many ways, and cannot well do without them?

This example of Christ is all the more to be noted because it wholly wipes away all those false colors and vain pretenses that many allege as reasons to show that there is little reason they should love their wives. Some of their pretenses are these:

1. Their wives are of a far lower rank than1276 themselves; should they then perform duty to their inferiors? Those who marry their kitchen maids, or others far beneath their station, commonly allege this pretense.

Answer. I might reply that marriage raises a wife to the rank of her husband, and that it was his own folly to marry one so lowly. But for the purpose and point in hand, let anyone tell me whether the supposed disparity between them and their wives is in any degree comparable to that which is between Christ and the church; yet Christ does not think it too much to do duties of love to his church.

2. There is nothing in their wives worthy to be loved.1277

Answer. This very thing, that such a one is your wife, is matter enough to make her worthy of love. But what was there in the church to make her worthy of Christ’s love? If it is said that she is endowed with many excellent graces, which make her lovely in Christ’s sight, I answer that of herself she has none of those graces. Christ has bestowed them on her, and so made her lovely. And so you ought to endeavor, by using all the good means you can, to make your wife correspond to your love; but in any case, to love her.

3. Their wives give just cause to be hated because of their1278 irritability, stubbornness, insolence, and other such intolerable vices.

Answer. No cause should seem just enough to move a husband to hate his wife, nor any vice seem intolerable to him: with good he ought to overcome evil. If notorious sins seemed intolerable to Christ, or if he thought any cause just enough to provoke hatred, many who are of his church would often draw his hatred on themselves. But Christ hates not one member of his church.

4. There is no hope that I will ever receive any help from my1279 wife, or any benefit from her.

Answer. There is little love in those who can conceive no hope, for love “hopes all things.”1280 Yet this is just the case with Christ. The church is so utterly unable to help or benefit him that he may justly say he cannot hope to receive anything from her. Christ loves the church for her own good, not for his; so ought husbands. Thus, if Christ’s example is well weighed and observed by husbands, it will afford matter enough to remove every doubt or scruple raised to turn their affections away from their wives. Fitly, therefore, has the apostle set it before husbands, both to direct them how to love their wives and also to move them to do so.

§. 76. Of a man’s love for himself, a motive to provoke him to love his wife.

The pattern of a man’s self tends to the same purpose as Christ’s example. Great is the affection that a man bears to himself, to his own flesh, his own body. He never hates, but always loves himself. No sore, no disease, no pain, no stench that the flesh brings on a man can make him hate it; rather, all manner of infirmities make him pity it, tend it, and cherish it all the more. This is a work of nature: the most heathenish and barbarous people that ever were do it. Now since a wife is to a man as his body and his flesh (for “the two will be one flesh”), and since God has commanded men to “love their wives as their own bodies,” these conclusions will necessarily follow from this motive:

1. He who does not love his wife is more led by the instinct of nature than by the express charge of the God of nature. Nature’s instinct moves him to love his body, but God’s express charge does not move him to love his wife.

2. He who does not love his wife is worse than an unbeliever and a barbarian, indeed, worse than a beast. For all these love their own bodies and their own flesh; but a wife (by God’s ordinance) is as a man’s body and his flesh.

3. “He who loves his wife loves himself.” The apostle himself1281 lays down this conclusion in these very words. From this, by the rule of contraries, this will also follow: he who does not love his wife does not love himself.

4. He who does not love his wife cannot help but bring woe and injury on himself. For the damage and injury that falls on a wife through any neglect of duty on her husband’s part falls also on him, just as the injury that falls on the body through any negligence of the head falls also on the head.

If these are not motives enough to provoke a husband to love his wife, I do not know what can be enough.
